surface_text: Transition metal (TM) catalyzed cross-coupling reactions are the utmost versatile and reliable methods for the production of many industrially important fine chemicals. The utilization of transition metals nanocatalysts in organic transformations, specifically the Suzuki, Heck, and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions, have enticed the vigilant eye of researchers and technologists due to; (i) high surface area, (ii) higher number of surface atoms leading to large number of catalytic active centers, and (iii) chemical stability. Moreover, being colloidal, nanomaterials combine the properties of both homogeneous and heterogeneous. i.e., solubility in different solvents and ease in the separation of catalysts. This improves the overall catalytic efficiency and cost. Therefore, these pseudo-homogeneous nanocatalysts are gaining a great deal of attention due to their broad substrate scope and ease of handling. This review article focuses on the recent advances in developing nanostructured catalysts and their utilization for selective carbon–carbon bond-forming reactions, e.g., Suzuki, Heck, and Sonogashira coupling reactions. The main focus is laid on the reactions catalyzed by nanocatalysts derived from transition metals such as Pd, Pt, Cu, Ag, Ni, Fe, Au, and Zn, expounding the conception and rationale based on the reactivity improvement and the recyclability of the nanocatalysts are presented here. The heterogeneous catalysis, essential in daily chemical transformations, is demonstrated, implicating significant functions presented by the nanocatalysts, related pros and cons, recyclability, and efficiency.

Recently, heterogeneous metal catalysis has been gaining much attention due to its superior catalytic activity, broad substrate scope, and ease of handling [13]. The nanocatalysts are easy to recover by filtration or centrifugation, allowing reusability of the catalyst after the completion of the reactions [3,14,15]. A great part of the former heterogenous catalysis community is emerging into the nanoparticle community, as highlighted in the special issue of the prestigious journal ‘‘Chem. Rev.”(nanocatalysts) [16]. Moreover, nanocatalysts-based transformation is considered a nonhazardous and greener approach, which is desirable for sustainability and economic viability [17]. In addition, nanocatalysts that are built up on TM nanoparticles (NPs) such as Au, Cu, Pd, and their alloys can drive a wide range of C C cross-coupling reactions and C-Het (N, S, N) bond formations with enhanced catalytic activity, broad substrate scope, and improved yields [15]. These catalyst systems are generally free from ligands and the requirement of air and moisture-sensitive conditions [15]. Materials in the nanosize regime bear the highest surface area and the highest number of surface atoms that can be further tuned through the synthesis method employed. This leads to higher catalytic efficiency due to; (i) increasing the contact between the substrate and catalytic center, (ii) offering many catalytic active sites per unit volume as compared to bulk heterogeneous counterpart, (iii) higher zeta potential values, and (iv) due to unique surface chemistry associated with the nanomaterials [18,19].

Since these supports and resulting nanocatalysts bear a high surface area, even small amounts of dispersed metal NPs onto support can lead to higher efficiency when compared with their bulk counterpart (larger size particles) [35–37]. Moreover, the dexterity to integrate the precise nano-sized (1 to 100 nm (Fig. 2) [38,39] objects into the nanostructured composite affords unprecedented opportunities to generate multiple catalytic interfaces with the elaborated spatial arrangement on a single platform to exploit their synergistic effects [40].

To conclude, size is one of the key parameters influencing any catalyst’s catalytic performance, especially transition metalsbased nanocatalysts in different chemical reactions [102]. Its influence is complicated in many cases, such as if the rate-determining step is the dissociation of an intra-molecular bond of a reactant molecule, then it is expected that the metal atom has a lower coordination number and exhibits higher catalytic activity [103–109]. Metal atoms with smaller coordination numbers on the surface have stronger adsorption energy, which could reduce the activation barrier to dissociate the reactant molecules and hence accelerate the catalytic process. The size-dependent catalytic activity is favored when the dissociation step acts as the rate-determining step. While in some cases, this trend is opposite to the above statement, in that case, the metal surface atoms have lower coordination numbers, dramatically dissociate a chemical bond, and tightly bind the dissociated species. Still, unfortunately, this tightly binding could poison the surface of the catalyst to slow down the rate of the chemical reaction when coupling with another species during the catalytic reaction cycle [84,103,106,107].

In the case of supported metal catalysis, the support materials have been considered to be inert, and their prime role was to increase the stability of the metal particles by immobilizing and dispersing them to improve the active surface area. Later, the Tauster group introduced the term strong metal-support interaction to elaborate on the unexpected chemisorption properties of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 }$ on noble metal NPs supported by $\mathrm { T i O } _ { 2 }$ [63]. Further, the importance of the support materials has been explored at a fundamental level, commonly utilizing model catalysts. In short, the role of the support materials in catalysis is somewhat more complex and yet to be explored. Support material can play direct or indirect roles during a catalytic transformation. These provide precise defect sites onto which the metal NPs can be immobilized in the case of metastable particles [131]. In addition, the support can enable the electronic interactions between metal NPs and provide functionalities to the nanomaterials, such as acidic sites or basic sites that improve the stability, activity, and selectivity of the catalyst [132,133].

Polanski et al. developed a novel methodology for a coppersupported Pd nanocatalyst by transferring nanoparticles to the target Cu by intermediate carrier SiO [188]. The as-prepared bimetallic Pd/PdO/Cu nanocatalyst was then used for a series of Sonogashira reactions. The Pd/PdO/Cu was a highly efficient and selective catalyst for the reaction between aryl halides and various terminal acetylenes, giving yields from 63 to 100 % of the corresponding products (Scheme 16) [188]. Ultrasonication was employed to prevent the aggregation of NPs and retain the cat alytic activity. Moreover, the recycling of catalysts was facilitated through catalyst separation from the reaction mixture using centrifugation. In addition, a known amount of phosphine ligand was used in each round of the cycle to stabilize and inhibit catalyst deactivation. The performance of the nanocatalysts was proved to be unchanged within the two repeated cycles (100 % conversions). The role of Cu was regarded as two folds; (i) as solid support and (ii) as co-catalyst. The high catalytic activity of the bimetallic nanocatalysts was linked to the coexistence of PdO species, which was developed in the Pd/Cu system as revealed by X-ray photo electron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis [188].

Initially, a silica eggshell was fabricated using a slightly modified sol–gel method. The supported catalyst with narrow pore size distribution and a large surface area showed high catalytic activity towards the Sonogashira reaction of acyl chlorides with terminal alkyne (Scheme 29). The high activity is imputed to the strong synergizing effect between highly dispersed $\mathtt { C u } _ { 2 } 0$ NPs and mesoporous silica [242].

Notably, the precise control over the size and the amount of stabilizer for Au NPs are crucial parameters for enhancing their cat alytic activities. As the size of Au increases from 1.0 nm to 5.0 nm, the catalytic efficiency decreases from 87 % to 10 % [252]. Conversely, controlling the size up to 1.0 nm required an excessive amount of stabilizer, reducing the reaction efficiency and producing less product yield. In conclusion, the smaller size Au NPs leads to excellent catalytic activity, whereas a higher amount of stabilizer inhibits the reaction [255]. Kang et al. reported his important contribution by introducing graphene as an interface layer for plasmonic Au NPs and active catalysts (Pd nanodots) [256]. This visible-light-driven C C coupling reaction achieved high catalytic efficiency with Pd-rGO-AuNPs. The signifying role of the graphene interface layer is shown in (Fig. 11). These results designate the design and engineering of interfaces that are significant to obtaining the highest catalytic activity using nanocatalysts [256].

Song et al. reported water-dispersible Au@Pd core–shell and Au-Pd alloy NPs for the Heck coupling reaction [22]. In a conventional Heck coupling reaction, Pd (0) phosphine complex system has been employed as an effective catalyst in controlling the reactivity and selectivity in the reaction, which enters the catalytic cycle of the C C bond coupling reaction among unsaturated hydrocarbon and aryl halides. In the last step, bases were added to eliminate halides and reduce Pd(II) to Pd(0) [257]. For instance, styrene, methyl acrylate, and n-butyl acrylate were applied as unsaturated hydrocarbon and iodobenzene was utilized as aryl halide (Scheme 30). Au@Pd NPs presented a 99 % yield of the product after many times recycling of catalytic reactions. Cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB) was introduced as an additive to improve the activity of the catalyst. The cationic surfactant enhanced the catalytic activity effect by chelating the Pd NPs, a phosphine-free catalyst. [258] Song and co-workers utilized four different types of Au@Pd core–shell NPs at room temperature, as a result, the emulsion phase surrounded the Au core-NPs. Due to sharp branched arms, Au@Pd core–shell NPs were active in a relatively small amount throughout the whole catalytic reactions [22].

Silver (Ag) nanoparticles catalyzed organic transformations have also attracted the interest of researchers in the past ten years because of the unique catalytic properties of Ag NPs such as efficient reactivity, specific selectivity, prolonged stability, and easy recyclability during catalytic reactions [273,274]. The application of heterogeneous AgNPs in general organic transformation reactions has proven to be an effective strategy in developing crosscoupling reactions in terms of efficiency and selectivity [274]. The hybrid NPs of bimetallic Pd-Ag supported on carbon quantum dots (CQDs) is an emerging nanohybrid efficient catalyst for the Suzuki coupling reaction of aryl halides like bromides and chlorides under ligand-free ambient environments (Scheme 35). [275] The synergistic activity of the nanohybrid catalyst showed enhancement of cross-coupling reaction in a short time (<1 h) with the highest yields (>90 %). The nanohybrid catalyst showed heterogeneous character and enabled easy isolation and recyclability [275].

Zhang’s group has developed a novel method to produce periodic mesoporous silica (PMO) supported Ni(II) organometallic nanocatalyst [311]. The PMO was functionalized with diphenylphosphine ligands and was then utilized as a support to immobilize Ni NPs through coordination interaction. The MPO structure allowed high dispersion of Ni (II) active sites, and the embedded phenyl groups onto the silica walls improved the surface hydrophobicity and promoted the adsorption of reactant molecules onto Ni NPs in an aqueous media. The as-prepared catalyst was employed together with CuI as a co-catalyst in the Sonogashira coupling reaction to produce aryl alkynes in good to excellent yields (Scheme 46). The nanocatalyst exhibited good recyclability, showing no significant activity loss after three repeated cycles.

This article demonstrates that the TM-based NPs catalyzed C C cross-coupling reactions have witnessed phenomenal growth in the past decade (Fig. 1). The C C coupling transformation finds its utility in producing biomaterials, fine chemicals, natural products, and medicine [315]. More specifically, the Suzuki, Heck, and Sonogashira reactions have been widely exploited to generate diverse structural frameworks and chemical entities. Since homogeneous Pd catalysts are far from industrial realism, heterogeneous metal nanocatalysts have emerged as a promising alternative owing to their superior catalytic activity, broad substrate scope, and ease of handling. Moreover, the ease of recovery and reusability makes their use a non-hazardous and greener approach, which is important for sustainability and economic viability. For a higher catalytic activity, stability, and recyclability of the heterogeneous metal nanocatalysts system, careful design of the nanocatalysts size, shape, and morphology is important. Likewise, the architectures of well-defined nanostructured supporting materials have also made meaningful advancements in the field. Moreover, the dexterity to integrate the precise nano-sized (1 to 100 nm objects into the composite nanostructured affords unprecedented opportunities to generate multiple catalytic interfaces in a single nanostructured catalyst to exploit the synergistic effects between these catalytic interfaces. Mechanistic understanding of a chemical process is equally important. The organic transformations usually follow multistep complex reaction pathways, which need to be fully understood to understand the role of nanocatalysts. A pedagogical approach is required to empower the synthetic chemist with the suitable software and computational chemistry tools needed to design their reaction, prediction flowcharts, and probe reaction pathways was envisioned. Computational chemistry tools such as first principle ab initio and density functional theory could be a strong means to predict the mechanism and kinetics of the chemical transformation. Computational modeling of nanocatalysis due to the variety of nano sizes of the NPs becomes quite complex. Therefore, the theoretical modeling would be an excellent addition to optimize the large number of trials required to explore various configurations corresponding to the different sizes of NPs [316]. Acquiring ‘chemical accuracy’ through computational modeling would necessitate considering all aspects of the catalyst environment, such as support, pressure, temperature, solvent, and other surface-bounds species [317]. The atomistic approaches, combined with machine learning tools, can achieve the desired accuracy required to shape optimum nanocatalysts [318].

Similarly, the dynamic model for understanding reaction condi tions in a real reaction environment, such as atomic mobility within each NPs can also be employed. Finally, new numerical tools are in high demand to understand the assembly of NPs into super architectures and their influence on catalytic reactions [319,320]. Artificial intelligence technology could be a viable solution to solve grand challenges in organic transformations which need in-depth chemical intuition. Advanced hardware, enhanced algorithms, and growing storage capacity would allow scrutinizing variables beyond the ability of human beings and detection of hidden patterns in insignificant and core scale datasheets. The future of advancement and approaches will ultimately assist the engineering and design of nanocatalysts for the efficient routes (retrosynthesis and prediction of products) with their improvement (optimization of reaction parameters) to identify new chemical matter.

An organic additive, Diazine Black (DB), was employed as a leveler for microvia filling using copper electroplating. DB is a derivative of Janus Green B (JGB), which is a common leveler used for copper fill of submicron or micron circuit metallization in electronic products. This study determined the optimal DB concentration for achieving the best filling performance. The electrochemical behavior of DB and its interaction with other additives, such as a suppressor and an accelerator were characterized using galvanostatic measurements. These electrochemical analyses helped explaining the filling mechanism of the plating formula containing the DB. Various surface morphologies and the crystalline orientation of the plated copper films caused by different DB concentrations were characterized by a scanning electron microscope (SEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD), respectively. The corresponding chemical activity of the surface atoms of the plated copper films caused by different DB concentrations was characterized using a test of etching rate.

Because the diameter of the microvia has shrunk to less than 65 -m, and even as low as 50 -m, several metallization technologies such as filling with resin and conductive paste have not met the demands of process integration [1,2]. Instead, researchers believe that a more promising technology is to fill microvia using copper electroplating because this filling technique has been employed successfully to fabricate the interconnections of IC chips, such as via and trench metallization [3–13]. The microvia filling technology using copper electroplating is implemented using a specific plating formula that contains a suppressor, an accelerator, and a leveler [14–17]. The suppressor and the accelerator are basic additives for the microvia filling; the addition of a leveler can significantly improve the filling yield and extend the operative range of the accelerator concentration [16,17].

Janus Green B (JGB) is a familiar leveler that bears one quaternary ammonium cation and one chloride ion. It preferentially adsorbs at the protrusion to inhibit the copper deposition rate because of the selective adsorption of the quaternary ammonium cation [18]. Therefore, a proper addition of JGB results in a copper deposit with a mirror-like surface. It is an effective reagent for carrying out a void-free filling in dual damascene metallization [4,5,7,8,10]. With regard to the electrochemical and adsorptive behaviors of JGB on the copper electrodeposition, Li et al. [18] and Bozzini et al. [19] presented detailed results using various instruments to identify the molecular structures of adsorbed JGB and the byproduct thereof. In addition, JGB can interact with polyethylene glycol (PEG) to form a composite suppressor whose adsorptive behavior is strongly convection dependent [16,17]. Hence, the addition of JGB can significantly enhance the filling performance of a plating formula because the forced convection acting on the board surface is always stronger than that at the bottom of the microvia during electroplating [20,21]. The behavior of the convection-dependent adsorption (CDA) of a plating formula has been demonstrated to be an indicator that can determine whether the plating formula is a good candidate or not for the microvia filling [17,22,23].

Fig. 1 shows the molecular structures of DB and JGB. They are very similar, except for that DB has a functional alcohol group. Alcohol may be oxidized by $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 }$ or by anodic current to be a carboxyl group, which forms a chelating complex with metallic ions and has the ability to form hydrogen bonds with each other or with $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } .$ Hence, small amounts of precipitate always appear in the plating solution after electroplating. Table 1 lists the plating results obtained from various plating formulas, showing that only two formulas resulted in BUF of microvia. One formula had 0.3 ppm SPS and no DB, and the other formula had 1 ppm SPS and 1 ppm DB. The rest of these formulas did not led to BUF but to conformal deposition. PEG–Cl is a well-known suppressor, and SPS–Cl has been confirmed to be an accelerator for copper electrodeposition [5,7,8,10,26–52]. Hence, the results listed in Table 1 indicate that the BUF behavior is caused by a synergistic interaction between the suppressor and the accelerator and that when the accelerator concentration is high, a leveler is an indispensable additive for achieving BUF.

The SPS concentration must be low for the BUF of microvia when DB is absent in the plating solution. Considering the function of SPS–Cl, the failure in the microvia filling caused by the high SPS concentration is attributable to the loss of synergy between suppression and acceleration; that is, the ratio of acceleration to inhibition is too high to effectively inhibit copper deposition on the board surface. This is also the reason why the surface appearance of the copper deposit is not bright and smooth but matte and rough.

However, the conformal deposition caused by the high SPS concentration, as in case 7 listed in Table 1, can be turned into BUF, that is, case 8 listed in Table 1, due to the presence of 1 ppm DB. This result implies that the addition of 1 ppm DB enhances the inhibiting effect of PEG–Cl and in turn relieves the accelerating effect of SPS–Cl. The electrochemical role of DB is characterized in Section 3.2.

SPS concentration was increased from 0.3 to 1.0 ppm, the filling performance correspondingly decreased, especially in the case of a big microvia, as shown in Fig. 2c and d. The surface ofthe copper deposit also became more uneven than that ofcase 3. Many hill-like copper deposits were formed on the surface and a doughnut-like copper deposit was formed around the opening of the filled microvia. This result implies that the accelerator dominates copper deposition under this condition. Therefore, copper was preferentially deposited around the opening of the microvia due to a protrusive structure and the locally high current density. These negative results can be overcome by adding 1 ppm DB into the plating solution. A mirror-like copper surface as well as an excellent filling performance was obtained in case 8, as shown in Fig. 2e and f. The addition of 1 ppm DB could not only enhance the filling performance of the plating formula with 1 ppm SPS, but it could also flatten the plated Cu surface thoroughly. In addition, adding DB reduced the extent of overplating on the filled microvia. In particular, the doughnut-like copper deposit completely disappeared due to the addition of DB. This result strongly suggests that the good performance stems from the interaction among PEG, SPS, DB, and chloride ions.

However, when SPS was absent and DB was present in the plating solution, a conformal deposition occurred, as shown in Fig. 2g and h. An extremely rough copper surface is seen in Fig. 2g and h, although the doughnut-like copper deposit around the opening of the microvia does not appear. This result implies that the interaction between the inhibitor and the accelerator must exist such that equal deposition rates in a locally vertical and lateral direction can function well. This outcome also suggests that the leveling effect does not result from the leveler itselfbut from the interaction among the suppressor, leveler, and accelerator.

Fig. 3 shows potential variations in galvanostatic measurements on a Cu-RDE at two rotating speeds. The individual additive was injected into the base electrolyte in sequence. Fig. 3A shows that DB interacts with chloride ions to be a depolarizer for copper deposition. This electrochemical behavior is different from that of JGB, which exhibits a slight inhibition of copper deposition in the presence of chloride ions [16,18]. The deposition rate was Cu(II) diffusion-controlled before PEG was added in the plating solution because the cathodic potential decreased as the rotating speed increased $( \mathrm { i } . \mathbf { e } . , \Delta \eta < 0 )$ . After PEG was injected into the plating solution, the cathodic potential suddenly dropped by a wide margin, and the value of- equaled zero. These results mean that the main contribution for inhibiting copper deposition comes from PEG–Cl, and the deposition rate of copper is not Cu(II) diffusion-controlled but charge-transfer-controlled owing to the existence of PEG–Cl. Interestingly, after SPS was subsequently injected in the plating solution, the value of $\Delta \eta$ thereupon became positive, suggesting that forced convection is unfavorable to the copper deposition. This phenomenon stems from a convection-dependent competitive adsorption ofadditives, whose original occasion is attributed to the potential-dependent adsorption of chloride ions [16,17,23,26].

Fig. 3B shows that the cathodic potential was not significantly changed after SPS injection, implying that there was no significant interaction among DB, chloride ion, and SPS at the low potential. The CDA behavior (i.e., - > 0) only occurred after PEG was also present in the plating solution. To further clarify the interaction of these additives, the injective sequence was changed again, as shown in Fig. 4. There was no potential difference (i.e., $\Delta \eta = 0 )$ until SPS was injected into the plating solution, showing that copper deposition is not diffusion-controlled in the presence of PEG–Cl–DB. This result, combining with that of Fig. 3, also strongly suggests that the CDA behavior, which leads to BUF, is caused by the interaction of these four additives. This synergy ofadditives results in a slow copper deposition on the board surface and a relatively rapid copper deposition at the bottom of the microvia, which is characterized by the positive $\Delta \eta$ shown in Figs. 3 and 4. Fig. 4 also shows that DB does not enhance the inhibiting effect of PEG–Cl on copper deposition, which is different from that ofJGB [16]. The synergy of these additives stems from the adsorptive and transport characteristics of chloride ions and from the competitive interaction between the suppressor, accelerator, and leveler [5,7,8,10,26–52]. All the organic additives need to interact with chloride ion to exert individual function on copper deposition [5,7,8,10,26–52]. The establishment ofthe synergistic interaction between these additives reflects the positive $\Delta \eta .$

Fig. 5 shows the influence of DB concentration on filling performance. The filling performance of a plating solution is defined by a ratio percentage of two heights, $\mathrm { i . e . , } \left( h _ { 2 } / h _ { 1 } \right) \times 1 0 0 \% ,$ , where h is the copper thickness plated inside the microvia and $h _ { 1 }$ is the thickness ofdielectric layer plus the thickness ofcopper plated on the top surface of PCB [37]. A small amount of DB could markedly improve the filling performance of the plating formula composed of 200 ppm PEG, 60 ppm Cl−, and 1 ppm SPS. The optimal DB concentration causing the best filling performance ranged from 0.5 to 1 ppm, depending on the diameter of the microvias. Similar results were also obtained from the system usingJGB as a leveler [17]. When the DB concentration was higher than 1 ppm, the filling performance declined with the DB concentration, particularly in the big microvia. This result is attributed to the CDA behavior [16,17,23,26] caused by the synergy of these additives, which is characterized by the $\Delta \eta$ values recorded by curve (c) shown in Fig. 5. Three representative - values were evaluated from Fig. 6.

The trend of the $\Delta \eta$ value with the increased DB concentration varies with the variation in filling performance. The positive value of $\Delta \eta$ implies that that the rate ofthe copper deposition is inversely proportional to the strength of forced convection [16,17,23,26], which leads to a slow copper deposition on the board surface and a relatively rapid copper deposition at the bottom of the microvia. Hence, the larger the $\Delta \eta$ value, the better will be the filling performance. These results also reveal that $\Delta \eta$ defined in this study is a useful indicator to evaluate the filling performance ofa plating solution employed for microvia filling. However, this evaluation tool is conditional, that is, a leveler must be present in the plating solution [26]. If there is no leveler in the plating solution, a poor filling performance may be obtained, even though a positive $\Delta \eta$ value is correspondingly obtained, as confirmed in Fig. 2c and d. It is notable that the positive $\Delta \eta$ value was obtained at lower cathodic potential because of the leveler-free plating solution, as recorded by curves (a) and (b) shown in Fig. 6. A significant continuous depolarization was observed in the case ofthe leveler-free solution. In other words, this plating solution was accelerator dominated. Hence, copper was preferentially deposited on the board surface, such that a conformal deposition occurred, as shown in Fig. 2d.

The depolarization behavior proceeding with the plating time was immediately suppressed by adding DB, as recorded by curves (c)–(f) of Fig. 6, indicating that the steady-state cathodic potentials were immediately shifted from the range of approximately 0.55 to 0.56 V to the range of approximately 0.6 to about 0.64 V. In addition, an  wave that represents a transient surface composition change, which varies from an accelerator-dominated composition to a leveler-dominated one, appears in Fig. 6. The transient time depends on the DB concentration and the strength of convection. A higher DB concentration or a stronger forced convection leads to a shorter transient time. Moffat et al. [53] proposed a model to explain the competitive adsorption between an accelerator and a leveler and simulated similar transient curves during plating.

The surface flatness of the copper deposit caused by the participation of DB in the plating formula with multiple components did not vary with the increase in the DB concentration until the DB concentration was higher than 15 ppm. These results were demonstrated by the SEM images, as shown in Fig. 8. As can be seen from Fig. 8, as the DB concentration increased, the surface flatness of the copper deposit was maintained until the DB concentration increased to 16 ppm. The plating formula that contained a DB concentration higher than 10 ppm would forfeit the synergistic effect on forming a mirror-like surface, implying that a high concentration of DB dominated the surface composition on the plated copper, resulting in an SEM image similar to that shown in Fig. 7a.

A leveler, namely DB, employed for microvia filling was tested in this study. An excellent filling performance is obtained from a copper plating formula composed of 200 ppm PEG, 60 ppm Cl−, 1 ppm SPS, and 1 ppm DB. This plating formula not only results in BUF of microvias but also leads to a mirror-like copper surface. According to electrochemical analyses, the root cause for achieving BUF in the plating solution was attributed to the CDA behavior ofthis formula.

Although DB is a derivative of JGB, their electrochemical behaviors are somewhat different. DB cannot enhance the suppression of PEG–Cl on copper deposition, whereas JGB can do that. Nevertheless, DB can effectively suppress the acceleration of SPS–Cl on copper deposition in the presence of PEG. The preferential orientation of the plated copper films is changed from [1 1 1] to [2 2 0] because of the addition of DB, which causes a decrease in the etching rate of the plated copper film and results in fine grains and mirror-like copper surfaces.

Leveler is one of the most important additives for super-conformal copper electroplating, which has been widely applied in the fabrication of nanoscale (or microscale) interconnect features in integrated circuits (ICs) and printed circuit boards (PCBs). Because the structure-property relationship of the leveler is not clear, the development of novel leveler with high microvia filling performance is very time-consuming and challenging. In this study, a series of triphenylmethane-based (TPM-based) molecules with different nitrogen-containing groups have been designed, synthesized, and investigated as novel levelers for superconformal copper electroplating. Their structure-property relationships are investigated by electrochemical analyses, contact angle measurements, and microvia filling electroplating experiments. It is found that the steric hindrance and the type of the nitrogen-containing groups (tertiary amine or quaternary ammonium with counter anions) in a leveler not only affect its adsorption ratio and strength on the copper interface, but also affect its adsorption preference on different copper crystalline plane. In combination with Cl−, polyethylene glycol (PEG, suppressor), and bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS, accelerator), all TPM-based levelers show excellent microvia filling performances in copper electroplating and their effective concentrations are related to their antagonistic ability against the accelerator SPS.

According to the additives’ different electrochemical effects in the electroplating, the additives were categorized as accelerators, suppressors, and levelers, respectively. Bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) [3,4] and its reduced monomer sodium 3-mercapto-1-propanesulfonate (MPS) [5,6] are most widely used accelerators. In electroplating, the accelerators can reduce the cathodic polarization and facilitate the copper reduction [7,8]. The suppressors are usually polyether compounds, such as polyethylene glycol (PEG) [9,10], polypropylene glycol (PPG) [11,12], or their copolymers [13,14]. In contrast to the accelerators, the suppressors synergistically work with chloride ions to increase the cathodic polarization and thus suppress the copper reduction. Leveler is another important additive used in the electrolyte to fulfill the super-conformal electroplating, which usually are nitrogencontaining molecules and positively charged in the acid electroplating solution. As reported, the levelers can adsorb at the highdensity charge region of the cathode to inhibit the copper deposition and level the copper surface [15]. In addition, the use of a leveler in the microvia filling electroplating solution can greatly expand the application concentration range of accelerators [16].

Currently, most of the reported levelers are nitrogen-containing dyes, such as the Janus Green B (JGB) [17], Alcian Blue (ABPV) [18,19], and Diazine Black (DB)[16] etc., or non-dye heterocyclic aromatic molecules, such as 2-amino-4-methylbenzothiazole (AMBT)[20] and 2-mercaptopyridine (2-MP)[21,22] etc. Because the structure-property relationship of the leveler is not clear yet, the development of novel leveler with high microvia filling performance is very time-consuming and challenging. More and more research groups began to purposefully design and synthesize various nitrogen-containing levelers to study their structureproperty relationship [23–27]. In our previous study, we reported a triphenylmethane-based leveler TPM-1, in which three pyrrolidine rings (nitrogen-containing functional groups) were linked by a triphenylmethane (TPM) backbone [28]. It was found that the small molecule with three saturated tertiary amines already be able to show strong inhibition effect and promising microvia filling performance in the copper electroplating experiments.

The electrochemical properties of TPM-based levelers were investigated with GMs and CVS methods. Fig. 2 shows the GMs with different injection orders of Cl−, PEG, SPS and TPM-based levelers. As shown in Fig. 2a, with the addition of 40 ppm $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } } ,$ 200 ppm PEG, and 2 ppm SPS in sequence, the cathode potential went through three changes: rising, sharply decreasing, and slowly rising again. The results are consistent with the literature reports [5,7]: Cl− itself is a depolarizer; however, the Cl− and PEG will synergistically form a barrier layer on the cathode and significantly suppress the copper reduction; SPS is a depolarizer in the presence of Cl−, which can gradually replace the suppressor layer on the cathode leading to a slowly potential increase.

Following the addition of SPS, 1.484 μmol/L TPM-based levelers were injected into the electroplating solution. The cathode potential drops from 0.559 to 0.673 and 0.712 V for TPM-1 and TPM-2, respectively, which imply that at the same concentration, the inhibition effect of the quaternary ammonium TPM-2 was much stronger than the tertiary amine TPM-1. Comparing the molecular structures of TPM-1 and TPM-2, two differences were found: the quaternary ammonium structure and the I− ion. It has been reported that counter anion in a leveler influence its electrochemical behavior and I− can inhibite the $\mathsf { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ reduction [29– 33]. To distinguish the stronger inhibition ability of TPM-2 was induced by the ammonium structure or I−, we designed and synthesized a new molecule TPM-5, which have the same cationic structure as TPM-2 but with Cl− instead of I− as the counter ion. When TPM-5 was injected in the copper electroplating solution, the potential drops from 0.559 to 0.654 V (fast adsorption) and then slowly moves back to 0.547 V(gradually deactivated by the SPS through the ion pairing interactions)[34–36]. The result indicates that though with the same cationic skeleton, TPM-5 has a much weaker inhibition effect against SPS than TPM-2. As shown in Fig. 2a, the steady potential after addition of TPM-5 is close to the initial value before the leveler injection, which means the adsorption of TPM-5 on the copper surface is weak and the adsorbed leveler was replaced by SPS gradually in the electroplating process. From the GMs of TPM-2 and TPM-5, it can be concluded that the extraordinarily strong inhibition effect of TPM-2 should be related to the anion I− instead of causing by the quaternized pyrrolidine group. In addition, from Fig. 2a, we can see that the inhibition effect of TPM-5 is also weaker than TPM-1. Therefore, by comparing the molecular structures and inhibition abilities of TPM-1, TPM-2 and TPM-5, it was found that the methylated quaternary ammonium structure actually weakens the leveler’s inhibition effect instead of strengthening it, and the exist of I− is the cause of dramatical improvement of the molecule’s inhibition ability.

To further verify the strong inhibition effect of TPM-2 and TPM-4 was caused by the I− alone or the synergistic effect of I− and the TPM-based counterpart, equivalent amount of I− as in TPM-2 and TPM-4 was injected into the electroplating solution. As shown in Fig. 2a, the addition of I− alone in the presence of Cl−, PEG, and SPS leads a further polarization from 0.559 to 0.662 V, which means I− has a certain kind of antagonistic against SPS, however, the inhibiton ability is much weaker than that of TPM-2 and TPM-4 as shown in the GMs. The results clearly indicate that the strong inhibition effect of TPM-2 and TPM-4 was caused by the synergistic effect of I− and its counterpart rather than I− itself alone. To further confirm whether the synergistic effect is related the quaternary ammoiunm structure, TPM-1 I− and TPM-3 I− with a molar ratio of 1:3 have aslo been injected together into the electroplating solution, respectively. As shown in Fig. 2a, with iodide ions in the electrolyte, the potentials of TPM-1 and TPM-3 also dramatically decreased to 0.710 V and 0.713 V, respectively. The polarization of TPM-1 I− and TPM-3 I− behaved very similarly as TPM-2 and TPM-4. Since TPM-1 and TPM-3 have no quaternary ammonium structure, the strong inhibition effect of TPM-2 and TPM-4 should be caused by the synergistic effect of I− and the whole structure of the TPM-based counterpart, rather than specifically interacted with the quaternary ammonium structures.

As shown in Fig. 2b, following the addition of Cl−, the subsequent injection of TPM-based levelers leaded to potential decreases of approximately 93 mV (for TPM-1), 75 mV (for TPM-2, TPM-4, TPM-1 I−, and TPM-3 I−), 100 mV (for TPM-3), 88 mV (for TPM-5), and 49 mV (for I−), respectively. Then 200 ppm PEG was added into the electroplating solution. For all TPM-based levelers, the potentials sharply decreased to approximately 0.702 V, which were much lower than the potentials obtained by PEG and Cl− in the absence of TPM-based levelers (approximately 0.667 V, as shown in Fig. 2a). The results imply that the TPM-based levelers synergistically interact with halides and PEG to form stronger barrier layers than those formed by PEG and Cl−. While for the I−,the potential gradually moved back to 0.678 V after the sharp decrease, which is higher than that induced by TPM-based leveler. Finally, SPS was added into the electrolyte and it was found that with TPM-1, TPM-3, TPM-5, and I− presented in the electroplating solution, the cathodic potentials increased by 37 mV, 108 mV, 143 mV, and 39 mV, respectively. While for the electroplating solution contain TPM-2, TPM-4, TPM-1 I−, and TPM-3 I−, instead of increase, the cathodic potential even slightly decreased. These results indicated that with the participate of I−, the TPM-based levelers could synergistically interact with PEG and Cl− forming much stronger barrier layers than those formed by TPM-based levelers without I−. SPS can hardly replace the complex inhibitors composed of PEG, Cl−, and TPM-2 (or TPM-4, TPM-1 I−, TPM-3 I−), which further demonstrated that the combination of iodide ion and TPM-based levelers rather than any of them alone strongly improve the leveler’s inhibition effect and quenched the activity of SPS on the cathodic surface. To make the interactions more comprehensible, a schematic diagram was provided in Fig. 3.

To charactrized the effect of the leveler concentrations on its electrochemical properties, cyclic voltammetry measurements with various concentrations of TPM-based levelers (or I−) in an electroplating solution containing 2 ppm SPS, 40 ppm Cl− and 200 ppm PEG have been carried out. As shown in Fig. 4, the increase of the TPM-based levelers (or I−) concentration all leads to a further polarization. For TPM-1, the addition of 0.05 ppm leveler not only decreases the absolute current density, but also changes the relative current density values in the forward (negative-going) and backward (positive-going) sweep. As reported, the current densities in the return sweep larger than the forward values indicate a positive feedback for the copper electroplating [38,39]. In addition, when the concentration of TPM-1 reaches as high as 8 ppm, an evident negative differential resistance (NDR) phenomenon was observed, which has been widely used to explain the mechanism of extremely bottom-up filling of Cu or other metals with one suppressor as the additive in electroplating [38,40–42]. Similarly, NDR has also been observed with other TPM-based levelers at relatively high concentrations (above 2 ppm for TPM-2 and TPM-4; above 8 for TPM-3; above 20 ppm for TPM-5). Though ternary additives (leveler, suppressor, and accelerator) were used in this research instead of one additive system reported in literature, extremely bottom-up microvia filling effect has also been otained with high concentrations of TPM-2 or TPM-4 (as shown in Figs. 7–2f, 7–2g, 7–4f, and 7–4g), which imply a gradual breakdown of the suppression starting from the microvia bottom. NDR is observed for all high concentration TPM-based levelers, however, only TPM-2 and TPM-4 result in the extremely bottom-up filling. One possible explanation is that due to the strong inhibition strength caused by the synergistic effect of I− and the TPM-based counterpart, the suppression layer formed by high concentration of TPM-2 (or TPM-4) plays a predominant effect on the cathod surface and overshadowed the effect of SPS (as shown in Fig. 3e and f). While for other TPM-based levelers (or I−), the antagonistic effect of SPS and the inhibitors contributes together to achieve the super-conformal electroplaitng, as described by the curvature enhanced adsorbate coverage (CEAC) [36] or convection-dependent adsorption (CDA) [43] mechanisms.

In this study, a series of novel triphenylmethane-based molecules (TPM-2 to TPM-5) with varied nitrogen-containing functional groups were synthesized and investigated as levelers for copper super-conformal electroplating. The structure-property relationships of the TPM-based levelers have been studied in detail with electrochemical analyses, surface activity measurements, and microvia filling electroplating experiments. It was found that all TPM-based levelers show inhibition effect in the copper electroplating and their antagonistic ability against SPS followed in the order of TPM-2 TPM-4 TPM-1 TPM-3 TPM-5. The inhibition ability of the TPM-based levelers positively correlated to their adsorption ratio on the copper interface. Electrochemical measurements demonstrate that the strongest inhibition effect of TPM-2 and TPM-4 was caused by the synergist interaction of the TPMbased structures and the counter ion I−; the replacement of a fivemembered pyrrolidine ring (TPM-1) by a six-membered piperidine ring (TPM-2) leads to a decrease of the leveler’s inhibition ability; the quaternization of a tertiary amine (TPM-1) with Cl− $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ as the counter ion leads a much weaker antagonistic effect against SPS (TPM-5). Based on the results, it can be concluded that the minor adjustment of the nitrogen-containing group’s structures in a leveler has a significant impact on its electrochemical properties and microvia filling performance. The steric hindrance and the type (tertiary amine or quaternary ammonium with counter anions) of the nitrogen-containing groups need to be comprehensively considered when one designs new levelers for the super-conformal copper electroplating.

This work investigated the influence of Sodium 3- (benzothiazole-2 -ylthio)- 1- propanesulfonate (ZPS) as a single additive on performance of copper foil. Electrochemical analysis indicates that ZPS is of accelerating effect during electroplating. Chronoamperometry and ex situ SEM confirm that Copper growth obeys 3D diffusioncontrolled instantaneous nucleation and growth process, with ZPS significantly increasing the density of active sites. A comprehensive theoretical framework combining density functional theory calculations, molecula dynamics simulations, and in situ infrared spectroscopy elucidates an adsorption-capturing acceleration mechanism: ZPS can adsorb on copper surface and “catch” free Cu<sup>2+</sup> to the active sites to accelerate the electrochemical reduction process coupled with adsorbed Cl<sup>−</sup> . Furthermore, a Turing oscillation growth model, supported by finite element simulations and AFM analysis, is proposed to describe the morphological evolution, wherein ZPS preferentially accumulates at valley regions, improving surface flatness through cyclic peak-valley transfer, though with inherently limited ultimate smoothing. Structurally, XRD shows ZPS promotes Cu (220) orientation, while HRTEM confirms the presence of twin boundaries, and lattice fringe measurements reveal a transition from (111)-dominated to (220)-dominated regions upon ZPS addition. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) further indicates grain refinement (mean size from 3.29 μm to 2.60 μm) and increased twin-boundary density, which contribute to strengthening via Hall-Petch and dislocation-blocking effects. In terms of performance, ZPS improves surface morphology and reduces roughness. Mechanical properties are optimized at 30 mg/L ZPS, with tensile strength reaching 331 MPa and elongation 3.78 %. Finite-element simulation of high frequency signal transmission demonstrates that the lowered roughness effectively mitigates the skin effect, reducing signal loss. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive mechanistic understanding of ZPS and dem onstrates its potential as a single additive for producing high-performance electrolytic copper foils.

Additives usually consist of organic molecules, which plays roles mainly on the interface between substrate and electrolyte. Thus, it is significantly important to apply specific additives to modulate the nucleation and growth process of copper foil and control the surface morphology to improve the performance of copper foil. As for proposed additives, Zhang et al. [10] studied the influence of DPS and hydrolysis animal protein on surface morphology and mechanical property, while Xiao et al. [11] applied SPS, SH110, gelatin to change surface roughness and tensile strength of copper foil. Alexandrov [12] et al. studied the effect of two composite additives (gelatin-polyacrylamide and thiourea-polyacrylamide) on surface roughness, tensile strength of copper foil. Sun [13] et al. applied three composite additives (SPS, HEC, collagen) to fabricate copper foil with low roughness. Despite the development of diverse additives (surfactants, polymers, dyes, proteins, etc.), poor mechanistic insight has rendered additive design largely empirical, necessitating exhaustive experimental screening with little predictive guidance.

As investigation method progresses, theoretical calculation [14], spectrum technology [15], microscopic technology [16] are widely used to gain deeper understanding of additives during copper electrodeposition, providing guidance for researchers. An et al. [17,18] coupled in situ Raman spectra and infrared spectra, DFT (density functional theory) calculation to study triphenylmethane-based levelers during copper electroplating and proposed difunctional mechanism of coordination and adsorption, providing insights into future leveler molecular design. Wheeler et al. [19] used ab initio MD simulation method and found that the adsorption strength order is $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } > N a ^ { + } > M P S > H _ { 2 } O . }$ . The addition of Cl⁻ results in the decline of copper substrate work function, indicating that electrons can transfer more readily from the metal to surface-active species. Meanwhile, sulfide bond of MPS adsorbs onto the copper substrate, whereas the sulfonate group tends to attract ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ and reduce $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ with Cl<sup>−</sup> adsorption layer. Broekmann [20] investigated the accelerating mechanism of SPS by STM and found that SPS adsorbs on copper sub strate by disulfide. Laterally, SPS will break into two MPS molecules, among which one side (sulfide bond) adsorbs on copper substrate and the other side (sulfonate group) catches $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ , consistent with Ref [19]. The desorbed MPS will be oxidized to SPS or PDS. Overall, emerging advanced research technology provide support for the underlying mechanism of electroplating additives.

In this work, a novel accelerating additive, namely, accelerator (benzothiazole-2 -ylthio)- 1- propanesulfonate (ZPS) is introduced to prepare copper foil. Electrochemical analysis method, including cyclic voltammetry, electrochemical impedance spectra, was used to study the effect of ZPS in cathode surface. Chronoamperometry and ex situ SEM was used to investigate the nucleation and growth process. DFT calcu lation, molecular dynamics (MD) simulation and in situ infrared spectroscopy is used to study the accelerating mechanism on the cathode surface. Besides, growth model of copper foil under the influence of ZPS was established based on finite element (FE) simulation. The phase structure and surface morphology under the influence of ZPS is also investigated, while tensile strength and elongation of copper foil is evaluated. Based on FE simulation, the skin effect is studied for copper foil with different surface roughness.

After the introduction of ZPS, the onset potential shifted positively. When ZPS concentration was 40 mg/L, the onset potential was increased to about −0.425 V, indicating that ZPS is of depolarization effect during copper electrodeposition. However, it should be noted that the increasing trend is slowing down with ZPS concentration. Density functional theory (DFT) calculation, molecular dynamics simulation (MD) and in situ infrared spectroscopy were applied to study the interface behavior of ZPS and adsorption-capturing accelerating mechanism was proposed.

Based on above analysis, adsorption-capturing accelerating mechanism was proposed. During electroplating, ZPS adsorbs well on copper substrate by multiple sites (heterotoms S and $- S O _ { 3 } ^ { - } )$ , different from typical accelerator SPS, which breaks into two MPS molecules on copper surface and adsorbs by sulfide bond [16,20]. Therewith, $- S O _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ captures $\mathrm { { C u } ^ { 2 + } }$ moving to the cathode surface, after which $\mathrm { { C u } ^ { 2 + } }$ obtains electrons and is rapidly reduced through “bridging effect” of adsorbed Cl<sup>−</sup> on copper surface, verified by electrochemical tests, similar to the accelerating effect of SPS. Besides, px and py orbits of Cl<sup>−</sup> have large overlap with dyz and dxz orbits of $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ , while pz orbits interact with dz2 orbits of $\mathrm { { C u } ^ { 2 + } }$ . The d p hybridization between $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ and ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ creates electron transport channels and facilitating electron transfer (bridging effect) (Fig. 2j).

This contrast between the locally emerging fast process and the ubiquitous slow process satisfies the activator-inhibitor conditions for Turing-type reaction-diffusion patterns [43,44]. Under the influence of ZPS, the shape evolution exhibits the transfer of valley and peak (Fig. 3a). Further analysis reveals that ZPS surface coverage was improved at the valley position due to geometric change (fig. S23), leading to a higher growth rate at valley position after the introduction of ZPS and the surface flatness is improved as so. However, when valley grows up to the same level as peak, the accumulated ZPS is still higher than original peak position, resulting the continuous accelerated growth (fig. S24) and the original valley changes into peak. In this circumstance, the ZPS will be accumulated in newly-formed valley (original peak) and accelerate the local growth. As a result, ZPS surface coverage exhibits oscillation behavior (Fig. 3c) and shape evolution is characterized by continuous peak-valley transfer, which illustrates that the improved surface flatness is limited. Furthermore, the respective Turing pattern was visualized to better illustrate the application of Turing model. Fig. 3d shows the 3D shape evolution under the influence of ZPS. The fast deposition process area with high ZPS coverage and slow deposition process area with low ZPS coverage evolution were shown in Fig. 3e and fig. S25. The process area evolution and ZPS coverage evolution exhibit typical Turing patterns characterization (spots, stripes), and the transfer between peak and valley arises from the slow geometric evolution of the surface.

Based on above analysis, Turing oscillation growth mechanism was proposed. On one hand, the accumulation of ZPS on valley position improve the flatness. On the other hand, the continuous change between valley and peak (oscillation) indicates that the boosting effect of addi tives on surface flatness is limited, overcoming previous diffusionadsorption theory based on suppressor-type additives, in which the surface flatness should be continuously improved to plane $( R _ { \mathrm { z } }$ tending to 0). To verify the mechanism, the cross-sectional profile of copper foil was calculated from AFM images used to measure copper layer deposited with different deposition time (Fig. 3F and 3g). The almost unchanged surface roughness with deposition time confirms the limited improved flatness of copper foil under the influence of ZPS due to the transfer of valley and peak.

To directly observe the internal interface structures at the atomic scale, high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) was employed to investigate the microstructural evolution of copper foils influenced by ZPS (bis-(sodium sulfopropyl)-disulfide) [46]. HRTEM observations consistently revealed the presence of twin boundaries on the copper foil surfaces, irrespective of ZPS addition (Fig. 4b and 4c). Quantitative measurements of lattice fringe spacings in the twin-boundary regions demonstrated a distinct crystallographic transition: in the absence of ZPS, the twin-boundary vicinities were predominantly characterized by (111) planes; upon ZPS introduction, the regions transformed to (220) planes (Fig. S26-S29). This finding is in agreement with the XRD analysis, confirming that ZPS facilitates the preferential growth of (220)-oriented grains. Consequently, the enhanced mechanical properties are attributed to the synergistic effects of the favorable slip characteristics associated with the (220) texture and the strengthening contributions from the high-density twin boundaries. Furthermore, the cross-sectional Inverse Pole Figure (IPF) orientation maps (d1, e1) from EBSD tests indicates that ZPS has a limited effect on grain orientation, with only a slight enhancement of (220) texture. The obtained Cu (220) is of better for improving elongation of copper foil compared with Cu (111) and Cu (200) plane [47] owing to more glide planes [48].

The influence of ZPS on grain size was investigated by EBSD. The Image Quality (IQ) maps (d2, e2) show that the addition of ZPS reduces the grain size and induces high density boundaries. Specifically, the mean grain size decreases from 3.29 μm to 2.60 μm (d4, e4). According to Hall-Petch strengthening mechanism, grain boundaries act as strong barriers to dislocation motion. Grain refinement dramatically increases the total grain boundary area, leading to sharp increase in strength. As a result, the improved grain boundaries density by ZPS is conducive for enhancing mechanical performance. Furthermore, twin grain boundaries, as a special type of high-angle grain boundary, are characterized by low interfacial energy and high stability, and they exhibit a stronger strengthening effect due to their unique symmetric structure. As revealed by fig. d3, e2, the introduction of ZPS increases the density of twin boundaries (red lines), thereby further enhancing both elongation and tensile strength.

The copper foil without ZPS is uneven and full of large copper grain size, while the surface flatness is improved and the grain size is reduced with ZPS rising from 10 mg/L to 20 mg/L, which is due to ZPS boost the nucleation growth, resulting in more compact and even growth of copper foil. When ZPS was 30 mg/L, copper foil becomes compact and flat and there is no obvious improvement with ZPS increased to 40 mg/L, indicating that accelerating effect of ZPS is achieved the most (Fig. 5b), in accordance with CV analysis and EIS analysis. Apart from surface morphology, the surface roughness was also illustrated (fig. 5c, S30). $R _ { \mathrm { z } }$ declines from 2.603 μm to 1.627 μm with ZPS from 0 mg/L to 40 mg/L, further demonstrating that ZPS can improve copper foil morphology.

Elongation and tensile strength are key indicators to evaluate the performance of copper foil [50]. Fig. 5d shows the influence of ZPS concentration on mechanical performance of copper foil. The elongation for copper foil obtained in VMS was 2.89%. After adding ZPS, there is an increasing trend (from 3.53% to 3.78%) with the rising ZPS concentration until 40 mg/L. ZPS can accelerate the nucleation and growth process so as to increase the number of copper grain and refining the grain size, which is beneficial to boost the elongation [51]. As for tensile strength, similar results can be found. Tensile strength increases from 295 MPa to 331 MPa with ZPS concentration rising from 0 mg/L to 30 mg/L and then sees a slightly decrease to 327 MPa with 40 mg/L ZPS, which is due to copper foil grain refined by ZPS provides more grain boundary hindering the crack propagation, thereby improving the tensile strength [52]. However, overhigh ZPS leads to grain further reduced, weakening the elongation to some extent [51]. The mechanical performance of copper foil from this work was compared with copper foils from researches in recent years (Fig. S31) and it is obvious that single additive ZPS is beneficial to improve copper foil properties with elongation of 3.78% and tensile strength of 331 MPa obtained by 30 mg/L ZPS.

In this study, additive Sodium 3-(benzothiazole-2-ylthio)-1-pro panesulfonate (ZPS) has been systematically investigated for copper foil electrodeposition. Cyclic voltammetry and electrochemical impedance spectra indicate that ZPS is of accelerating effect during electroplating. Chronoamperometry and ex situ SEM shows that the 3D diffusion controlled instantaneous nucleation and growth model is not changed but the active sites are increased by ZPS. At present, the acidic copper sulfate solution is more commonly used for copper electroplating deposition [1], and the main components of the Virgin Make-up Solution (VMS) are copper sulfate (CuSO<sub>4</sub>), sulfuric acid (H SO ), and chloride ions (Cl<sup>−</sup> ) [10]. However, in through-hole electroplating, the orifice of through hole has higher current density and higher mass transfer [11]efficiency than the middle of through hole, resulting in very uneven metal deposition of through hole, which affects electrical signal transmission of the circuit and reduces the service life of electronic devices. Researchers have found that this problem can be solved by adding a variety of additives to the VMS, which has sparked increasing interest in the study of copper electroplating additives [12]. The additives of copper electroplating are generally divided into three categories: inhibitors (i.e. polyethylene glycol (PEG) [13–15], polypropylene glycol (PPG) [16] or their copolymers), accelerators (such as bis(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) [17,18], or 3-mercapto-1-propanesulfonate (MPS) [19,20]), and levelers (i.e. Janus Green B (JGB) [11,21–23], Diazine Black [24], Alcian Blue, Safranin T [25], 2-mercaptopyridine [26,27], or 2,2-Dithiodipyridine [28]). With the synergistic effect of the three additives, a bright and uniform thickness of the electroplating inside and outside through hole is obtained. In previous work, our group reported aliphatic amine organics [29–31] and large conjugated molecules [32–39] as copper electroplating levelers, and all of these levelers performed excellently.

In this work, a family of water-soluble carbazole derivatives were synthesized in high yield. Electrochemical tests were employed to explore the ability to inhibit the reduction and deposition of copper ions. In theoretical calculations, molecular orbital calculations of carbazole derivatives demonstrated the ability of carbazole derivatives to adsorb onto copper surfaces. Furthermore, molecular dynamics simulations visualized the adsorption behavior of carbazole derivatives on copper. After through-hole electroplating experiments, the effect of compound Cz-BPDB as a leveler was demonstrated by various instruments. Metallographic microscopy was applied to test throwing power (TP) values. SEM and XRD were respectively employed to observe the flatness of electroplating surface and the dominant crystal orientation of electroplating layer. In addition, to investigate the mechanism of through-hole electroplating, nucleation model theory, molecular properties, and electrochemical properties were further analyzed. This work increased the options for copper electroplating levelers with carbazole materials as a new plating leveler and contributed to the continuing development of the copper electroplating mechanism.

# Insights into the synergistic effects of safranine in an acidic copper bath on through-hole void-free filling for high-quality electronics interconnection
Additives: Complex and effective synergistic effects
Keywords: Acidic copper electronic plating Safranine Synergistic effect Through-hole void-free filling Molecule action mechanism

In this work, we develop a novel safranine (SA)-based acidic sulfate copper electronic plating process for through-hole copper void-free filling for high-quality electronics interconnection, and both the molecule actions and synergistic effects of safranine (SA) are carefully explored. Cyclic voltammetry experiments at rotating rates of 200 r/min and 1200 r/min demonstrate that SA itself can accelerate the electro-reduction of copper ion, heighten the inhibiting effect of polyethylene glycol (PEG) and acceleration effect of bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS). The addition of SA to the virgin make-up solution (VMS) containing PEG and SPS makes the relative electric charge (ΔQ) between the low and high rotating rates be increased from 1.27 ± 0.04–22.53% ± 0.05, indicating the higher copper electronic plating amount at the center than that at the mouth of through-hole. In situ Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy together with theoretical calculations further illustrate that the molecule SA is adsorbed on the copper surface through the N atom in the aromatic ring, PEG and SPS can heighten the adsorption of SA on the Cu surface, and both PEG and SPS both synergistically influence with SA to achieve the void-free copper filling of through-hole.

With the rapid development of electronic products, advanced fabrication technologies for high-density interconnect (HDI) in the printed circuit board (PCB) are widely applied in 5 G communication, energy devices, wearable devices, and other booming fields [1–3]. Metallization of through-hole (TH) is one of the core technologies to realize the conduction of different layers in HDI-PCB [4,5]. Acidic sulfate copper electronic plating is the most universal process for the metallization of TH [6–9]. TH copper thickening combined with resin plugging and TH void-free copper filling are the two common metallization technologies. For the TH copper thickening combined with resin plugging technology, only a homogeneous and conformal copper coating (about 20 µm) on its side wall is needed [10–14], then epoxy resin is used to fill the TH. For the TH void-free copper filling technology, copper coating is fully filled inside the TH without any void. It is worth noting that TH may crack under long-term heating due to the different thermal expansion coeffi cient between the resin and copper, resulting in the blocked signal transmission. Therefore, compared with TH copper thickening combined with resin plugging technology, TH void-free copper filling technology behaves the advantages of higher reliability and better signal transmission quality. Nowadays, with the acceleration of communication speed, more heat is generated when the signal processing, the copper void-free filling of TH has therefore been widely employed for improving the heat dissipation efficiency.

The main difficulty in copper filling is the formation of voids in TH with higher aspect ratio due to the uneven local current distribution and tanglesome convection environments caused by the specific geometry of TH [15–17]. The copper deposition amount at the mouth is usually higher than that at the center of TH, resulting in the coating in a void or seam. Therefore, it is particularly crucial introducing the organic additives in the acidic sulfate bath to modulate the copper deposition process at the mouth and center. The key to blind hole filling is the bottom-up growth of copper coating. The key to TH filling is that copper coating rapidly deposits at the center of TH wall until the center is connected to form a butterfly shape structure (two blind holes), and then the two blind holes are filled separately. The accelerator of bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) and suppressor of polyethylene glycol (PEG) are the commonly used additives in the acidic sulfate bath [18–25]. Suppressor, mainly distributed at the mouth of TH, inhibits the copper ion electro-reduction at a definite potential which results in the decrease of reduction current density. Accelerator, mainly distributed at the center of $\mathrm { T H } ,$ promotes the copper ion electro-reduction at a definite potential which results in the increase of reduction current density. It is still difficult to realize a void-free copper filling from the bath with only these two additives, and therefore the other additive is further needed. Zheng et al. [12] reported that poly (1-vinyl imidazole co 1, 4-butanediol diglycidyl ether) (VIBDGE) could further heighten the inhibiting ability of PEG in copper electronic plating. Li et al. [13] presented that a copolymer comprising of pyrrole and 1,4-butanediol diglycidyl ether (PBDGE) also could enhance the inhibiting ability of PEG during copper electronic plating. Wang et al. [14] introduced that gentian violet (GVT) behaved with the synergistic inhibiting effect with PEG and the antagonistic effect with SPS. Although considerable studies have been carried out to show the superior performance of additives, up to now, the synergistic action mechanisms of additives are still not clarified.

Organic additives play an important role in regulating <sup>fi</sup>lm growth and properties in Cu electrodeposition. 3‑Mercapto‑1‑propane sulfonate (MPS) and its dimer bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) are representative accelerators that promote Cu electrodeposition rate. Cu has been widely used as metallization material in the semi conductor industry owing to its low electrical resistivity and high electromigration resistance. Cu metallization is usually performed by electrodeposition, which e<sup>fi</sup>ciently yields high quality <sup>fi</sup>lms by a relatively simple and inexpensive process. Electrolyte for Cu electrodeposition typically contains small quantities of organic additives, which are essential to regulate <sup>fi</sup>lm growth and properties. Additives are grouped into accelerators, suppressors, and levelers according to their roles in controlling the deposition rate. Among them, 3‑mercap to‑1‑propanesulfonate (MPS) and its dimer bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) are the most representative accelerators in Cu electrodeposition [1].

The accelerating e<sup>f</sup>ect of SPS or MPS has been explained by two mechanisms [2]. One describes competitive adsorption between accel erator and suppressor; the displacement of suppressor inhibition layer by SPS or MPS facilitates the approach of Cu ions to electrode surface, enhancing the deposition rate $[ 3 - 7 ]$ . The other mechanism focuses on direct catalytic reduction of $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ ion to $\mathrm { { C u } ^ { + } }$ ion by forming Cu(I) (thiolate) complex [8–11]. The reduction of ${ \mathsf { C u } } ^ { 2 + } { \mathsf { t o } } { \mathsf { C u } } ^ { + }$ is known as the rate-determining step of Cu electrodeposition [12]. Vereecken et al. reported that the amount of $\mathrm { { C u } ^ { + } }$ near electrode surface is a key factor determining the deposition rate in Cu electrodeposition [13,14].

Herein, the formal reduction potential of SPS $( \operatorname { E q } .$ . (3)) was obtained, and the cell potentials of Eqs. (1) and (2) were estimated by spectroscopy. The formal reduction potential of SPS was obtained by measuring the chemical equilibrium constants of thiol–disulfide interchange reaction between MPS/SPS pairs and reference thiol/disul<sup>fi</sup>de pairs, lipoic acid (Lip) and mercaptoethanol (ME). A defect free copper interconnect is crucial for ensuring the electrical connection and transmission of high density interconnect printed circuit boards. Leveling agent is a key regulatory factor for achieving dense cop per super filling from bottom to top in blind holes during the electroplating process of high-density interconnect boards. Here, two small molecule five-membered heterocyclic compounds with different side chains, namely 3- amino-5-mercapto-1,2,4-triazole (AMT) and 2–5-methyl-1,3,4-thiadiazole (MMT), were selected to be as levelling agents to study their effect on the copper filling behavior on blind holes. Electrochemical tests including cyclic voltammetry solvation (CV) and linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) were firstly used to analyze the inhibitory effect of two leveling agents on copper deposition and it was indicated that the MMT has a more significant inhibitory effect on the copper deposition than the AMT. Subsequently, the influence of different concentrations of MMT on the inhibition of copper deposition and the blind hole filling performance were also further analyzed by LSV, CV, and constant current measurement (GM), where an optimal concentration of 7 ppm was obtained for the maximum inhibitory ability on the copper deposition accompanied by the best blind hole filling ability. The characterization analysis from the field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM), atomic force microscopy (AFM), and X-ray diffraction (XRD) also illuminates that the MMT leveling agent can effectively reduce the surface roughness of copper filled with micropores and promote the selective growth of copper coatings along the (11 1) crystallographic plane. The adsorption behavior of the levelling agent on the cathode surface during electrodeposition was further also studied by the quantum chemical calculations and molecular dynamics sim ulations combined with the in situ electrochemical surface enhanced Raman spectroscopy (EC-SERS) experiments. It has been suggested that the thiol, sulfur, and alkyl groups in the leveling agent MMT molecule are nucleophilic groups, providing preferred active sites for adsorption reactions and thus generating effective inhibition ability on copper deposition formation. Thermal shock experiments based on tin immersion showed the copper layer obtained under the addition of the levelling agent MMT has excellent reliability. The comprehensive results indicated that 2-mercapto-5-methyl-1,3,4-thiadiazole (MMT) was an effective levelling agent for the blind hole supperfilling.

Blind hole copper electroplating is the primary technology used in the connectivity manufacturing process for printed circuit boards (PCB), semiconductor integrated circuit (IC) chips, and IC packaging substrates [1–3]. The issue of achieving complete filling of high-quality plated copper has become increasingly essential in light of the progress made in integrated and miniaturized electronic devices. This is particularly relevant as high-density interconnect printed circuit boards (PCBs) are transitioning towards through-hole and micro-hole designs with larger depth-to-diameter ratios [4]. In the process of copper plating on such PCB micro vias with a larger depth-to-diameter ratio, there is a very significant difference between a current’s density distribution inside and on the surface of the micro vias. In such an environment, the copper electrodeposition rate in the pore area will be significantly greater than that in the micropores’ bottom region, which will result in the coppe layer covering and sealing the pore area in a preferential manner, leading to internal defects in the pores. In order to achieve bottom-up superfilling of the micropores, a synergistic effect of different addi tives is required, namely accelerators, inhibitors, levelling agents and chloride ions. Accelerators are generally small molecule organic sul phides containing specific functional groups of (-S–S-), sulfhydryl (-SH) and sulphonic acid $\left( - S O _ { 3 ^ { - } } \right)$ groups, which typically preferentially adsorb at the micropore’s bottom and can hasten the electrodeposition of copper at the hole’s bottom. SPS and MPS are both common accelerator $[ 5 , 6 ]$ . During copper electrodeposition, the inhibitor is usually adsorbed on the cathode surface and interacts with chloride ions to increase the overpotential, thereby achieving the inhibitory effect on the surface deposition of copper, Inhibitors are mainly macromolecular polyether or polyols [7]. The most prevalent inhibitors are polyethylene glycol (PEG), but in addition to PEG there are also polypropylene glycol (PPG) and triblock copolymers of PEG and PPG [8–10]. Levelling agents can be added in very small amounts compared to inhibitors to achieve a strong inhibiting effect and rapid deactivation, leaving the surface flat and smooth. Meantime, levelling agents also show an inhibiting effect o copper deposition but there is no substitute for inhibitors, which can be compared to short-acting inhibitors, while inhibitors show a moderate inhibiting effect and deactivate slowly, and throughout the plating process, the levelling agent gradually covers the copper surface, domi nating the completion of superconformal deposition [4,7]. Traditiona levelling agents such as Janus Green B (JGB), Diazine Black (DB) Methylene Blue (MB), Alsin Blue (ABPV) [11–14]. However, these dye conventional levelling agents are prone to decomposition at high tem peratures, which makes the plating process not easy to control increasing the cost and also leading to copper plating quality problems. In response to the above problems, researchers have continued t develop new environmentally friendly high-performance small molecul copper plating levelling agents, such as benzyl quaternary ammonium containing compounds phenylacetyl chloride (BZC) [15], 2,2-dithiodi pyridine (DTDP) [16], 4,6-dimethyl-2-mercaptopyrimidine (DMP) [17], tricyclazole (TCA) [18], 1-(4-hydroxyphenyl)-2-tetrazole-5-thion (HPTT) [19]. Synthetic macromolecule polymers such as copolyme synthesized with pyrrole and 1,4-butanediol diglycidyl ether (PBDGE) copolymer, synthesized with imidazole and 1 4-butanediol diglvcidy ether (IBDGE), copolymer synthesized with 1-vinyl imidazole and 1,4 butanediol diglycidyl ether (VIBDGE) [20 22] and so on. These new copper plating levelling agents are phenotyped with good levelling properties. These results from the electrochemical analysis and theoretical calculations fully demonstrate that MMT is an effective levelling agent for PCB blind hole filling.

Electrodeposition plays a vital role in advanced chip manufacturing as it is a key technology for electrical interconnects. With the rapid development of technology, the length of metal wiring inside the chip has been significantly extended, at the same time, the number of layers inside the chip has also continued to increase. To improve energy efficiency and performance, the size of transistors and metals must continue to shrink [1–4]. However, this process inevitably exacerbates the size effect (grain boundary and interface diffusion of electrons in metals), significantly increases the current load and resistance, and causes serious RC delay and thermal damage to chip performance. Metal cobalt interconnect layer is mainly prepared by electrodeposition technology. In the process of metal cobalt electrodeposition, additives are key components that can adjust the cobalt deposition rate in via and trench, improve the uniformity of the deposited cobalt film, and thus improve chip performance [6–9]. However, due to the confidentiality of the technology, there are relatively few related studies and reports, but this does not affect its importance and application prospects. Li et al.
