In this study, SO was used to chemically modify the commonly used leveling agent polydimethyldiallylammonium (PD) in through-hole electroplating, resulting in a more effective leveling agent, PDS, which improved the throwing power (TP), leading to through-hole circuit boards with better metal coverage in difficult-to-reach areas. Furthermore, theoretical and experimental studies were conducted to understand how the −SO structure influences the leveling ability of the leveling agent. The study demonstrates that the −SO - modified additive significantly enhances the copper plating process, resulting in thicker and more uniform deposits in through-holes, which are critical for ensuring high-quality circuit boards.Additionally, this study elu cidates the mechanism of action of the leveling agent on the copper surface, providing theoretical support for the development of copper plating leveling agents. The leveling ability differences between the leveling agents PD and PDS were investigated using Cyclic Voltammetry, constant current method, and Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy. Additionally, the optimal concentrations of the additives were determined. Quantum chemical calculations were employed to analyze the electrostatic potential, HOMO/LUMO orbitals, and differential charge density on the Cu (111) surface for both leveling agents. These theoretical analyses provided insights into the reasons behind the differing leveling abilities of the two agents.

With the rapid development of the electronics industry, an increasing number of consumer products, such as computers, electronic watches, wearable devices, smartphones, and communication equipment, are becoming more intelligent, lightweight, and miniaturized[1–3]. In these advanced electronic products, the Printed Circuit Board (PCB) is a critical component, serving as the main conduit between various electronic elements, enabling them to connect and work together in a coordinated manner. The metallization of PCBs, which enables the interconnection of electronic components, is particularly crucial[4,5]. Through-hole electroplating plays a vital role in this process, with copper electroplating emerging as the mainstream choice for PCB interconnection due to its excellent conductivity and low cost[6]. However, current copper electroplating technology faces challenges in meeting the ever-increasing demands of PCB manufacturing, which has become a bottleneck limiting the improvement of PCB performance [7,8].Therefore, the preparation of high-quality through-hole plating and high-density interconnect circuit boards holds significant industrial and economic importance[9].

Currently, the most widely used technology in the through-hole plating process of circuit boards is acid copper plating, which typically involves a conventional acid copper plating solution containing copper sulfate, sulfuric acid, and trace amounts of plating additives[10]. Traditional electroplating additives can be categorized into suppressors, accelerators, and levelers[11–13]. In the context of through-hole electroplating, the key substance capable of enhancing the TP value is the leveler, which, as a crucial component in the acid copper plating solution, requires only a small addition to effectively increase the TP value [14,15]. As a critical metric for assessing the performance of throughhole copper plating, the TP value is calculated as the ratio of the copper thickness on the surface to the copper layer thickness inside the hole [16]. The traditional calculation method is divided into six-point method[17,18], and the specific measurement method is described in detail later.

When the cathodic overpotential is low, research has found that the capacitive loop of the leveling agent PDS is significantly larger compared to PD, indicating that PDS has a stronger inhibitory effect on the deposition of copper ions and can provide a better leveling performance[34]. The PDS molecule shows a maximum in differential charge density near the sulfur atoms, significantly affecting the distribution of differential charge density on the Cu surface. In contrast, PD lacks these structural features, resulting in weaker surface interactions and less effective inhibition.

This study improves the common leveling agent PD used in acid copper plating by incorporating $\mathrm { { S O } _ { 2 } }$ and investigates the leveling performance of both leveling agents through CVS, GMs, EIS testing, and more. The introduction of the − ${ \bf - } S 0 _ { 2 }$ structure effectively enhances the leveling capability of the leveling agent and creates new active sites on the Cu surface. The enhancement of leveling capabilities by the intro duction of the $- s 0 _ { 2 }$ structure was further substantiated through differential charge density calculations. Additionally, electrochemical experiments confirmed that the optimal concentration for both PD and PDS is 100 mg/L. SEM observations of the copper layers plated at this concentration revealed a significant reduction in porosity, indicating that both additive molecules effectively decrease the porosity of the plating layer. Observations from the profilometer showed that the copper layers were smoother and the crystallization more refined. This study demonstrates that the introduction of the − ${ \bf - } S O _ { 2 }$ functional group into PD leveling agents significantly improves their leveling performance. Theoretical calculations reveal that the $- S O _ { 2 }$ group enhances molecular adsorption and introduces additional interaction sites, leading to a more uniform adsorption layer and stronger inhibition of $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ deposition.Furthermore, comparative experiments show that the $S O _ { 2 ^ { - } }$ modified PD exhibits superior leveling efficiency and deposit uniformity compared to commercially available leveling agents. These findings highlight the potential o $\dot { \mathbf { \eta } } - \mathbf { S } \mathbf { O } _ { 2 }$ modification as a novel approach for designing next-generation copper plating additives.

The 1-(4-carboxyphenyl)-5-mercapto-1 h-tetrazole (CMHT) as a novel leveler for the overfilling of micro-blind vias was investigated in acidic copper electroplating. The synergistic effect between CMHT and other additives were confirmed through chronoamperometry, cyclic voltammetry and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy. The results showed a convection-dependent interaction between the CMHT and suppressor (propyleneoxide (PO)-ethylene oxide (EO)-propylene oxide (PO), named PEP). Metallographic section testing demonstrated that the CMHT not only have excellent microvia filling performances, but also only have 19.1 μm thin surface Cu for micro blind vias with a diameter of 150 µm and a depth of 80 µm by the electrodepositing 60 min of 2 A/dm<sup>2</sup>. The quantum chemical calculations experiments revealed also that the CMHT parallel orientation of the benzene ring and tetrazole heterocycle can enhance the effective adsorption area. The obtained results from electrochemical test and quantum chemical calculations were in reasonably good agreement

Copper plating process is widely applied in PCB and TSV industries due to its excellent conductivity properties and low cost. Currently, several important electronic interconnection applications encompass processes such as electroless copper plating, blind via plating, and through-hole plating. A significant issue associated with blind via plating is the relatively thick copper layer on the surface, which prevent effective and complete filling of the blind vias. On the other hand, the miniaturization requirements of 3D packagings force manufacturers to adopt multiple layers wiring interconnection structure to reducing the interconnect line length and corresponding signal loss. In other words, the vertical copper interconnection without void or seam can improve the signal transmission rate and saving the installation components area for PCB miniaturization [1–4].

In order to achieve high filling performance by CuSO -based elec trolyte systems, the leveler have become the fundamental choice for via fill applications due to it can prevent premature sealing of holes [5–8]. Typically, when using amine-containing glycidyl ethers as leveler, ad vantages such as improved surface appearance and void-free filling of blind vias are observed. However, these levelers are associated with a slower copper filling rate and can result in excessively thick copper layers on the surface. For example, the depth of the diameter of micro blind is about 100um and the surface copper is generally 20 \~ 25 μm, which is not easy to prepare fine circuit. In contrast, compounds such as imidazole and polyepoxides, when utilized as levelers, have demon strated advantages including a rapid filling rate for blind vias and a thinner copper layer on the surface [5–10]. The CMHT has a relatively small molecular weight and it contains thiol groups (−SH) and nitrogencontaining heterocycles. Considering the structure of CMHT tetrazoles is similar to imidazole as shown in Fig. 1, therefore, it is necessary to study the conditions for obtaining excellent blind hole filling effect by controlling the plating temperature, selecting appropriate current density and time, and making the additives in the plating solution have a high synergistic effect.

Additives take on critical significance in electroplating, even though they are employed in small quantities. They exert notable efects on the performance exhibited by the plating solutions and coatings. Surfactants are capable of reducing the surface tension of the plating solution such that the plating solution can spread more smoothly on the substrate surface. Moreover, surfactants facilitate the release of hydrogen gas adsorbed on the cathode surface such that the occurrence of pinholes and pitting on the coating surface can be reduced and a smoother surface can be generated. This results in finer grain size and denser coatings, leading to increased hardness and glossiness.<sup>14</sup> However, at higher concentrations of brighteners in the plating solution, the metal ions are greatly afected or complexed by a large number of brightener molecules during the discharge process, severely hindering the normal deposition process. This intensifies the hydrogen evolution reaction and leads to a decrease in coating hardness and glossiness.<sup>20−22</sup> In accordance with the comparative analysis, thiourea, which showed a greater improvement in coating hardness and glossiness, served as the brightener for the plating solution system.

ABSTRACT: The copper connectivity technique is essential for achieving electrical interconnection in wafer level packaging (WLP), system in packaging (SiP), and 3D packaging. The essential processing material for copper connectivity is a copper sulfate electroplating solution in which organic additives play a crucial role in the regularity of copper electrodeposition. In this study, electrochemical tests, X-ray difraction, 3D profiling, and scanning electron microscopy were used to investigate the leveling efect and mechanism of polyquaternary ammonium urea-containing polymer (PUB2) in the process of copper electrodeposition on-chip copper connections. PUB2 has excellent polarization ability on the target surface, remains unafected by the sulfur additive SPS and poly(ethylene glycol), and displays a strong ability to regulate the copper deposition rate of through-holes and surface wiring. The waviness of the wafer surface wiring was reduced from 130 to approximately 70 nm after optimizing the PUB2 concentration, and the surface roughness was reduced from 10 to approximately 7 nm. The coating was dispersed evenly, and the rate of through-hole filling was improved by 57%. This study not only examined PUB2 leveling performance and mechanisms but also devised a research method and system for electroplating additives to facilitate the development and application of new electroplating additives.

Microchip technology has entered the post-Moore era, and chip packaging technology has continually evolved. Transitioning from two-dimensional packaging, such as the double-line inline and square flat packaging of the last century, we have now entered an era ofultrahigh-density three-dimensional packaging. Compared to two-dimensional packaging, three-dimensional packaging enables higher chip density, shorter transmission distances, and lower chip power consumption.<sup>1,2</sup> Copper is used as an interconnecting material based on its low resistivity and strong electromigration resistance. In comparison to traditional aluminum interconnects, the electromigration resistance of copper interconnects is improved by 2 orders of magnitude, significantly enhancing the reliability of integrated circuits (ICs).<sup>3</sup> Copper electroplating stands as a fundamental technology for interconnecting devices, including ICs, IC packaging substrates, and printed circuit boards (Table 1).

However, copper sulfate plating solutions often cause problems such as uneven coating, defects, and faults during microhole plating. Therefore, plating solutions often contain various additives for auxiliary plating, including Cl<sup>−</sup>, accelerators, inhibitors, and leveling agents to improve the plating performance of copper sulfate plating solutions and meet the plating requirements of diferent scales and diferent conditions to obtain an ideal copper plating layer.<sup>4−7</sup> Research at home and abroad mainly focuses on organic additives, such as accelerators and inhibitors. Additionally, dye leveling agents such as Jenner green B (JGB) have been studied extensively and organic amine leveling agents are novel leveling agents that have started attracting significant attention.<sup>8−11</sup> Dow et al. considered that the convection-dependent adsorption behavior of a plating solution can be used as an indicator to determine whether the plating solution is suitable for micropore filling<sup>12</sup> and Chang et al.<sup>13</sup> studied the leveling efect of 2-mercaptopyridine. It was determined that 2-mercaptopyridine has a stronger inhibitory efect on Cu deposition than JGB. Considering the complexity and broad variety of chip processes, there are diferences between the plating solutions used for diferent plating processes, plating machines, and semiconductor manufacturers. As a result, plating solutions are typically customized develop ment products. However, there are three main issues associated with the research on leveling agents both domestically and internationally. First, current research mostly uses theoretical calculations, electrochemical methods, and electroplating experiments to investigate the mechanisms and efects of electroplating additives. Unlike traditional electrodeposition, chip copper interconnection involves precise deposition in a narrow space or surface at the micronano level. The morphology and uniformity of the copper deposition layer have a direct impact on the electrical performance of the copper interconnection line, thereby influencing the overall chip performance.<sup>14,15</sup> Its characteristics mainly include small electroplating dimensions, dificulty in filling microholes with uneven current density, and high coating quality requirements. However, there is a distinct lack of comprehensive research on electroplating with structured wafers, which renders most research results unable to be applied in practice. Second, copper sulfate electroplating leveling agents are primarily composed of dye organic polymers such as JGB, which tend to generate significant pollution. With the development of wafer-level, system-level, and 3D packaging, the performance ofelectroplating additives is facing increased scrutiny and evaluation. As a result, the industry is urgently requiring the development of novel electroplating leveling agents. Third, the majority of the existing research is focused on developing independent research models for wafer surface wiring and through-hole filling. However, in practical IC manufacturing, through-hole filling and wiring are performed concurrently, which causes a gap between study findings and application.<sup>16−18</sup> Therefore, it is crucial to develop an application-based screening and evaluation strategy for electroplating additives.

2.3. Hull Cell Plating Tests. Hull cell experiments were conducted to examine the efect of various PUB2 additive concentrations on the morphology of electroplated copper. A copper plate served as the cathode, and phosphorus copper served as the anode. The primary solution had a current density of 1 ASD and contained the following ingredients: 220 g/L $\mathrm { C u S O _ { 4 } } , \mathrm { 5 5 ~ g / L ~ H _ { 2 } S O _ { 4 } } ,$ additive inhibitor polyethylene glycol (PEG)-2000 at 100 ppm, accelerator SPS at 4 ppm, and Cl<sup>−</sup> at 50 ppm. Electroplating tests were conducted with PUB2 additives at concentrations of 0, 10, 30, 50, 70, and 100 ppm.

2.5. Wafer Filling and Wiring Tests. For this analysis, phosphorus copper served as the anode and a wafer served as the cathode. The plating mixture was 220 g/L $\mathrm { C u S O _ { 4 } } ,$ 55 g/L ${ \mathrm { H } } _ { 2 } S { \mathrm { O } } _ { 4 } ,$ 100 ppm of PEG-2000 additive inhibitor, 4 ppm of SPS accelerator, and 50 ppm of Cl. Wafer plating tests were conducted with PUB2 additives at concentrations of 0, 10, 30, 50, 70, and 100 ppm. The wafer slice dimensions were 3 × 3 mm with anode and cathode spacing values of 10 mm and a current density of 1 ASD.

3.1. JGB and PUB2 Additive Electrochemical Behaviors in Electroplated Copper. The CV curves for the JGB and PUB2 additives are presented in Figure 1. It is clear that the basic copper sulfate solution’s oxidation peak area is lowered by additives and that PUB2 addition reduces the solution’s redox peak area to its minimum value. The amount of copper being deposited is represented by the oxidation peak areas in the CV curves.<sup>19</sup> It can be concluded that PUB2 has a better inhibitory efect than JGB in terms of preventing the precipitation of $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + } .$

The results are reversed when PUB2 is added, and the copper deposition rate on the wafer surface is lower than the through hole filling rate, demonstrating that PUB2 has a stronger inhibitory efect on the copper deposition rate on the wafer surface than that in the through-holes. This inhibitory efect increases as the PUB2 content increases, and the growth rate gradually slows after the PUB2 content reaches 50 ppm. The PUB2 concentration in the through-holes is significantly lower than that on the surface of the coating as a result of PUB2’s strong adsorption on the surface of Cu and slow difusion into the microchannels of through-holes. 19,21−23

Without PUB2 addition, the entire coating has a burnt appearance with obvious faults that improve with increasing pole spacing. The surface flatness and brightness of the coating are significantly enhanced by the addition of PUB2 and these properties improve with an increasing concentration up to a certain point. The optimal efect is achieved when the PUB2 additive is diluted to between 30 and 50 ppm. The brightness and flatness ofthe coating rapidly decrease as the PUB2 additive concentration increases beyond this point. When the PUB2 additive concentration reaches 100 ppm, the coating develops flaws at small electrode spacing values and loses brightness.

Figure 8 indicates that the PUB2 additive enhances the plating impact on the wafer surface and significantly increases the regularity ofthrough-hole filling. When PUB2 is not applied, the wiring edge has burrs, protrusions, and unevenness and the through-holes and closed holes have uneven filling. Wiring roughness and homogeneity significantly improve as the PUB2 additive concentration increases. The optimal efect is achieved when the PUB2 additive concentration is between 30 and 50 ppm. When the PUB2 additive concentration increases further, the coating becomes uneven and develops pinholes. Addition ally, the rate of through-hole filling slows considerably, leading to unsatisfactory outcomes.

(2) The incorporation of PUB2 significantly enhances through-hole filling and wafer wiring efects. This is primarily due to PUB2 inhibiting the deposition rate of Cu atoms, refining the grain size, and promoting a more uniform grain distribution. The wafer surface waviness decreases from approximately 130 to 70 nm, the surface roughness decreases from approximately 10 to 7 nm, and the through-hole filling rate increases by 57% when the concentration of PUB2 ranges from 10 to 30 ppm.

It is well-known that organic additives can efectively improve the quality of electroplating, especially in coating uniformity and filling completeness. Additive mixtures facilitate the super-filling of holes by adjusting the overpotential and the kinetics of plating in damascene copper electrodeposition [19]. The accelerator and various levelers were investigated in copper micro-via filling, and the convection-dependent adsorption of additives was proposed [20,21]. In cobalt electrodeposition, the cobalt nucleation and the morphology of nanograin were also afected by organic additives and electrolytes [22,23]. The group of additives for metal electrodeposition mainly contains accelerators and inhibitors. The selective adsorption (such as convection adsorption) of accelerators and inhibitors causes a higher deposition rate at the bottom of the hole than the rate outside the hole. leading to a complete hole filling [24]. The accelerator for metal electrodeposition, such as 3-mercapto-1-propane sulfonate sulfonic acid (MPS), is a crucial additive in the copper hole filling [25]. Previous studies indicated that MPS molecules adsorbed on the surface of the co er la er through the sulfhydryl group, while the sulfonic acid group captured copper ions in solution to accelerate the deposition of copper [26]. Cobalt performs close electron-donating and -accepting ability similar to copper so similar additives could be chosen during electrodeposition. However, current studies on the mechanism of MPS are still insuficient to explain cobalt pillar electrodeposition and the cobalt hole filling. On the other hand, inhibitors are usually necessary for metal electrodeposition. The inhibitor molecules can selectively adsorb on the surface of the metal laver or generate complex with metal jons to improve the quality of the metal coating and electrodeposition eficiency [27]. For instance, polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) undergoes a convection-dependent adsorption inhibition efect on cobalt electrodeposition [28]. The PVP molecule has great absorption at sites with strong convection (such as the upper part of the hole). In contrast, the sites with weak convection (such as the bottom of the hole) has relatively low PVP absorption, thereby making PVP a suitable additive in the hole filling for cobalt electrodeposition [28]. However, PVP brings an inherent suppressing efect on the overall deposition rate and the quality of the deposited cobalt layer, so the practical application of

PVP is hindered in the manufacture of cobalt devices. In this article, competitive adsorption of MPS and PVP in cobalt electrodeposition was proposed first and cobalt pillar was successfully realized. Notably, the morphology of cobalt particles was modified and the uniformity of the cobalt layer was improved.

The cobalt electrodeposition was conducted in a 500 mL bath with a direct current from the DC power supply (INT-ERLOCK IPD-3305SLU). Cobalt electrodeposition was performed in the solution containing 0.3 mol/L $\mathrm { C o S O } _ { 4 } { \cdot } 7 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } 0$ 0.57 $\mathrm { m o l / L H _ { 3 } B O _ { 3 } } ,$ and 0.84 mmol/L $\mathrm { C o C l } _ { 2 } { \cdot } 6 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } 0$ . PVP (100 g/L) and 1 g/L MPS were prepared in advance for the injection in the electroplating solution before electrodeposition. $\mathtt { R u O } _ { 2 ^ { - } }$ coated titanium was connected to the cathode of the power and 2 L/min airflow was used to improve the convection in the electroplating solution. Cobalt was electrodeposited on the copper layer on a printed circuit board (PCB) with photopolymer film after imaging transfer at a current density of $1 0 \mathrm { m A } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } .$ . The depth of the hole in the photopolymer film was 50 µm and three diferent diameters of the holes were 100, 80, and $6 0 \mu \mathrm { m } .$ , respectively. A scanning electron microscope (SEM, HITACHI S3400) was used to analyze the morphology, while a metallographic microscope (ASIDA-JX23RT, China) was used to observe the top view and cross-section of the cobalt pillar. The crystal phases of the coating were measured by an X-ray difractometer (Rigaku MINIFLEX 600). The roughness tests of the coating were observed by a 3D measuring laser microscope (Olympus S4100) and the contact angle was measured by a contact angle tester (JY-PHa, China).

The efect of MPS on cobalt electrodeposition was investigated to observe the electrochemical behavior with electrochemical measurements. As shown in Figure 1a, the oxidation peak current density (from 1.72 to $2 . 0 8 \mathrm { A } / \mathrm { d } \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 } )$ and the cobalt oxidation area increases when 7 mg/L MPS is added to solution I. The change of the peak current density and oxidation area indicates the promotion of the cobalt electroplating process. In addition, the potential during cobalt deposition is shifted positively, revealing that MPS with a depolarization efect accelerates the electrodeposition of cobalt. With the addition of MPS, the stripping peak current density further increases to enhance the depolarization behavior during cobalt electrodeposition. The GM tests were also employed to verify the depolarization efect of MPS in cobalt electrodeposition (Figure 1b). As shown in Figure 1b, the potential shifted positively from −1.476 V to −1.362 V after the addition of $7 { \mathrm { m g / L } } { \mathrm { M P S } }$ . This potential pattern indicates that MPS has a significant acceleration efect on cobalt electroplating.

The electrochemical performance of the solution with MPS and PVP is further investigated to analyze the com petitive adsorption behavior of MPS and PVP. The inhibitive efect and adsorption behavior of PVP in cobalt electrodeposition has been reported in the previous work and the oxidation peak current density reduces obviously with the addition of PVP in the solution without MPS [28]. In this work, as shown in Figure $^ { \mathrm { 1 b , } }$ the inhibition behavior of PVP is also observed in the solution with MPS because the potential sharply dropped by 33 mV after the addition of 5 mg/L PVP. In addition, as presented in Figure 2a, the oxidation peak current density decreases when 5 mg/L PVP is injected into the plating solution with 7 mg/L MPS. In contrast. the decrease of the peak current density in the previous work is higher in the plating solution without MPS [28]. Overall, solution II containing both 7 mg/L MPS and 5 mg/L PVP still exhibits an inhibition behavior on cobalt electrode osition although the inhibi tion of PVP is attenuated by MPS. Meantime, in Figure 2b, a current density of −1.6 V for the solution with the addi tion of both MPS and PVP is generall lower than the one with only MPS or without additives. The above changes of the oxidation peak current density, deposition potential, and electrodeposition current density are attributed to the dynamic adsorption status of MPS and PVP molecules in the plating solution. In the first stage, the adsorption spon taneously occurred after MPS was added to the solution. In the presence of MPS in the solution, the sulfhydryl groups for the transfer of electrons and sulfonate groups for cap turing the metal cations synergistically contribute to accel erating the de osition of metal cations [42,43]. However, the adsorption sites of MPS are partially replaced with PVP when PVP is added in the solution with MPS because PVP is attracted to the cathode surface and weakens the accel eration level of MPS. In the previous work, convection dependent adsorption of PVP was verified to cause the diverged deposition rate between the bottom and the out side of the holes [28]. Therefore, the cobalt deposition rate on the outside of the hole could be relatively inhibited by PVP. Meanwhile, MPS, as a relatively small molecule, is able to difuse into the hole easily and accumulate in the bottom of the hole. As a result, the deposition rate of cobalt increases at the bottom of the hole.

Multiple studies have reported that MPS molecules adsorb on the surface of the copper layer through the sulfhydryl groups, and the sulfonic acid group captures copper ions in solution to accelerate the deposition [45,46]. HOMO and LUMO of MPS were calculated in this work, and the energy values of HOMO and LUMO for MPS were −6.955 and −0.843 eV, respectively. The HOMO status of MPS in Figure 3d indicates that the thiol group of MPS possesses the major space of HOMO so the thiol group is probably the electrophilic attack site. Notably, the value of the energy gap of PVP (6.28 eV) is close to that of MPS (6.122 eV), indicating similar chemical reactivities of PVP and MPS on the surface of cobalt. The computational result is consistent with the fact that MPS and PVP sustain competitive adsorption in cobalt electrodeposition.

Based on the above electrochemical characterization and quantum chemical calculation, the mechanism including three stages is proposed for the cobalt pillar electrodeposition in Figure 5. In the first stage, cobalt atoms are electrodeposited on the bottom of the hole and then grow along the wall of the hole with the formation of the cobalt nanoparticles layer. In a solution with MPS and PVP, cobalt deposition is suppressed on the upper part of the hole but the rate of cobalt atom deposition is promoted on the bottom of the hole. In the second stage, MPS and PVP molecules both adsorb to the cobalt surface in the presence of chloride ions. In this way, PVP suppresses the growth of cobalt, especially in the area with stronger convection when MPS and PVP are added to the plating solution. In the third stage, the deposition of cobalt on the upper side of the hole is inhibited more than that in the hole. In fact, MPS with a small molecule structure easily difuses into the hole so that it accelerates the deposition process of cobalt. As a result, on the upper side of the hole, cobalt deposition is suppressed but on the bottom cobalt growth is accelerated, thereby leading to the balanced deposition rate and successful filling for regular manufacture.

With the aid of MPS and PVP, cobalt pillars are achieved by cobalt hole super-filling (Figure 6a and b). The cobalt electrodeposition was conducted in the bath and the cobalt pillar was fabricated in the solution with competitive adsorption of MPS and PVP (Figures S1 and S2). The cross-sectional slice and top view of the cobalt pillar were observed by a metallographic microscope. As displayed in Figure 6c, the diameter of the filled hole is 100 µm. In the case without additives, it is very hard to fully fill the hole that a large amount of cobalt is only electrodeposited on the upper edge (Figure 6d). The failed filling is caused by the stronger convection outside the hole of the photopolymer so that the cobalt deposition outside the hole is faster than that inside the hole and results in a conformal deposition. With the addition of 7 mg/L MPS and 300 mg/L PVP, the hole of the photopolymer is successfully filled to generate cobalt pillars. In cobalt pillar electrodeposition, 7 mg/L MPS was added in solution considering the depolarization efect of MPS and loss of MPS. PVP (300 mg/L) was chosen in order to ensure the efect of polarization and improve the morphology of the electrodeposited cobalt as a surfactant.

Besides, MPS and PVP have a considerable efect on the crystallization and morphology of the electrodeposited cobalt. As illustrated in Figure 7a, the solution without additives leads to scattered cobalt deposition, and the nanoparticles on the cobalt surface cover a wide range of sizes. In the solution with only 7 mg/L MPS, the result in Figure 7b indicates that MPS improves the formation of large size cobalt particles due to the acceleration of MPS in cobalt electrodeposition. As shown in Figure 7c, in the solution with only 300 mg/L PVP, the electrodeposited cobalt particles are refined to generate the flocculent structure on the surface. Notably, with the addition of MPS and PVP (Figure 7d), the cobalt particles turn to be electrodeposited compactly and uniformly because nano cobalt particles gradually grow to form the cobalt pillar. XRD patterns in Figure 7e show that (101̄0), (112̄1), (101̄1), (224̄0), and (314̄1) directions are observed for the cobalt growth with a hexagonal structure. In the solution with only PVP, cobalt electrodeposition is efectively inhibited wherein the XRD pattern of the copper substrate also appears. The XRD results indicate that MPS enhances the difraction peak intensity of the cobalt 224̄0 direction and PVP reduces it. The introduction of MPS accelerated the growth of the 224̄0 crystal plane, while PVP inhibited the growth of the 224̄0 surface due to the adsorption of MPS and PVP in the above discussion.

The addition of two additives could synergistically make the cobalt surface finer and uniform. The uniformity of the electrodeposited cobalt surface was further examined by 3D roughness tests. The value of $S _ { \mathrm { a } }$ represents the arithmetic mean of the height values of all the peaks and troughs and a lower $S _ { \mathrm { a } }$ value indicates a better uniformity of the surface. As shown in Figure 7f and $^ { \mathrm { g , } }$ the $S _ { \mathrm { a } }$ value of the electrodeposited cobalt in solution with additives is significantly lower than the one without additives, verifying that the coexistence of MPS and PVP promotes uniformity of the cobalt surface. In addition, the wettability of the plated metal surface was evaluated. In Figure 7h and i, the contact angle of the solution on the cobalt substrate without additives is more than $7 5 ^ { \circ }$ and the surface contact angle is less than $3 6 ^ { \circ }$ with the addition of MPS and PVP. The wettability of the plating solution on the cobalt surface was substantially improved, which might be attributed to the interfacial reaction and hydrogen release in cobalt electrodeposition [47]. In summary, the additives efectively improved the uniformity of the electrodeposited cobalt and make the cobalt layer finer.

MPS and PVP as additives exhibit the function of acceleration and inhibition during cobalt electrodeposition, respectively. They undergo competitive adsorption behavior in cobalt electrodeposition and some adsorption sites of MPS are replaced by PVP. The adsorption site was calculated by quantum chemical calculations. The amide groups of PVP and thiol groups of MPS are probably the adsorption sites in cobalt electrodeposition. Besides, the amide groups of PVP mainly contribute to the HOMO orbital as a probable main electrophilic attack region. The cobalt pillars with diferent diameters are successfully fabricated with the use of competitive adsorption between MPS and PVP. In this way, the additives of cobalt electrodeposition can efectively control the process of electrodeposition and a uniform cobalt deposition could be obtained. Cobalt electrodeposition has great potential in system-in-package, and this work facilitates the theoretical research and application of cobalt pillar in electronic interconnection. Synthesis of additives and more theoretical studies focusing on the working mechanism of the additives in cobalt electrodeposition are expected in the future.

Achieving uniform through-hole filling by copper electrodeposition is important for the fabrication of printed circuit boards (PCBs), and the development of suitable additives is a key process to realize eficient electrodeposition. Five isoindigo (IID) quaternary ammonium salts were synthesized using isoindigo molecules as the core skeleton. Electrochemical tests, theoretical calculations, and molecular dynamics simulations demonstrated that the isoindigo derivatives have the ability to act as leveler and exhibit electrode absorption capacity, among which IID-C4-QL showed the best inhibition of copper deposition as well as the best cathodic adsorption ability The high through-hole filling and excellent leveling performance of IID-C4-QL were confirmed by actual electroplating tests.

In order to achieve the bottom-up filling efect without defects in the through-hole, the main option is to add functional additives during copper deposition,<sup>9</sup> which are usually classified into three categories according to the functions they perform in copper plating: inhibitors, levelers and accelerators.<sup>10–13</sup> Inhibitors are mainly polyether compounds, such as polyethylene glycol (PEG), polypropylene glycol (PPG), and most of the large organic molecules with their molecular weights in the range of 6000–10 000, which mainly inhibit the deposition of copper.<sup>14,15</sup> The most common accelerator is sodium polydithiodipropane sulphonate (SPS), which is able to synergize with chloride ions to increase the rate of copper deposition and refine the copper crystalline particles, resulting in a bright copper coating.<sup>16,17</sup> Levelers are the most complex of the additives and a special kind of inhibitor, which can further enhance the dispersing ability of the plating solution and the flatness of the copper layer.<sup>18,19</sup> A series of dye-based levelers with large conjugation planes, such as diketopyrrolopyrrole derivatives, anthraquinone derivatives, 3,3<sup>0</sup>-bicarbazole derivatives, etc., have been reported in previous works of our group,<sup>2,20,21</sup> and it is hypothesized that molecules possessing good planarity as well as large conjugation are better at leveling.

The synthesized isoindigo quaternary ammonium salts (IID-QAS) were electrochemically tested to evaluate their inhibitory performance and convective adsorption, and the energy band gap and adsorption energy of five quaternary ammonium salts were calculated by combining quantum chemical calculations and molecular dynamics simulations to analyze their adsorp tion behaviors on the surface of copper, and the better quaternary ammonium salts were screened out from them for the next step of the actual copper plating test. The TP values were measured by making metallographic gel of copper plated through holes, and the morphology of the copper-plated surface was analyzed by SEM and XRD, which was corroborated via the electrochemical test. The results showed that IID-C4-QL had outstanding inhibition performance in the electrochemical test, and had a leveling efect in the actual copper-plating, which visually improved the TP value, refined copper grain size on the copper surface, and made the surface bright and flat, and the optimum amount of the quaternary ammonium salt was 1.5 ppm. The use of isoindigo derivatives as novel levelers broadens the application scope of isoindigo dyes and lays the foundation for exploring other conjugate structures that can be used as electroplating levelers.

Cyclic voltammetry is one of the commonly used methods for analyzing the inhibitory efect of additives on metal electrodeposition.<sup>24</sup> The negative peak in the curve represents the cathodic reduction peak of copper ions, while the positive peak represents the anodic stripping peak of copper. The peak areas in the copper deposition zone and the copper stripping zone correspond to the deposition amount of copper ions and the stripping amount of metallic copper, respectively, and these two quantities are directly proportional.<sup>25</sup> Therefore, the deposition of copper ions is represented by the positive peak area, and the smaller the positive peak area, the stronger the inhibitory efect of the additive on copper ion deposition.<sup>26</sup> The results in Fig. 3 show that at a concentration of 2 mmol $\mathrm { L } ^ { - 1 }$ the peak areas of all six additives (including JGB) decreased compared to VMS, indicating that all additives have inhibitory efects. Table 1 calculates the peak areas of all positive peaks using integration, where the peak areas of IID-C4-QL, IID-C4- DMAP, and IID-C4-Bpy are all smaller than that of JGB.

The three IID-QAS with the best inhibitory performance (better than JGB) were selected to test the efect of concentration change on the inhibition ability and compared with the cyclic voltammetry curves of JGB as shown in Fig. 4. In summary, five isoindigo quaternary ammonium salt derivatives were synthesized in this paper using isoindigo as the parent body to explore their application as levelers in PCB through-hole plating. The results of electrochemical experiments show that five IID-QAS exhibit diferent degrees of copper deposition inhibition, among which IID-C4-QL has the best inhibition performance and strong convective adsorption ability. Theoretical calculations and molecular simulations show that IID-C4-QL has the strongest adsorption capacity among the five compounds. In the actual copper plating test, the highest TP value of 120.77% can be obtained with the addition of IID-C4-QL at 1.5 ppm, and the SEM results show that IID-C4-QL can obtain the flattest layer at the same concentration, while the addition of more than 1.5 ppm will compete with SPS for adsorption, resulting in the ‘‘cavity phenomenon’’ and decrease of the TP value of the layer. XRD results show that the addition of IID-C4-QL transforms the crystallographic orientation of the copper layer from (220) to the most stable (111) crystallographic plane. The present work enriches the study of isoindigo on this field and exploits the great potential and scope of isoindigo derivatives for acid plating applications.

Plating additives utilized in acid copper sulfate plating predominantly encompass inhibitors, accelerators, and levelers, each playing pivotal roles in the copper plating process through distinct mechanisms.<sup>12,13</sup> Inhibitors form a polymer film on the plating surface, curtailing copper deposition, commonly comprising poly ether chain compounds like polyethylene glycol (PEG).<sup>14,15</sup> Accelerators expedite copper deposition in conjunction with chloride ions, typically represented by sulfonate compounds such as sodium polydithiodipropane sulphonate (SPS).<sup>16</sup> Among these additives, levelers assume paramount importance and are extensively researched for their ability to selectively impede copper deposition during plating, thus optimizing copper filling in vias and achieving a flat copper layer.<sup>17</sup>–<sup>19</sup> Presently, common levelers predominantly consist of organic dye molecules like Janus Green B (JGB) and DPP.<sup>20,21</sup> However, limitations such as planarity issues afecting adsorption performance and incomplete understanding of underlying mechanisms highlight the need for further research in this area.<sup>22,23</sup>

The adsorption capacity of quaternary ammonium salt leveler molecules primarily relies on their positively charged regions. It is proposed that synthesizing quaternary ammonium salts from nitrogen-containing heterocyclic molecules with conjugated structures could enhance adsorption eficiency, thereby improving the leveling efect. Quinacridone quaternary ammonium salts were synthesized using N-methylimidazole, quinoline, and 4-dimethyl aminopyridine. Furthermore, methylation of the quaternary ammonium salt derived from 4-dimethylaminopyridine was conducted to introduce four charges, aiming to investigate the impact of charge density on leveling eficacy. Thus, this study involved the synthesis of quinacridone aromatic heterocyclic quaternary ammonium salts, as depicted in Fig. 1, and elucidated their mechanism. The inhibition efectiveness of pigment-derived levelers depends on their charge dispersion and adsorption onto electrode surfaces. In this chapter, we employ density-functional theory (DFT) calculations and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to explore how four quinacridone aromatic heterocyclic quaternary ammonium salt molecules interact with copper surfaces. By analyzing energy band gaps, electron densities, and adsorption behaviors, we aim to understand the diferences in inhibition eficacy among these molecules.

The electrostatic potential (ESP) for the four compounds was calculated and plotted in Fig. 7. The dark blue region signifies the positive charge-rich area of the molecule, which tends to adsorb onto the copper plate surface, aiding in charge dispersion to enhance cathodic electrochemical polarization. N-methylimidazole, with the strongest alkalinity, exhibits the highest positive charge after quaternary ammonium salt formation, reaching an ESP of 0.211 eV. This indicates stronger adsorption capability and charge accommodation ability. Quinoline and 4-dimethylaminopyridine, both pyridine derivatives, form large O-systems due to benzene ring and pyridine O-electron overlap. Quinoline’s alkalinity is slightly lower than that of pyridine, reflected in its ESP of 0.189 eV. The ESP of the quaternary ammonium salt of 4-dimethylaminopyridine is at 0.183 eV. Upon methylation of 4-dimethylaminopyridine to obtain 4-trimethylaminopyridine salt, an additional positive charge is introduced. This significantly increases the electrostatic potential to 0.339 eV. However, with two positive charge centers, the charge dispersion is relatively dispersed, and molecular stability may be compromised. This could explain why $\mathrm { D C Q A \mathrm { - } C _ { 8 } \mathrm { - } D M A P \mathrm { - } M e }$ exhibited poor inhibition performance in electrochemical tests.

Molecular dynamics simulation is employed to assess the adsorption state of additives on copper crystal surfaces, determining their adsorption dificulty through calculated binding energies. In Fig. 8, quaternary ammonium salt molecules exhibit non-flat adsorption on the copper plate due to intramolecular charge repulsion and site resistance. However, $\mathrm { D C Q A - C _ { 8 } \mathrm { - M I } }$ achieves nearly flat spreading on the copper plate, with its quinacridone parent partially parallel to surface copper atoms. This optimal adsorption distinguishes $\mathrm { D C Q A \mathrm { - } C _ { 8 } \mathrm { - } M I } ,$ while $\operatorname { D C Q A - C _ { 8 } - Q I }$ also demonstrates good adsorption due to its larger quinacridone ring, despite hindered flat spreading. Conversely, $\mathrm { D C Q A  – C _ { 8 } – D M A P }$ and $\mathrm { D C Q A \mathrm { - } C _ { 8 } \mathrm { - } D M A P \mathrm { - } M e }$ display chaotic adsorption states, hindered by increased site resistance from the dimethylamino substituent on the pyridine ring. This limits their charge adsorption ability, particularly for $\mathrm { D C Q A \mathrm { - } C _ { 8 } \mathrm { - } D M A P \mathrm { - } M e }$ , which has the most positive charges, resulting in the weakest inhibition efect.

# Study of 5‑Alkynylpyrimidines as Cobalt Superfilling Inhibitors

ABSTRACT: Electrodeposition technology is the key core technology for achieving micro/nanoscale interconnection in high-end chip manufacturing. Recently, cobalt interconnect structures have been the ideal choice for constructing electronic pathways in process nodes below 14 nm due to the fact that cobalt has a smaller electron mean free path compared to copper; thus, studying the electroplating filling behavior of cobalt in micronano scale space has become a hot topic in the field of chip manufacturing. In this article, an electroplating solution containing a new 5-alkynylpyrimidine (5-EP) as an inhibitor is designed for electrochemical tests, including cyclic voltammetry and linear sweep voltammetry. The results indicate that the 5-EP significantly inhibits cobalt electrodeposition. The change in the nucleation mode of cobalt in an electroplating solution with the inhibitor (5-EP) was revealed by chronoamperometry, where cobalt atoms nucleate in a three-dimensional continuous manner instead of three-dimensional instantaneous nucleation. In situ enhanced Raman spectroscopy is used to further analyze the adsorption of the inhibitor (5-EP) molecules on the cobalt surface during the electroplating process from a spectroscopic perspective. The energy gap value of the additive molecule obtained through quantum chemical calculations is $\begin{array} { r } { \triangle E = E _ { \mathrm { L U M O } } - \bar { E _ { \mathrm { H O M O } } } = 3 . 3 0 2 ~ \mathrm { e V } , } \end{array}$ indicating that the additive molecule has high reactivity and higher adsorption strength at the metal interface. The calculated electrostatic potential (ESP) values of the molecule range from a minimum of −47.29 kJ/mol to a maximum of 70.89 kJ/mol. Lower ESP values imply higher electron density. Molecular dynamics simulations calculate the adsorption energy of the additive molecule (5-EP) on Co(100) to be −133.96 kcal/mol, indicating that the 5-EP molecule has good adsorption capability. Electroplating experiments reveal that the addition of 6 ppm 5-EP to the plating solution enables defect-free filling of blind holes. Finally, it is also revealed by characterization tests (scanning electron microscopy/atomic force microscopy/X-ray difraction) that the inhibitor (5-EP) efectively reduces the surface roughness of the cobalt coating and, meantime, promotes the preferential growth of cobalt along the 100 and 110 crystal planes.

Damascene copper plating technology has remained the best choice for metal interconnects in logic chips and memory chips.<sup>1</sup> As semiconductor processes advance toward 10 nm and below, the use of copper as a conductor material begins to encounter issues with RC delay, which severely impacts the interconnect performance of chips. This has led to bottlenecks in process technology at the 10- and 7-nanometer nodes,<sup>2,3</sup> necessitating the search for new alternative interconnect materials. Researchers have found that metals such as Co, Ni, Mo, and Nb show greater potential than Cu.<sup>4</sup> However, when considering other parameters such as process and material costs, only Co is highlighted as a promising material. It has been reported that Co has already been used in the contact interconnect layers at the 10 nm node and is also considered suitable for use as a conductor in higher metal layers.<sup>5</sup> Compared to copper, cobalt has a shorter mean free path for electrons and a higher melting point. At the nanoscale, cobalt interconnects exhibit minimal size efects and superior resistance to electromigration.<sup>6</sup> The deposition quality of chip interconnect materials has a crucial impact on the final performance of the chip, directly afecting the chip’s yield, reliability, and stability. This places higher demands on the chip interconnect process. Electroplating technology is the primary technique for forming micro and nano interconnect structures.<sup>7</sup> In this complex process, additives play a critical role in regulating the deposition quality and behavior of metals.<sup>8</sup> Similar to the traditional Damascene copper interconnect process, the cobalt interconnect plating system also requires additives that can increase the metal deposition overpotential to achieve void-free superfilling in micro and nano structures.<sup>9</sup> The cobalt superfilling additives reported to date often contain unsaturated carbon bonds, nitrogencontaining functional groups, or a combination of both. The nitrogen-containing functional groups exist in the forms of amines $( - \mathrm { N H } _ { 2 } , \mathsf { \Gamma } - \mathrm { N H } )$ , oxime groups $( - \mathrm { C = N - O H } )$ and nitrogen-containing heterocycles. Utilizing the S-shaped negative diferential resistance (S-NDR) mechanism for ultraconformal deposition, Mofat et al.<sup>10</sup> observed bottom up filling of cobalt in 8 μm × 56 μm silicon through-holes. They achieved this by utilizing polyethylenimine (PEI) as an inhibitor. Jungkyu Kang et al.<sup>11,12</sup> found that void-free filling could be achieved even in low aspect ratio trenches in the presence of benzimidazole (BZI) and 2-mercaptobenzimida zole (MBI). An et al. demonstrated the potential application of nitrogen-containing organic heterocyclic molecules, nitro blue tetrazolium chloride (NBT)<sup>13</sup> and malachite green (MG),<sup>14</sup> as inhibitors. Their research found that the heterocyclic structures of the additive molecules preferentially adsorb on the cathode surface, serving as a mechanism to inhibit cobalt deposition. Huang et al.<sup>15−17</sup> utilized electrochemical methods such as EQCM and cyclic voltammetry to investigate the inhibitory properties of oxime-containing compounds, including cyclo hexanedione dioxime (CHD), furandione dioxime (FD), and dimethylglyoxime (DMG), on cobalt electrodeposition. To meet the high-performance demands of current electronic devices, copper electroplating in blind vias must achieve flawless filling without cracks and gaps. This typically involves superfilling or botom-up filling techniques, where superfilling refers to a deposition process during electroplating in which the copper deposition rate at the botom of the blind vias is significantly higher than at the opening and surface, thereby achieving perfect filling of the vias [5]. To accomplish superfilling, an acidic copper sulfate system is com monly used in industrial applications. In this system, the choice of additives is crucial, primarily including accelerators, suppressors, and leveling agents. Accelerators, usually sulfur-containing organic compounds, adsorb on the electrode surface, refine the copper crystal structure, and promote copper nucleation. Their primary function is to combine with chloride ions to achieve depolarization, thus increasing the cathodic current density [6–9]. The most widely studied and used accelerators include SPS and MPS [10, 11]. Sup pressors, such as polyether polymers (e.g., PEG and PPG) [12–14], mainly inhibit the deposition of copper during electroplating by adsorbing on the surface of the plated parts and preventing the difusion of ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ [15–17]. In systems containing both accelerators and suppressors, the role of leveling agents is indispensable. Leveling agents typically include certain nitrogencontaining organic compounds [18, 19], such as the dye-type leveling agents JGB [20], DB [18], ABPV [21, 22], and heterocyclic non-dye leveling agents such as 2-amino-4-methylbenzothiazole [23] (AMBT) and 2-mercaptopyridine [24, 25] (2-MP). Their main func tion is to work synergistically with suppressors to inhibit copper deposition on the surface of the plated parts, optimize current density distribution, enhance filling eficiency, and thereby prevent premature hole sealing that leads to voids [25–30]. Although the most efective leveling agents are often commercial secrets, high costs and poor environmental friendliness in the market make the development of new leveling agents both time-consuming and labor-intensive. Consequently, to date, only a few superfilling leveling agents have been specifically reported [31–33].

In this study, the electrochemical performance of additives was evaluated using a CHI 760e electrochemical workstation. The employed testing methods included cyclic voltammetry (CV), linear sweep voltammetry (LSV), and galvanostatic measurement (GM). All electrochemical tests were conducted within a threeelectrode system, schematically illustrated in Fig. 2, where the working electrode was a 3-mm-diameter platinum rotating disk electrode (Pt-RDE), the reference electrode was a saturated mercurous sulfate electrode (SMSE), and the counter electrode was a platinum wire. The electrolyte base plating solution (VMS) comprised $\mathrm { C u S O } _ { 4 } { \cdot } 5 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ at 220 g/L, ${ \mathrm { H } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { S O } } _ { 4 }$ at 60 $\mathrm { g / L } ,$ and chloride ions at 60 mg/L, with the testing temperature controlled at $2 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ using a water bath thermostat. In this research, bis-(3-sulphopropyl) disulfide (SPS) was used as an accelerator, polyethylene glycol (PEG, $\mathrm { M W } = 1 0 , 0 0 0 )$ as a suppressor, and the synthesized CDT as a leveling agent. The experimental potential range for cyclic voltammetry (CV) was set from − 0.6 to 0.1 V, with a scanning rate fixed at 10 mV/s. For linear sweep voltammetry (LSV), the experimental potential range was from − 0.4 to − 0.8 V, with the scanning rate also set at 10 mV/s. In the galvanostatic measurement (GM), the current density was fixed at $1 . 5 \mathrm { A } / \mathrm { d } \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 } ,$ , and additives were sequentially injected into the base plating solution for measurement over a duration of 3000 s.

Based on the research and analysis presented, it can be inferred that CDT can serve as a leveling agent for micro-via filling in PCBs. To evaluate the filling efficacy of CDT as a leveling agent, electroplating experiments were conducted at various concentrations of CDT and compared with a commercial JGB formulation. Figure 11 shows the cross-sectional optical microscopy images of the micro-vias after electroplating. As depicted in Fig. 11a, without the addition of a leveling agent, a significant void is observed at the botom of the via, resulting from uneven current density due to varying convection intensities. With the injection of 1 mg/L CDT, the filling performance of the micro-vias notably improves. As illustrated in Figs. 11b–f, the optimal micro-via filling performance occurs at a CDT concentration of 5 mg/L, consistent with the previous electrochemical testing results. When the CDT concentration is increased to 6 mg/L, the filling rate decreases, and the performance deteriorates, indicating that there is a specific operational concentration range for the leveling agent. If the concentration is too low, the inhibitory efect is insuficient, leading to void formation. Conversely, if the concen tration is too high, it disrupts the balance among the additives, resulting in poor filling performance. The JGB electroplating formula, commonly used in the industry, serves as a benchmark for comparing the filling performance of newly discovered leveling agents. Figure 11h shows the filling efect using the commercial JGB electroplating solution, which is inferior to the efect achieved with 5 mg/L CDT. The JGB formula results in some concavity and does not completely fill the blind vias, whereas CDT achieves superfilling of micro-vias, demonstrating its potential as an efective leveling agent.

The influence of different concentrations of CDT on the surface morphology of copper is depicted in Fig. 12. In the absence of CDT in the plating solution, the copper plating surface exhibits a rough, blocky, and distinctly porous appearance. Conversely, compared to the CDT-free condition, the addition of varying concentrations of CDT to the plating solution significantly improves the surface morphology of the copper plating (Figs. 12b–h). The formation of smooth planes is due to the modification of the plating layer after adding CDT, which initiates crystal refinement. However, when the CDT concentration is increased to 5 mg/L, a proliferation of small blocky crystals appears on the copper surface, becoming denser with increasing concentrations of CDT. These results indicate that CDT demonstrates its leveling capability efectively within a certain concentration range, but as the concentration of the leveling agent increases, the synergistic interactions among the additives are disrupted. Similar results have been reported in copper electrodepositing studies [18, 21].

In summary, we have selected the nitrogen-heterocyclic compound CDT as an electroplating leveling agent for copper micro-via filling. The synthesis of CDT was successfully confirmed by infrared, hydrogen nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, and gel permeation chromatography results. Quantum chemical simulations suggest that CDT possesses the potential to occupy metal vacant orbitals for adsorption. Moreover, molecular dynamics simulations indicate that CDT exhibits strong affinity for copper surfaces. Electrochemical tests revealed that the optimal working concentration of CDT is 5 mg/L. Chronopotentiometric measurements further demonstrated that CDT can synergistically suppress copper deposition when combined with other additives, exhibiting a potential diference as high as 20 mV, which indicates its strong inhibitory efect on copper electrodeposition. Electroplating tests show that the best plating results occur at a concentration of 5 mg/L, consistent with electrochemical findings. Field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) results showed that CDT can refine copper grain structures within an appropriate concentration range; however, when the concentration exceeds the optimal level, crystal agglomeration reoccurs. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) confirmed the efective adsorption of CDT on the copper surface, and the strong interaction between them provides a foundation for the suppression of copper deposition. Collectively, our research conclusively proves that CDT is a promising leveling agent for copper micro-via filling, providing theoretical guidance for the discovery and improvement of electroplating technologies for micro-via filling.

In this paper, five coumarin-based quaternary ammonium salts, including a new highly efficient through-hole (TH) electroplating leveler, were synthesized from environmentally harmless coumarin compounds. The inhib itory properties of five coumarin-based quaternary ammonium salts were tested by electrochemical method, leading to the selection of the optimal leveler (C2). The adsorption capacity, adsorption state and adsorption sites of different coumarin-based quaternary ammonium salts on copper surface were systematically analyzed, and the reasons for the different inhibition capacity of five coumarin-based quaternary ammonium salts with different molecular structures were explained. The effect of C2 content on throwing power (TP) was studied, when C2 content was only 0.6 ppm, TP value was greater than 100 %. The adsorption behavior of C2 on copper cathode and the interaction between C2 and other additives were studied by the galvanostatic measurements (GMs). SEM and XRD tests were conducted to analyze the effects of different amounts of C2 on the copper plating surface.

With the continuous improvement of the modern electronic indus try’s requirements for electronic components, the demand for electronic components such as electronic chips that achieve miniaturization and high efficiency has also increased. The realization of high-density interconnection between printed circuit boards (PCBs) through micropore connection is an important means to realize the miniaturization of electronic products, so as to obtain more excellent electrical conductivity and space performance [1–3]. Acid copper electroplating is a key technology for copper interconnects in through-holes (THs), and it is also an indispensable technology in the manufacturing process of PCB. In order to obtain a flat and smooth plating layer and efficient TH filling, electroplating additives need to be added to the electroplating solution [4,5].

Electroplating additives are generally divided into inhibitors (generally polyethylene glycol and other polyether compounds, such as polyethylene glycol, polypropylene glycol [6,7]), accelerators (generally containing S–H bonds or S–S sulfonate compounds, such as sodium 3,3′-dithiodipropane sulfonate, bis-(sodium sulfoethyl)-disulfide [8,9]) and levelers (generally N-containing compounds, such as Janus Green B, diketopyrrolopyrrole [10–16]).

In the process of copper plating, through the interaction of different plating additives, the microhole can be overfilled. In the current research on electroplating additives, electroplating levelers have attracted much attention due to their irreplaceable properties. The leveler is mainly adsorbed on the surface of TH and inhibits the deposition of copper ions on the surface of TH, but has less inhibition on the deposition of copper ions inside TH, so as to achieve the effect of conductive copper interconnection or bottom-up copper electroplating [17–19]. The current research on levelers mainly includes the research of new leveler molecules (small molecule compounds [20–22], quaternary ammonium compounds [23–26] and macromolecular polymers [27,28]), interaction of different electroplating additives [29] and the effect of leveler concentration on filling efficiency and copper electroplating surface morphology [30]. Among them, quaternary ammonium salts have received more attention as leveler due to their superior leveling performance. For example, Myung JunKim [31] synthesized choline-based quaternary ammonium salt levelers and used them in TSV (Through Silicon Via) electrodeposition copper, Jinge Lv [32] designed and synthesized three water-soluble naphthalimide derivatives (NPI) and used them as levelers for microporous electrodeposition. Van Quy Dinh [33] used sulfonated diallyl dimethyl ammonium bromide copol ymer to fill the TSV bottom-up electrodeposition for 5 min to achieve no gaps. These studies have shown that quaternary ammonium compounds have good application prospects in the field of electroplating levelers, but it is still a difficult task to develop electroplating levelers with small additive amount, good leveling effect and environmental friendliness.

In our previous work, we found that the large plane quaternary ammonium salt leveler has more efficient leveling performance than the general quaternary ammonium salts, when the concentration is 0.2 ppm (0.278 μmol/L), a very efficient leveling effect can be achieved [34]. Combining the previous work, and the working principle of the leveler −- the leveler molecules are adsorbed on the copper surface during the electrodeposition process to inhibit the electrodeposition of copper ions [14,34,35], we speculate that $^ { 4 , }$ 4-bipyridine can be used to connect rigid planar molecules to synthesize larger coplanar quaternary ammonium salts. If such large flat molecules can be adsorbed on copper surfaces, they have the potential to be effective levelers [15,34]. As a common natural product, coumarins (Fig. 1) are planar compounds with two conjugated six-membered rings, and its $^ { 7 }$ position is relatively electron-rich, indicating that its $^ { 7 }$ position is prone to electrophilic substitution reaction. When a hydroxyl group is present, it is easy to undergo substitution reaction with dibromoalkane, thereby further reacting with $^ { 4 , }$ 4-bipyridine to obtain a coumarin-based quaternary ammonium salt.

Herein, five coumarin-based quaternary ammonium salts were synthesized by connecting coumarin-based compounds with pyridine-like compounds, including the first synthesis of large plane dicoumarinbased pyridinium quaternary ammonium salt C2 through a four-step reaction. The results of cyclic voltammetry (CV) test and polarization curve test show that C2 can be used as the preferred leveler. The band gap and electron cloud density distribution of five coumarin-based quaternary ammonium salts were obtained by quantum chemistry calculation and molecular dynamics simulation, in order to study the relationship between the molecular structure and inhibitory ability of these levelers. The experimental results of TH copper plating show that in a certain range, the content of C2 has a positive correlation with the TP value of TH electroplating, and can make the surface morphology of copper plating layer more smooth, and optimize the orientation of the crystal surface of copper particles. GMs results show that C2 can exert inhibition alone and has strong convection-dependent adsorption (CDA) behavior. In summary, this study synthesized five coumarin-based quaternary ammonium salts and, for the first time, investigated their application as novel electroplating levelers in acid copper plating. Electrochemical measurements were used to analyze the copper plating inhibition ability of five coumarin-based quaternary ammonium salts, leveler C2 with double coumarin structure had the strongest inhibition performance. Quantum chemical calculation and MD simulation show that leveler C2 has the strongest adsorption capacity and the most adsorption sites on copper surface, which is the reason why C2 has the strongest inhibition ability. TH copper plating results show that the leveler C2 has good leveling performance, only need 0.6 ppm addition, can get 103.36 % through-hole TP value. The interaction between C2 and other additives and the mechanism of action were further explored by GMs test. The results of SEM and XRD show that the leveler C2 can make the surface of the copper plating layer smoother and optimize the orientation of the copper crystallographic plane. In this work, a new coumarin compound was synthesized for the first time and used as an electroplating leveler, which expanded the application range of coumarin compounds and the design field of molecular structure of electroplating leveler. It is hoped that it can be used as the basis for the development of efficient leveler molecules in the future.

Abstract: Levelers are indispensable additives for achieving void-free, bottom-up superconformal copper filling of microvias. Establishing the molecular-level correlation between leveler structure and performance is therefore essential to the continued advancement of microelectronic copper-plating technology. Herein, nitro blue tetrazolium chloride (NBT) is identified as an efficient leveler for copper microvia superfilling. A multiscale strategy—combining electrochemical measurements, X-ray photoelectron spec troscopy (XPS), density functional theory (DFT) calculations, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations—is employed to elucidate the action mechanism of NBT and pinpoint its electroactive sites. Electrochemical tests show that NBT markedly suppresses copper deposition and, together with polyethylene glycol (PEG), effectively resists competitive ad sorption by bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS), thereby enhancing the microvia superfilling performance of the PEG–SPS–NBT additive system. DFT results reveal that the nitro groups and tetrazolium rings constitute the primary adsorption centers on the copper surface; the nitro groups additionally strengthen intermolecular interactions between NBT and PEG. MD simulations further confirm that NBT anchors onto the Cu(111) surface predominantly through these $\Nu { \cal O } _ { 2 }$ groups and the tetrazolium ring, while co-adsorbed PEG enhances the overall adsorption strength of NBT. The electroplating experiment demonstrates that NBT can act as an effective leveler for microvia superfilling. Moreover, XPS analyses further confirm the synergistic co-adsorption of NBT and PEG and verify that the $\Nu { \cal O } _ { 2 }$ groups and tetrazolium rings are the dominant adsorption sites of NBT. Collectively, the electroplating, XPS, electrochemical, DFT, and MD findings clarify the structure–activity relationship of NBT and provide rational guidelines for designing next-generation copper-plating levelers.

Industrial practice predominantly relies on organic additive systems to locally regulate the deposition rate for achieving superfilling of microvias. In two-component systems the competitive adsorption of a suppressor and an accelerator is often sufficient for sub-100 nm Damascene features [7–9]; larger microvias, however, require a third component—a leveler— to suppress copper deposition at high-current-density sites (feature mouths and protrusions), thereby ensuring void-free bottom-up growth and surface planarization [10–12]. Among the numerous levelers reported, Janus Green B (JGB) is the most classic, as it can achieve not only superfilling in microvias [13] but also high throwing power (TP) electroplated in through-holes [14]. Additionally, previous studies have demonstrated that the azo group and the positively charged quaternary-ammonium group are the primary active functional groups in JGB [13,15].

However, growing evidence indicates that, beyond the classic active groups— positively charged quaternary-ammonium and azo groups—auxiliary modification groups such as electronegative substituents or heteroaromatic rings can markedly reinforce leveler adsorption [20], alter the diffusion ability of molecules [21,22], and enhance synergism with other additives [23]. Dow et al. compared JGB with its derivative Diamond Black (DB), revealing significant electrochemical differences despite the two molecules differing by only a single peripheral functional substituent [24]. Similarly, Wang et al. observed that Safranine T (ST), which lacks several peripheral functional substituents present in JGB, exhibited significantly reduced through-hole throwing power compared to JGB [25], whereas Zhu et al. restored microvia superfilling by introducing hydroxyl (-OH) groups into ST [20]. Therefore, using density functional theory (DFT) calculations and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to unravel how individual functional groups dictate adsorption energetics and electron distribution is very necessary. For example, many research groups have used DFT and MD simulations to examine how different modifying functional groups affect the leveling performance of tetrazolium derivatives, because the tetrazolium scaffold is an excellent leveler backbone: the tetrazolium ring carries an intrinsic positive charge comparable to that of quaternary-ammonium groups, while offering high structural stability and low cost. Lei et al. used DFT calculations to show that introducing N/O heteroatom substituents alters the electronic structure of tetrazolium derivatives, increases their electron activity, and thereby markedly improves microvia superfilling [26]. Similarly, combined DFT and MD studies by Wei et al. revealed that electronegative groups such as $\Nu { \cal O } _ { 2 }$ and I redistribute the electrostatic potential of the tetrazolium backbone, create additional chemically active sites, and strengthen intermolecular interactions, ultimately enhancing microvia filling [23]. In the same vein, Teng et al. [27] combined DFT with experiments to elucidate how various tetrazolium derivatives interact synergistically with a propylene-oxide–ethylene-oxide–propylene-oxide (PEP) triblock copolymer; highly electronegative substituents were found to promote stronger cooperation with the suppressor PEP and thus further boost superfilling performance.

As is well known, nitro blue tetrazolium chloride (NBT), a commercially available tetrazolium dye, has demonstrated excellent performance as a leveler in through-hole copper filling [28–30]. In contrast, blind microvias present a far more challenging environment: with only one opening, electrolyte circulation is severely restricted, the diffusion layer thickens, and a pronounced ohmic and activation overpotential gradient develops. These factors make void-free filling in blind microvias significantly more difficult than in through-holes. To date, however, the suitability of NBT for blind-microvia superfilling has not been reported, nor has its structure–performance relationship been elucidated—an omission that limits the molecular-level insight into tetrazolium-based levelers and the rational design of cost-effective additives. Accordingly, NBT was chosen as the leveler in this study to assess its effectiveness in copper superfilling of microvias, of which the molecular structure is shown in Figure 1. By combining electrochemical analyses, electroplating experiments, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), MD simulations, and DFT calculations, we elucidate how NBT’s NO<sub>2</sub> groups and tetrazolium ring govern the adsorption on Cu(111) and synergism with PEG and other species. The insights provide rational guidelines for engineering the next-generation, robust, and economical levelers.

All quantum-chemical calculations were carried out with Gaussian 09, using the B3LYP functional. Geometry optimizations for the isolated NBT molecule, a PEG fragment, and the ${ \mathrm { N B T } } { \mathrm { - } } { \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ complex were carried out with the def2-SVP basis set, and single point energies were refined at the def2-TZVP level to improve accuracy. Electrochemical measurements were carried out to investigate the effect of NBT on cathodic polarization, as shown in Figure 2. From the GM curves at 1000 rpm, it can be seen that injecting just 10 ppm NBT immediately shifts the electrode potential negatively by approximately 160 mV, demonstrating that NBT strongly inhibits ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ reduction (Figure 2a). With further increases in NBT concentration, the cathodic potential shift becomes more pronounced, indicating that NBT’s inhibition strength is concentration-dependent. Moreover, pronounced electrode-potential oscillations occur at 100 rpm but are largely attenuated at 1000 rpm, indicating that adsorbed NBT forms labile complexes with ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { + } / { \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ whose stability is governed by $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ mass transport rather than by NBT diffusion.
