To elucidate the cooperative action of NBT with the suppressor PEG, GM and CV were performed (Figure 3). The addition of 200 ppm PEG alone shifts the potential by approximately 210 mV in the negative direction (Figure 3a), reflecting formation of a dense $\mathrm { P E G } / \mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ adlayer that impedes ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ access to the cathode [37]. Upon introducing 10 ppm NBT into the PEG bath, the potential shifts an additional ∼36 mV negative at 1000 rpm, indicating synergistic co-adsorption of NBT and PEG and the formation of a more compact suppressor film (PEG–NBT) [27]. Because NBT adsorption is diffusionlimited (at low concentration), its inhibitory effect is substantially weaker under low convection (100 rpm) than high convection (1000 rpm), resulting in a large difference potential $\Delta \mathfrak { n } _ { 1 }$ of about 30 mV and underscoring the mass-transport sensitivity of the process. Increasing the NBT concentration in the PEG bath further enhances cathodic polarization. The potential difference $\Delta \mathfrak { n }$ between 100 rpm and 1000 rpm gradually narrows. Importantly, ∆η remains positive, indicating that under these conditions the system transitions from NBT-diffusion control to being governed by the adsorption/desorption behavior of the PEG–NBT suppressor film. However, at high NBT concentrations, pronounced electrodepotential oscillations still occur, reflecting that the denser PEG–NBT adlayer forms stronger complexes with $\mathrm { C u } ^ { + } / \mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ and it remains sensitive to convection.

The CV profiles further validate the strong synergistic suppression by PEG and NBT (Figure 3b). Compared with the PEG-only baseline, the onset of copper deposition shifts progressively negative as NBT concentration increases, confirming enhanced inhibition. Unlike NBT alone (Figure 2b), the PEG–NBT curves display a large $\Delta \mathrm { E _ { h y s } }$ value that largens with rising NBT concentration, while the $\mathrm { E _ { r e c o v e r } }$ remains essentially constant across all NBT concentrations—indicating the formation of a potential-sensitive PEG–NBT complex film. Higher NBT concentrations produce a denser suppressor layer that is more resistant to breakdown by electrode potential. Taken together, the PEG–NBT suppressor exhibits pronounced sensitivity to both convection and potential—properties that favor PEG–NBT-selective coverage at the microvia mouth rather than microvia bottom and promote void-free superfilling. This is due to the fact that the PEG–NBT concentration is relatively low at microvia bottom (weak convection) compared to the microvia mouth (strong convection), making the suppressor film at microvia bottom more susceptible to potential-induced collapse and thereby facilitating ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ reduction. Conversely, at the microvia mouth the higher local PEG–NBT coverage resists breakdown and, once collapsed, rapidly re-forms, ensuring sustained suppression [38,39].

Although NBT and PEG exhibit electrochemical behaviors that facilitate the superfilling of microvias, the achievement of efficient microvia superfilling electroplating often necessitates the synergistic effect of SPS. Specifically, SPS focuses on accelerating copper deposition at the bottom of the microvias, while PEG–NBT is responsible for suppressing copper deposition in the microvias’ entrance region. GM for the PEG–SPS–NBT additive system (Figure 4a) further confirmed the distinct yet synergistic functions of each component. After the electrode-potential drop caused by 200 ppm PEG, injection of 1 ppm SPS partially breaks through the PEG– $- \mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ film, producing a marked depolarization [40]. Subsequent addition of 10 ppm NBT immediately reverses this trend: the potential shifts to values even more negative than those recorded with PEG alone, indicating that the PEG– NBT co-adsorbate effectively resists displacement by SPS and restores a robust suppressor layer. The differences between the depolarization curves at 100 rpm and 1000 rpm indicate that the system still exhibits a certain sensitivity to convection $( \Delta \mathfrak { n } _ { 4 } , \Delta \mathfrak { n } _ { 5 } , \Delta \mathfrak { n } _ { 6 } > 0 )$ , which is consistent with the characteristics of PEG–NBT adsorption being diffusion-limited.

The CV curves validated the observations obtained from the GM curves, as shown in Figure 4b. Relative to the PEG–SPS baseline, increasing NBT concentration again shifts the copper deposition onset to more negative potentials and produces a larger $\Delta \mathrm { E _ { h y s } }$ value, while the $\mathrm { E _ { r e c o v e r } }$ remains unchanged across all NBT concentrations. This behavior indicates that higher NBT concentrations generate a denser PEG–NBT suppressor film that not only resists breakdown by applied potential but also effectively withstands SPS attack. Collectively, these electrochemical features indicate that the PEG–NBT layer remains strongly adsorbed at the microvia mouth (as discussed above in Figure 3b)—blocking SPS there—and confines accelerator action to the convection-limited via the bottom, thereby achieving void-free, bottom-up superfilling.

Molecular electrostatic potential (ESP), defined as the potential energy experienced by a unit positive test charge in the electrostatic field of a molecule, is a convenient descriptor for analyzing intermolecular electrostatic interactions. As illustrated in Figure 6a,b, the lowpotential regions (blue) lie on the nitro groups (Nitro/Nitro<sup>′</sup>), whereas the high-potential regions (red) appear mainly on the tetrazolium rings themselves $( \mathrm { { T } } z / \mathrm { { T } } z ^ { \prime } )$ and on the methoxy-substituted phenyl rings (Ph3-Meo/Ph3<sup>′</sup>-Meo<sup>′</sup>). Because the nitro groups are strongly electronegative, its inclusion redistributes charge and makes the ESP surface more symmetric (Figure 6b), thereby improving the ability of NBT to interact electrostatically with the copper surface or with additives such as PEG [44].

To fully predict a leveler’s performance, one must assess not only its electronic active sites but also its interactions with other species and their corresponding adsorption sites. Accordingly, DFT calculations were carried out to investigate NBT’s interactions with $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ ions and with the suppressor PEG. Atom in Molecules (AIM) and interaction region indicator (IRI) calculations were carried out for the ${ \mathrm { N B T } } { \mathrm { - } } { \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ complex, while the NBT–PEG interaction was analyzed with the independent-gradient model based on Hirshfeld parti tion (IGMH), as shown in Figure 7. As shown in Figure $^ { 7 } \mathbf { a } ,$ the shortest contact between $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ and NBT is the Cu–N bond to the tetrazolium nitrogen (1.994 Å). The Cu–O distance to the methoxy group is longer (2.177 $\mathring \mathrm { A } )$ , indicating that the Cu–N interaction is stronger than the Cu–O one. To evaluate the bond nature, we calculated the bond-critical-point (BCP) parameters (Table 1). For both Cu–N and Cu–O bonds, the electron density at the BCP (ρ ) is below 0.10 a.u. and the Laplacian of electron density $( \nabla ^ { 2 } \rho _ { \mathrm { B C P } } )$ value is positive, showing that the two bonds for Cu–N and Cu–O are ionic bonds [47,48]. However, only the Cu–N bond has negative energy density $\left( \mathrm { H } _ { \mathrm { B C P } } \right)$ and negative potential energy density (Vr ), which confirms that the Cu–N bond is the stronger bond [49]. IRI analysis (Figure 7b) reveals blue isosurfaces between ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ and the tetrazolium nitrogen, as well as between ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ and the methoxy oxygen, indicating strong Cu–N and Cu–O interactions. The two-dimensional IRI map (Figure 7c) further supports these observations, confirming robust coordination between NBT and $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ ions. These findings indicate that NBT coordi nates predominantly with ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ via the nitrogen atom of the tetrazolium ring, forming a strong ionic bond that retards ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ reduction. This selective coordination promotes NBT adsorption at Cu-rich sites—such as microvia mouths or cathode protrusions—thereby efficiently inhibiting local deposition.

An effective leveler must not only coordinate with $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ but also work synergistically with suppressors such as PEG to further enhance cathodic polarization. DFT calculations (Figure 7d) reveal that NBT–PEG interactions are dominated by van der Waals forces and a key hydrogen bond between the nitro oxygen of NBT and a hydroxyl hydrogen of PEG. The presence of this hydrogen bond drives the PEG–NBT binding energy to as high as −30.98 kcal/mol, significantly exceeding the −15.19 kcal/mol reported for the INT–PEG system (Wei et al. [23]) and the −26.47 kcal/mol for HPTT–PEP (Teng et al. [27]). The strong NBT–PEG affinity underpins the pronounced synergistic suppression observed electrochemically and underscores the pivotal role of the $\Nu { \cal O } _ { 2 }$ groups in both reinforcing NBT chemisorption on copper and enhancing co-adsorption with ${ \mathrm { P E G } } ,$ thus improving overall leveling efficiency.

Peaks for the methoxy phenyl ring $( \mathrm { P h } 3 { - } \mathrm { M e o } / \mathrm { P h } 3 ^ { \prime } { - } \mathrm { M e o } ^ { \prime } )$ and the remaining fragments appear beyond $6 \mathring { \mathrm { A } } ,$ implying only weak van der Waals interaction. These results confirm that the electron-withdrawing nitro groups are the key chemisorption centers that give NBT its strong inhibitory effect, while the positively charged tetrazolium rings provide an additional electrostatic anchor.

To elucidate the effect of PEG on NBT adsorption at the Cu(111) surface, MD simulations were performed on systems containing both NBT and ${ \mathrm { P E G } } ,$ as shown in Figure 9. Under the cooperative influence of PEG, the entire NBT molecule adopts an almost flat orientation on the Cu(111) surface, resulting in markedly tighter contact compared to the PEG-free system. The RDF analysis confirms this rearrangement: The RDF peaks for both tetrazolium rings $( \mathrm { { T } } z / \mathrm { { T } } z ^ { \prime } )$ shift to distances below 3.5 ${ \mathring { \mathrm { A } } } ,$ indicating a transi tion from weak physisorption to strong chemisorption. By contrast, one methoxy group (Meo<sup>′</sup>) remains distant from the surface $( \mathbf { r } = 8 . 6 7 \mathring \mathrm { A } )$ , and the two remaining phenyl rings (Ph3/Ph3<sup>′</sup>) only partially adsorb in a tilted orientation. Overall, PEG markedly strengthens NBT’s interfacial binding, with the calculated adsorption energy rising from −128.27 to −191.51 kcal/mol—an enhancement of nearly 50%. In short, the MD simulations demonstrate that PEG markedly enhances the chemisorption of NBT on copper, most likely through the strong NBT–PEG interaction identified by DFT. This finding is fully consistent with the synergistic suppression behavior observed in electrochemical analysis and with the DFT calculations.

The study above indicates that NBT possesses the key attributes required of an electroplating leveler. To assess its practical performance, the microvia electrodeposition was carried out with 10–40 ppm NBT, and the cross-sectional results are given in Figure 10. At a low concentration of 10–20 ppm, NBT fails to support bottom-up filling: only little copper grows at the microvia’s bottom, while accelerated deposition at the mouth causes premature closure and large voids. This behavior is attributed to an insufficiently dense PEG–NBT suppressor film; its inhibition strength and potential sensitivity are too low, consistent with the narrow CV hysteresis observed in electrochemical analysis above.

However, when the NBT concentration is raised to 30–40 ppm, the filling mode switches to void-free bottom-up superfilling. The higher NBT level forms a denser, higherpotential-sensitivity PEG–NBT film that adsorbs preferentially at the relatively positive microvia’s mouth, strongly suppressing copper there. Meanwhile, SPS adsorbed at the microvia bottom—where convection is weak—accelerates copper deposition in that region, enabling void-free microvia superfilling. These plating results confirm the findings derived from electrochemical analysis, DFT calculations, and MD simulations: NBT synergizes with PEG to form a robust suppressor film that localizes at high-potential, high-convection regions, thereby enabling reliable void-free bottom-up copper filling of microvias.

Tween (TW) compounds, on account of their environmentally benign and non-toxic characteristics, were systematically studied as prospective eco-friendly suppressants in the process of copper plating for blind hole filling. The synergistic efects between TW and other additives were verified by means of chronopotentiometry, cyclic voltammetry, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy. The outcomes of the electrochemical tests revealed that the competitive adsorption behavior between bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) and TW is contingent upon the current density and the intensity of convection. Metallographic section analysis demonstrated that TW exhibits outstanding microvia filling capabilities for micro blind vias with a diameter of 150 µm and a depth of 80 µm. Notably, TW-80 was able to attain a filling rate of 96.15% following electrodeposition for 60 min at a current density of 2 A/dm<sup>2</sup>. Quantum chemical calculations suggested that the relatively smaller band gap and the clustered molecular structure of TW-80 are more conducive to its adsorption onto the electrode surface, leading to the formation of a barrier layer, which in turn restrains the deposition of copper.

In the realm of microelectronics manufacturing, acid copper electroplating for microvia filling has emerged as a pivotal process, ensuring reliable electrical interconnections within printed circuit boards (PCBs) and advanced packaging substrates [1–4]. The quality of via filling, characterized by void—free and uniform deposition, directly impacts the performance, reliability, and miniaturization potential of electronic devices [5–7]. To achieve this, a complex mixture of additives, including suppressors, accelerators, and levelers, is incorporated into the electroplating bath [8–11]. Among these, suppressors play a crucial role in controlling the deposition rate at diferent surface sites, preventing over—plating at the via openings and promoting bottom—up filling.

The additives utilized in the acidic sulfate copper plating process primarily consist of chloride ions (Cl-) [12], accelerators, suppressors and levelers. These additives interact with one another to enhance the performance of resulting formed copper plating layer [13, 14, 5, 15–17]. Previous research on suppressors for acid copper electroplating has predominantly focused on polymers and surfactants with diverse molecular structures. For instance, polyethylene glycol (PEG)-based polymers have been widely studied and utilized as suppressors due to their ability to adsorb on the copper surface and inhibit the deposition reaction [18, 19]. However, their high molecular weight and complex synthesis processes often lead to issues such as poor bath stability and dificulty in waste treatment, raising environmental concerns. Polyetheramine (PEP) has also been investigated as a potential suppressor, leveraging its unique amine-containing structure that allows for specific interactions with the copper surface [17, 20]. While PEP shows promise in adjusting the deposition rate, its relatively high cost and limited biodegradability pose challenges for large—scale industrial application. Additionally, ethylene—propylene copolymer (EPE) has been explored, as its alternating structure can provide a balance between hydrophobic and hydrophilic properties, influencing the deposition behavior [21, 22]. Nevertheless, EPE may sufer from inconsistent performance under varying electroplating conditions, and its efect on the quality of microvia filling in high—aspect—ratio scenarios remains suboptimal. Moreover, some non—ionic surfactants like Triton X—series have been investigated, but they may exhibit limited eficiency in microvia filling under high— aspect—ratio conditions and can also pose potential toxicity risks.

Tween compounds, a class of non—ionic surfactants derived from sorbitan esters and ethylene oxide, have found extensive applications across multiple industries. In the pharmaceutical industry, Tween compounds are commonly used as solubilizers and emulsifiers in drug formulations. They enhance the solubility of poorly water—soluble drugs, improving drug delivery and bioavailability. For example, in the formulation of oral suspensions and injectable emulsions, Tween 80 efectively stabilizes the dispersed phases, ensuring uniform drug distribution [23]. In the food industry, Tween compounds serve as emulsifiers, preventing the separation of oil and water phases in products such as margarine, salad dressings, and ice creams. They also contribute to the texture and shelf—life of food products [24]. In the cosmetics industry, Tween compounds are utilized in creams, lotions, and shampoos for their excellent wetting and emulsifying properties, facilitating the dispersion of ingredients and enhancing product stability [25]. Moreover, in the field of biotechnology, Tween compounds are employed in cell culture media to reduce surface tension, promote cell adhesion, and prevent cell aggregation [26].

Against this backdrop, considering their excellent emulsifying, dispersing, and wetting properties, as well as their relatively low toxicity and good biodegradability, Tween compounds present a compelling option for electroplating applications. However, their application as suppressors in acid copper electroplating for microvia filling has remained largely unexplored. This study aims to investigate the inhibitory efects of TW-20 and TW-80 (as shown in Fig. 1) and their synergistic efects with other additives through electrochemical methods, optical microscopy, and quantum chemical calculations. By doing so, it systematically evaluates Tween compounds as eco-friendly suppressors for acid copper electroplating in microvia applications, filling this research gap. The findings of this research are expected to contribute to the development of more environmentally friendly and eficient electroplating processes, meeting the growing demands of the microelectronics industry for sustainable manufacturing.

Following the determination of the inhibitory strengths of the two inhibitors, this study utilized the chronopotentiometry to predict the hole-filling capacity of the plating solution consisting of 60 mg/L Cl-, 6 mg/L accelerator, 4 mg/L HPTT and separate batches of 200 mg/L TW-20 or TW-80. The test results are shown in Fig. 4. The analysis of the test results indicated that the plating solutions containing distinct inhibitors all adhered to the convection-dependent adsorption (CDA) of additives [32], as evidenced by a notable negative shift in the stable potential measured at high rotation speeds. In other words, the inhibitors exhibit a stronger inhibitory efect under conditions of strong convection, thereby complicating the process of copper deposition. Furthermore, it can be inferred from Fig. 4 that the overpotential for copper deposition with TW-80 is higher than that with TW-20, which remains unafected by the intensity of convection. After comparing the potential diference Δη calculated for the two inhibitors at diferent rotation speeds, it becomes apparent that Δη for TW-80 consistently exceeds that for TW-20 at equivalent concentrations. According to the CDA mechanism, a higher Δη of the plating solution is associated with increased holefilling capability [32], suggesting that TW-80 is expected to have a more robust capacity for filling holes.

To further clarify the interaction of these additives, the synergistic efects of TW with other additives were further investigated through chronopotentiometry, as shown in Fig. 6(a-f). The analysis will be based on TW-80 since the structural similarity between TW-20 and TW-80. As illustrated in Fig. 6(b), the leveling agent HPTT does not influence copper deposition under either strong or weak convection intensities. Following the addition of TW, a slight negative shift in the deposition potential is observed. The subsequent introduction of SPS leads to a positive shift in the deposition potential. Finally, the addition of Cl- results in a rapid negative shift in the copper deposition overpotential and an increase in Δη to 20 mV, indicating the occurrence of convection-dependent adsorption (CDA) behavior.

Comparing the time intervals of 500–1000 s in Fig. 6(b) with the 1000–1500 s interval in Fig. 6(d) reveals that the simultaneous presence of HPTT and Cl- can accelerate the reduction of copper ions, whereas no such efect is observed when HPTT is present alone. Furthermore, a comparison between the intervals of 500–1500 s in Fig. 6(b) and 500–1000 s in Fig. 6(f) indicates that when only HPTT and TW are present in the VMS, HPTT diminishes the inhibitory efect of TW, suggesting an antagonistic interaction between the two. This antagonism reduces the adsorption capacity of both HPTT and TW in regions of strong convection, while exhibiting no significant impact under weak convection conditions. This implies that HPTT accelerates the rate of copper deposition outside blind holes, leading to an increase in the thickness of the deposited copper.

Moreover, when analyzing the time intervals of 500–2000 s in Fig. 6(d) alongside those of 500–1500 s in Fig. 6(f), it becomes evident that the addition of Cl- disrupts the antagonistic interaction between TW and HPTT. TW and Cl- preferentially combine to form a TW-Cl- complex, significantly enhancing the inhibitory efect on copper deposition. This suggests that in the simultaneous presence of Cl-, HPTT, and TW, Cl- preferentially associates with TW, thereby augmenting its inhibitory efect.

The Nyquist plots derived from the plating solutions containing TW-20, TW-80 and diferent concentrations of Cl- are depicted in Fig. 9, along with their corresponding equivalent circuit diagrams. It is important to note that, in order to provide a more objective reflection of the adsorption of inhibitors in the actual copper plating experiment for blind hole filling, the electrochemical impedance data were measured at a polarization potential of −0.65 V (vs. SMSE). The equivalent circuit diagram shows the diferent components representing resistance and capacitance in a system. Rs represents solution resistance, while CPE1 and R1 represent the capacitive arc in the high-frequency region. CPE1 represents double-layer capacitance, while R1 signifies electrochemical reaction resistance. Similarly, CPE2 and R2 correspond to another capacitive arc, indicating Cu + asd relaxation on the electrode surface [36–38]. The magnitude of R1 can indicate the challenges associated with copper ion deposition, enabling the assessment of Cl- concentration on TW's inhibitory capacity against copper deposition.

Cl- concentration can significantly enhance the inhibitory efect of TW-20 and TW-80 on copper deposition. Furthermore, when R1 attains its maximum value for TW-20 and TW-80, the associated Cl- concentration aligns with the concentration recorded in prior experiments. In contrast, the absence of additives in the VMS solution results in a R1 value of 4.004 Ω cm2. The comparison of the rise in R1 resulting from the introduction of TW and Cl- concentrations reveals that an elevation in Cl- concentration can more eficiently amplify the inhibitory efect of TW. This phenomenon is closely associated with the adsorption mechanism of TW on the electrode surface. As previously stated, when plating solutions contain higher concentrations of Cl-, TW interacts with Cl- and subsequently adheres to the cathode surface through chemical bonding. In this instance, TW exhibits high adsorption strength, leading to a potent inhibitory impact on copper deposition. Conversely, the absence of Cl- in the plating solution results in the adsorption of TW molecules on the electrode surface through electrostatic or van der Waals forces, which leads to a less robust adsorption and a diminished inhibitory efect on copper ion deposition.

Based on the aforementioned research findings and pertinent literature [20, 23], this study puts forward an adsorption model for TW-20 and TW-80, as shown in Fig. 13. In the absence of Cl- in the plating solution, TW molecules predominantly adhere to the electrode surface via electrostatic interactions and van der Waals forces, as illustrated in Fig. 3(a1) and (b1) in the supplementary materials. In this scenario, the intermolecular forces between TW molecules and the electrode surface are relatively weak, resulting in a reduced inhibitory effect of the resulting barrier layer on copper deposition. Upon the addition of Cl- to the plating solution, TW molecules engage with Cu + and Cl- to create complexes (TW-Cu + -Cl-). Consequently, it is not just simple TW molecules, but rather these complexes that adsorb on the electrode surface. The TW-Cu + -Cl- complexes adhere to the electrode surface via chemical bonding, resulting in a more potent inhibitory impact on copper deposition due to the formation of a barrier layer. The carbon–carbon double bond in TW-80 molecules specifically undergoes a reaction with Cl- and subsequently adsorbs onto the electrode surface through Cl-. This process leads to the formation of a barrier layer by the TW-80-Cu + -Cl- complex, which exhibits a more potent inhibitory effect in comparison to the barrier layer formed by the TW-20-Cu + -Cl- complex (Fig. 10).

The study shows that TW-20 and TW-80 have inhibitory efects on copper deposition, making them suitable for use as electroplating inhibitors. TW-80 demonstrated exceptional performance, with a plating solution comprising 220 g/L CuSO4·5H2O, 28.33 mL/L H2SO4, 30 mg/L Cl-, 6 mg/L SPS, 8 mg/L L, and 100 mg/L TW-80 achieving full filling of blind holes with a 150 μm diameter, resulting in a filling rate of 95.6%.

Electrochemical measurements have uncovered a convection-dependent synergistic efect between TW and L at low current densities. Moreover, a significant synergistic inhibitory efect was observed between TW and Cl-, suggesting that Cl- amplifies the inhibitory efect of TW on copper deposition. The coexistence of TW, L, and Cl- led to the most potent inhibitory efect.

Based on the research on Tween compounds as eco— friendly suppressors for acid copper electroplating in microvia applications, several key guidelines are proposed. Firstly, when selecting Tween compounds, factors like their hydrophilic—lipophilic balance, molecular weight, and branching structure should be carefully considered to ensure proper adsorption and inhibitory efects. Secondly, concentration optimization is crucial, as both too low and too high concentrations can negatively impact microvia filling quality, thus requiring systematic studies to find the optimal balance. Thirdly, using Tween compounds in combination with other electroplating additives and understanding their synergistic efects can enhance the overall plating performance, although their compatibility and interaction mechanisms need thorough investigation. Finally, environmental considerations are essential, including minimizing compound loss during bath operation and adopting appropriate biodegradation processes for waste treatment. By adhering to these guidelines, Tween compounds can be efectively applied, promoting more sustainable and eficient microelectronics manufacturing, and future research should further explore and optimize their application.

Abstract: Levelers, as an essential part of organic additives in copper electroplating, play a crucial role in the fabrication of sophisticated interconnects in integrated circuits, packaging substrates, and printed circuit boards. In this work, four N-heterocyclic oligomers were synthesized and characterized, along with investigations of their electrochemical behaviors and their synergism with other bath components. The corresponding effects of the oligomers on the deposited copper films were analyzed by morphological and compositional characterizations. The leveling mechanism of the oligomers was further discussed with the aid of quantum chemical calculations. The results exhibit that each of these N-heterocyclic oligomers holds a particular degree of leveling ability. The oligomer of 1,3-bis(1-imidazolyl)propane and 1,3-dichloro-2-propanol (IPIEP) is the best leveler for THs plating compared with the other three oligomers. It was found that the hydroxyl group in IPIEP enhances the hydrophilicity of the modified molecule and triggers a more stable complexation between IPIEP and H O−Cu(I)−MPS. Moreover, imidazole demonstrates a better practicality than piperazine. This work recommends the combination of N-heterocycles in planar conformation with modification by the hydroxyl group to synthesize high-performance straight-chain levelers

Under the synergistic effects of organic additives (brighteners, suppressors, and levelers), electroplated copper is uniformly deposited on the inner wall of through holes (THs) as the conformal layer or micro-through-hole filler [3]. The performance of electroplating copper film in THs is decided by the shape of holes, electrolyte formula, plating current, solution convection, etc. [4,5]. The conformal deposition in THs has been explained by the theory of secondary current distribution, but the via filling was considered abnormal and termed as super filling due to its behavior [6,7]. Moffat proposed and then revised the curvature-enhanced adsorbate coverage (CEAC) model based on the growth process, revealing the accelerating effect of the brightener in the bottom-up growth of vias [6,7]. Later, Dow discovered the convection-dependent property of levelers [8], and Broekmann found the N-type negative differential resistance (NDR) phenomenon in the bath solution [9]. These findings have established a systematic via-filling theory and emphasized the importance of levelers in copper electroplating.

Besides dye-based levelers, in recent years, organic oligomer levelers (nitrogencontaining heterocycles chained by linker groups) have attracted increasing attention in research and application [15,23,24]. Due to the unclear structure–property relationships of these oligomers, the need to develop new oligomer leveler machines with a high through-hole filling performance is very time-consuming and challenging. Several research groups have started to purposefully design various oligomer levelers to investigate their structure–property relationships in THs filling. Quaternary ammonium salts have been systematically studied because of their excellent via filling properties [25,26]. Broekmann used polymerizates of imidazole and epichlorohydrin (IMEP) as a model leveler to study the oscillatory behavior during electrodeposition and concluded that the leveling effect originates from the coordination between Cu(I) and the leveler, in which the hydroxyl functional group coordinates Cu(I) to form the IMEP−Cu(I)−MPS complex, inhibiting the activity of MPS [27]. In contrast, Bandas claimed that the activity of MPS is inhibited by electrostatic pairing with the N-heterocyclic leveler and the deposition of copper ions is occluded by the steric chemical structure of the oligomers [28].

The conventional mechanism of the levelers’ behavior proposes that the levelers directly adsorb on the tips or protrusions of the cathode to inhibit the deposition of metal ions [37]. In addition to the advantage of a shorter mean free path, some of the candidate metals can potentially provide performance gain through innovative integration schemes. The overall resistance of an interconnect structure is a result of not only the copper but also other materials used in the interconnect structure for a variety of purposes. Such materials include diffusion barrier, adhesion layer, capping layer and sometimes additional elements as the seed layer for copper plating. Therefore, using metals that can serve dual or multiple purposes may allow more volume for the conducting metal and thus a lower overall resistance and an improved RC delay. Furthermore, new materials that enable better integration and lower defectivities can improve the overall performance as well. For example, chemical vapor deposited (CVD) and atomic layer deposited (ALD) Ru was previously studied to replace the Ta diffusion barrier – Cu seed stack.<sup>7–9</sup>

Co has recently gained more and more attention as a material to replace the traditional Ta liner.<sup>10,11</sup> Compared with Ta, Co provides a better wettability of PVD Cu seed, enables a more conformal Cu seed coverage and therefore improves the extendibility of Cu electroplating in smaller dimensions.<sup>12</sup> In addition, the enhanced grain growth of Cu electroplated on Co seed<sup>13</sup> and the self-formation of a barrier layer enabled by the Mn diffusion through Co layer<sup>14</sup> potentially provide additional performance gain on the reliability of the interconnect structures.

Recently, selectively electroless deposited Co has been demonstrated to partially or completely replace the Cu in the small vias to improve the via resistance.<sup>15</sup> The bottom up fill of the via structures relied on the selectivity between the exposed underneath metal layer and the dielectrics for electroless deposition process. Electrolytic super conformal deposition of Co and Ni was reported using 2-mercapto-5-benzimidazolesulfonic acid (MBIS).<sup>16–19</sup> A potential dependent adsorption, passivation and desorption of the additive was found to result in a negative differential resistance in cyclic voltammetry and therefore multiple steady states at certain potentials. Super conformal deposition of through silicon vias (TSV) was enabled by controlling the deposition at such potentials, where the bottom and top of a TSV are plated at two different states. Super conformal NiFe filling into sub-50 nm interconnect trenches was demonstrated with a two component additive system using a polymer suppressor and a monomer accelerator.<sup>20</sup> More recently, three component commercial additive has been reported for the bottom up filling of Co for interconnect.<sup>21</sup>

A group of additives including saccharin and thiourea were previously studied for their impacts on the NiFe alloy deposition toward superconformal filling.<sup>20</sup> While polyethyleneimine (PEI) was found to show suppression effect, thiourea and benzenesulfinic acid showed only acceleration effect. In addition, mercapto-benezenimidazole and its sulfonic acid derivative showed suppression followed by acceleration effect. Comparing the molecular structures of these additives in Figure 1, it is clear that PEI only has paired amine groups, which are two CH groups apart. Thiourea and benzenesulfinic acid both have mercapto groups vie an isomerization and a disproportionation reaction,<sup>30</sup> respectively. When both mercapto group and paired amine (or imine) groups are present in the molecules, such as mercaptobenezenimidazole and its sulfonic acid derivative, both suppression and acceleration effects were observed. In addition, when one of the paired amine nitrogen is replaced by oxygen in mercapto-benzoxazole, the suppression effect was significantly weakened and only acceleration effect was observed. Finally, when the mercapto group was removed and only a sulfonic group is present in saccharin, neither suppression nor acceleration was observed. Based on this previous work, it can be speculated that a pair of amine (imine) group is responsible for a suppression effect and a mercapto group for acceleration.

The deposit leveller takes an important role in plating-related processes such as copper damascene interconnection,<sup>1–3</sup> copper pillar bumps,<sup>4,5</sup> and microvias.<sup>6,7</sup> Janus Green B (JGB) is the commonly used leveller which has been studied extensively. Kelly et $a I . ^ { 1 }$ and Cao et $a / . ^ { 8 }$ firstly proposed a four-component additive containing JGB to achieve the levelling efect and suggested a competitive adsorption relationship between these additives. Dow et al.<sup>9–11</sup> found that the inhibiting efect of JGB was enhanced in the presence of convection and proposed the convection-dependent adsorption (CDA) theory, suggesting that the CDA behaviour of the additive was a crucial factor to achieve bottom-up filling. Li et $a I . ^ { 1 2 }$ determined the structure of the reduction product of JGB by mass spectrometry (MS) and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), and proposed that the reduction product of JGB is the true leveller in the copper filling process. Mao et al.<sup>13</sup> provided molecular spectroscopic evidence on the reductive decomposition of the JGB azo group by in-situ attenuated total reflection-surface enhanced infrared spectroscopy. Hai et al.<sup>14</sup> further stated that the consumption of JGB should also include the reduction of heterocycles. In the present authors’ previous work, JGB-induced convection-dependence has been observed,<sup>15</sup> but molecular-level understanding of its genesis is still absent.

In this study, the JGB-induced convection-dependent filling process is visualised as benefitting from the CPBs in-situ observation platform. Cyclic voltammetry (CV), ultra violet-visible spectroscopy (UV-vis), and in-situ electrochemi cal surface enhanced Raman spectroscopy (EC-SERS) were performed to identify the decomposition of JGB. The weakening of the inhibitory capacity of JGB reduction product relative to JGB was confirmed by cyclic voltammetry stripping (CVS). Electrochemical and spectroscopic evidence supports the idea that inhomogeneous flow field inside the microvia leads to enhanced renewal of JGB and its reduction product on the higher flow rate side, and suppressed the deposition of copper on that side.

As a final component of this study, the diference in inhibition of copper deposition by JGB and JGB\_Red needs to be evaluated. The cyclic voltammetry stripping (CVS) method<sup>27</sup> was used to compare the changes in the inhibition ability of the plating solution when JGB or JGB\_Red was added to the basic plating bath (Figure 6).

Figure 6(a) illustrates typical CVS results used to evaluate additive inhibition capability. Additives with inhibition ability will slow down the deposition rate of Cu, which further leads to a decrease in the area of the Cu dissolution peak at around 0 V.

Figure 6(b) presents the trend of JGB and JGBRP inhibition factors with potential. The negative reverse potential was varied from −0.1 to −0.4 V to cover the potential window for JGB reduction as well as copper deposition. As shown in Figure 6(b), both JGB and JGBRP exhibited the ability to inhibit copper deposition. However, when the potential is shifted negatively to −0.3 V, the inhibition ability of both decreases significantly, which is attributed to the desorption of the leveller at more negative potentials.

JGB exhibits a consistently stronger inhibition ability than its reduction product, indicating that the inhibition ability of JGB can be maintained at a high level even if it decomposes when the raw material is suficiently supplied. Therefore, even with the generation of JGB\_Red in actual plating, the weakened inhibition ability of JGB can be compensated for as long as suficient convection is ensured.

So far, based on the above spectroscopic evidence and electrochemical studies, the convective dependence exhibited by JGB can be explained: JGB initially protonates in acidic solutions and subsequently becomes further decom posed during copper deposition, and the inhibition of the redox is much weaker. For regions with strong convection (e.g. mouth of the microvia,<sup>9,10</sup> and downstream of microcavity<sup>15,28</sup>), where suficient raw material supply can maintain the inhibition ability, the growth of copper can be slowed down, while, for the weaker convective regions (e.g. bottom of the microvia, and upstream of microcavity), the inhibition is rela tively weak, which will be preferred for copper growth.

In this paper, the mechanism of convection-dependent morphology induced by the leveller JGB has been investigated based on an in-situ observation platform simulating the work conditions of CPBs electrodeposition. The results of CV. UV-vis. and FC-SERS experiments indicate that the decomposition of JGB involves the protonation of the phenazine ring and the reduction of the azo group. The CVS studies further indicate that the reduction of JGB will result in a weak ening of its inhibitory capacity. Enhanced convection can ensure suficient supply of JGB to maintain its inhibitory capacity, while the decomposition of JGB in the weak convection region will deteriorate the capacity. This is believed to be the reason why the plating layer height distribution is afected by convection during the filling process. The revelation of this decomposition mechanism will contribute to the understanding of the role played by phenazine-type leveller, and facilitate the molecular design of leveller and the quality control of plating bath in the CPBs and microvia filling process.

In this study, a traditional copper electroplating formula was used to fill microvias, which indicated that when the concentrations of Janus Green B (JGB) and bis-(sodium sulphopropyl) disulphide (SPS) were both controlled at 6 mg L<sup>−1</sup>, through-holes and blind holes can be simultaneously and perfect filled with deposited copper by regulating the convection intensity. As a result, the dimple at the mouth of through-hole was only 5 μm, and the filling performance of blind hole was 88%. Galvanostatic measurements (GMs) and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) were employed to study the microvia filling mechanism. It demonstrated that the plating solution in the centre of the through-hole was nearly stagnant under the weak convection, which resulted in the accelerator SPS being preferentially adsorbed and further enhanced the copper deposition here. It led to the formation of butterfly-like deposited copper layer in the through-hole and finally filled the through-holes and blind holes simultaneously.

For through-hole plating, the relatively complex pulse electroplating technique has been commonly employed<sup>12–14</sup>. Zhang et al.<sup>15</sup> optimised the periodic reverse pulse plating process using numerical simulation methods, achieving conformal filling of through-holes with an aspect ratio of 10:1. Ning et al.<sup>16</sup> utilised horizontal pulse copper electroplating technology to successfully achieve conformal thickening of high-aspect-ratio through-holes and super-filling of blind holes, ultimately obtaining a smooth copper layer. Compared to the complex pulse electroplating process, direct current (DC) copper electroplating ofers advantages such as lower equipment costs, simpler operational parameters and higher process stability. Liu et al.<sup>9</sup> developed an electroplating solution formulation suitable for the simultaneous filling of through-holes and blind holes, which can be implemented using only a direct current (DC) power supply. Additionally, they optimised the process by improving the pattern plating method, thereby minimising the thickness of the surface copper. Zhao et al.<sup>17</sup> employed 1-dodecyl-2-methyl-3-benzylimidazolium chloride (DMBI) as a leveller, successfully achieving conformal thickening in through-holes and void-free filling in blind holes. In situ ATR-SEIRAS spectroscopy and electrochemical experiments revealed that DMBI inhibits the electroreduction of copper ions by competing with SPS. Currently, the simultaneous electroplating process for through-holes and blind holes primarily focuses on achieving conformal thickening of through-holes. However, this conformal thickening approach may lead to reduced signal transmission reliability and insuficient thermal performance during the long-term use of HDI<sup>18–20</sup>. To address these issues, it is necessary to achieve complete filling of through-holes. Therefore, this study aims to develop an acidic sulphate copper plating process based on a low-voltage DC power supply to achieve simultaneous and complete filling of through-holes and blind holes.

In this study, the commonly used SPS and JGB were employed as the accelerator and leveller, respectively. Based on a clear understanding of the efects of convection intensity and additive concentration on the copper plating filling performance, a novel method of optimising the filling efect through gradient regulation of convection intensity was proposed. This approach successfully achieved simultaneous and flawless filling of through-holes and blind holes, significantly enhancing the metallisation eficiency of HDI.

Generally, strong convection can eliminate concentration gradients in the plating solution, improving the quality of the deposited copper. Based on this, a microvia filling experiment was conducted under continuous strong convection and the results are shown in Figure 1.

It can be seen that a super conformal model had taken place in the blind hole, while the ‘butterfly-shaped’ filling model could not be achieved inside the through-holes, because, under strong convection, the plating solution flowed directly through the through-hole, which resulted in relatively strong convection in the centre of the through-holes like that on the PCB surface. Consequently, the distribution of additives inside and outside the through-hole was similar. According to the CDA model, the accelerator molecules could not accumulate in the centre of through-holes, which finally led to conforma copper deposition in through-holes. At this stage, the surface was relatively smooth. The copper deposition thickness inside the through-holes and on the PCB surface was approximately 15 μm, and the dimple at the mouth of the blind hole was 33 μm.

Given that the ‘butterfly-shaped’ filling model could not be achieved in the through-hole under continuous strong convection, the convection intensity was subsequently reduced to enhance the adsorption of accelerator molecules inside the hole. As shown in Figure. 2, copper electroplating for filling through-hole and blind hole were carried out under continuous weak convection.

For blind holes, appropriately strong convection was facilitated to increase the diference of copper deposition rate between the PCB surface and the bottom. Therefore, after the ‘bridge’ was formed inside the through-hole, switching to strong convection could enhance the filling performance of both through-holes and blind holes as well as improve the surface morphology of the deposited copper layer. To determine the optimal convection intensity switching time, the microvia filling results obtained at diferent switching times were investigated, as shown in Figure 4.

After electroplating for 40 min, the ‘butterfly-shaped filling trend in the through-hole was apparent, but the ‘bridge’ in the through-hole had not yet occurred, let alone the complete filling of the through-hole. It indicated that switching the forced convection from weak to strong before the ‘bridge’ formation would hinder the completion of through-hole filling, even if the ‘butterfly-shaped filling trend emerged. This result can be attributed to the unique geometry of through-holes. In the through-hole, accelerator molecules were dificult to adsorb onto the inner surface of the through-hole under the strong convection, which prevented the formation of the ‘bridge’. It indicated that only after ‘bridging’ was complete in the through-hole and transformed it into two symmetrical blind holes, could switching to strong convection be facilitated to achieve perfect filling and obtain smooth deposited copper layer. In addition, it could be concluded from Figure 4 that the optimal electroplating process was first electroplating for 60 min under weak convection, then switching to strong convection and continue electroplating for

The GMs were carried out in the optimal electroplating solution under diferent rotation speeds and the results are shown in Figure 7. It could be noted that the copper deposition potential increased gradually with the increase of rotation speed, which could lead to decrease of the copper deposition rate. Under both weak and strong convection, the copper deposition rate at the centre of the throughhole and the bottom of the blind hole is faster than that on the PCB surface. This indicates that SPS showed stronger adsorption strength than that of JGB in these regions. Actually, according to CDA theory, SPS preferentially adsorbed onto the surface where the convection was relatively weaker, such as in the centre of the through-hole and on the bottom of the blind hole, thereby accelerating the copper deposition rate in these regions. It finally resulted in the ‘butterfly-shaped’ filling in through-holes and the ‘bottom-up’ filling in blind holes.

Figure 9a,b represent the distribution of additives during the initial stage of through-hole filling and the copper deposition development stage inside the through-hole, respectively. In the initial stage of electroplating; due to the large molecular weight of the suppressor and the very weak convection inside the through-hole, most of the suppressor molecules adsorbed onto the surface outside the through-hole, while JGB molecules with positive charge accumulated at the mouth of the through hole, suppressing copper deposition in this region. Inside the through-hole, the leveller and accelerator molecules were uniformly distributed, and the concentration of the suppressor was relatively low, which resulted in the copper deposition rate inside the through-hole being higher than that on the surface. As the electroplating progressed, the adsorption of the accelerator molecules became dominant at the centre of the through-hole because the convection intensity here was relatively weak. Thus, the copper deposition rate at the hole centre was significantly increased, which ultimately resulted in the ‘butterfly-shaped’ filling.

Figure 9d illustrated the copper deposition process after achieving a ‘bridge’ inside the through-hole and switching to strong convection. At this stage, the ‘bridge’ had been achieved inside the through-hole and changed it into two symmetrical blind holes. Upon switching to strong convection, the concentration diferences of the components in the plating solution were eliminated, and chloride ions as well as additives on the copper surface were replenished and re-adsorbed. The accelerator preferentially adsorbed at the bottom of the blind holes, where the convection was weak. Meanwhile, the leveller and suppressor preferentially adsorbed on the surface and at the hole openings, where the convection was strong. This ultimately resulted in overfilling of the two symmetrical blind holes.

Electrochemical analysis coupled with CFD simulations enabled the development of a novel TH filling mechanism model. The model elucidated two critical phenomena: (1) a substantial convection gradient existed between the external and internal through-hole regions and (2) weak convection conditions promoted lower copper deposition potentials. These factors synergistically facilitated preferential copper deposition at the through-hole centre, initiating the charac teristic butterfly-shaped filling pattern. Following bridge for mation, the through-hole efectively transformed into two symmetrical blind holes, allowing subsequent strong convection to enhance both filling uniformity and surface quality.

ABSTRACT: Thiamine, a nitrogen-containing heterocyclic compound, is explored for the first time as a novel leveling agent in this study. Based on the density functional theory (DFT) calculations and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of the adsorption process of thiamine and the commonly used leveling agent JGB, the average values of the binding energies after equilibrium of thiamine and JGB are similar, which indicates that the thiamine molecules have strong bonding ability with the surface of copper and can be adsorbed tightly on the surface of copper. By cyclic voltammetry (CV) curve, thiamine was found to inhibit copper deposition and the inhibition efect was stronger than JGB. The chrono potential curve (CP) test found that the potential diference $\triangle \eta = 8 7 > 5 0$ mV at high and low speeds of thiamine, which indicates that thiamine has the potential to be used as a leveling agent. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) testing found that thiamine inhibited copper precipitation by inhibiting the reactions of $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + } \to \mathrm { C u } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { C u } ^ { + } $ Cu. Silicon through hole (TSV) technology, as one of the core technologies of 3D packaging, has been studied by a large number of scholars at present.<sup>1−3</sup> TSV is the interconnection of diferent chips and wafers by filling them with conductive metal through microvia. ABSTRACT: Acid copper electroplating stands as a core technology in advanced packaging processes, facilitating the realization of metal interconnects, bumps, vias, and substrate wiring between transistors. The deposition quality of copper interconnect materials has a crucial impact on the final performance of chips, directly influencing their yield, reliability, and stability. In this intricate process, additives play a pivotal role in regulating the deposition quality and behavior of metal copper. This mini-review comprehensively summarizes the recent research progress in the field of electroplating copper additives for advanced packaging, both domestically and internationally, delving into the types and mechanisms of various additive molecules, including accelerators, inhibitors, and leveling agents. Through in-depth research on these additives, we gain a profound understanding of their specific roles in the electroplating process and the intricate

Concerning the mechanism of superequivalent-angle electroplating filling, both the Curvature-Enhanced Accelerator Coverage (CEAC) model and the Convection-Dependent Adsorption (CDA) model can provide reasonable explanations for the flawless bottom-up filling process ofmicrovias. However, each model has its limitations (Figure 4).

CDA model:<sup>16</sup> It utilizes the convective intensity to influence the distribution of Cl<sup>−</sup> on the electrode surface in the plating solution, thereby determining the adsorption of additives. Specifically, strong convection increases the adsorption of Cl<sup>−</sup> on the electrode surface, thereby enhancing the adsorption of inhibitors and improving their inhibitory efect on the deposition of copper ions. In an environment with weak convection and low Cl<sup>−</sup> concentration, it is more conducive for the accelerator to enhance its depolarization efect, thereby expediting the deposition of copper. Consequently, there is a disparity in the copper deposition rates at the mouth and bottom of the hole, realizing the bottom-up filling of microvias.

CEAC model:<sup>17</sup> This model emphasizes changes in the geometric shape of microvias rather than the interaction of various additives. With the progression of the electroplating process, the hole surface undergoes internal contraction, leading to a reduction in the hole bottom surface area and a corresponding increase in curvature. At this stage, a significant amount of accelerator is adsorbed at the bottom of the microvia with a large curvature, further expediting the deposition of copper inside the hole and achieving bottom-up filling of microvias.

In an acidic copper plating system without the participation of additives, the copper layer on the surface of the PCB and the copper layer at the bottom of the microvia will increase simultaneously during the copper plating process, making it challenging to achieve overfilling of vias. In an acidic copper plating solution without additives, the obtained copper layer has poor brightness performance, and it is challenging to improve the overall leveling ability and deep plating ability of the plating solution. Therefore, additives are the core of the acidic copper plating system. Thus, for the acidic sulfate copper plating system, the pursuit of an efective, nonpolluting, and cost-efective additive formula becomes crucial for the entire system (Table 1). Additives are a critical factor in copper electroplating for via filling, representing the core of commercial formulations for copper via filling. The electrochemical characteristics of additives are crucial in altering the current distribution inside and outside the vias. Presently, the market dominance in copper electroplating via filling formulations lies in the hands of foreign companies like Atotech, Rohm & Haas, JCU, MacDermid, and Schlotter. In China, companies such as Good Way, Zhengtian wei, Sinyang, and others have also emerged. However, there is still a significant gap in bargaining power and technological R&D capabilities compared to major foreign enterprises.

In the current acidic plating solution system, the main components include one inorganic additive and three organic additives: chloride ions, accelerators, inhibitors, and leveling agents.<sup>20</sup> The concurrent presence of various additives in the electroplating solution system enables improved filling of microvias, ensuring better coating quality and achieving interlayer interconnection. Additionally, additives can enhance current eficiency, simultaneously regulate the deposition rate of copper in high and low current density areas, refine grains, and improve crystal orientation. Thus, achieving a more uniform and smooth coating. Furthermore, there are reports of accomplish ing copper electroplating for via filling using a single organic additive. For instance, researchers have proposed that SH110 is a combination of an accelerator and an inhibitor or leveling agent. It can form an adsorption film on the copper surface, exemplifying the inhibitory action of inhibitors. This inhibitory efect is more likely to occur in the strong convection region of the cathode, while its promoting efect primarily occurs in the weak convection region of the cathode.

4.2. Accelerator. Accelerator (also known as brightener) adsorbs in low current density areas such as the bottom of the hole. Cl<sup>−</sup> induces depolarization, lowering the overpotential of ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ and accelerating the deposition rate of copper at the bottom of the hole. Moreover, the accelerator accelerates the formation of crystal nuclei, ensuring a higher nucleation rate than the grain growth rate, leading to finer crystals and improving the smoothness of the coating surface. For example, in a plating solution without additives, copper atoms redeposit on existing crystal faces, generating new two-dimensional grains with a specific size, resulting in an overall layered structure. With the addition of SPS or SPS + Cl<sup>−</sup>, the resulting grains noticeably increase in size, with the deposition mode lying between preferred orientation and a layered structure.<sup>22</sup> The accelerator is primarily a small molecule compound containing sulfur, usually consisting of two parts. One part comprises thiol or disulfide bonds, and the other part is a sulfonic acid salt group. The most extensively utilized accelerators in the industry include sodium 3-mercaptopropanesulfonate (MPS) and 3,3′-Dithiobis-1-Propanesulfonic Acid Disodium Salt (SPS). When used in conjunction with PEG, it can coordinate to control the deposition rate of copper. In the process of the accelerator molecule exerting its accelerating efect, the thiol group plays an adsorptive role, while the sulfonic acid group performs the accelerating function. If the terminal functional group $\mathrm { i } s - \mathrm { O H } , - \mathrm { C O O H } , \mathrm { o r } - \mathrm { C H } _ { 3 } ,$ instead $\mathrm { o f } - \mathrm { S O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ , there is no transfer and acceleration capability, thus failing to achieve the goal of accelerating copper deposition.<sup>23</sup> The presence of chloride ions in the system accelerates the reaction rate of copper deposition by controlling the step of ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { + }$ generation, thereby expediting the copper deposition process. As accel erators, there are certain limitations on the content of SPS and MPS. If the content is too low, the acceleration efect is not noticeable, and holes are prone to form during the deposition process. An excessive amount can lead to an inconspicuous diference in concentration between the bottom and mouth of the hole, likewise failing to achieve the desired efect. In the majority of experiments, their concentration is generally a few ppm.

Garcia-Cardona et $\mathsf { a l . } ^ { 2 4 }$ pointed out through NMR that a Cu(I)-sulfonate complex is formed on the surface of the copper electrode. Since then, Cu(I)MPS has generally been recognized by the academic community as the substance that directly depolarizes the electrochemical interface in acid copper electroplating. Schmitt $\mathrm { e t } ~ \mathrm { a l . } ^ { 2 5 }$ also confirmed through electro chemical polarization and electroplating experiments that the concentration of $\mathrm { { C u } ( I ) M P S }$ is positively correlated with the copper electroplating rate. Through their research, Lan et al.<sup>26</sup> have demonstrated that mercaptopropanesulfonic acid copper-(II) complex MA exhibits depolarization efects in acidic copper plating solutions. Compared to SPS, MA exhibits fewer side reactions and possesses a wider linear range in its standard curve, resulting in stronger analytical capabilities. Therefore, in practical electroplating production processes, MA enables better monitoring and more precise supplementation. Additionally, replacing SPS with MA does not alter the coating crystallization characteristics, indicating that MA is a promising accelerator for copper electroplating applications.

4.1. Halide Ions. Halide ions are an essential component in the plating solution of the acidic copper plating system, commonly dominated by chloride ions. It mainly exists in the form of sodium chloride or hydrochloric acid in the copper plating solution. Although its required content in the plating solution is relatively low, it plays a significant role. Chloride ions enhance the conductivity of the system, facilitate the dissolution of phosphor copper anodes, reduce the formation of “copper powder” due to incomplete anode dissolution, improve the brightness and leveling ability of the coating, and enhance coating quality. Chloride ions play a dual role: inducing the capture of copper ions by the inner layer electron transfer of the accelerator MPS sulfonate ${ \mathrm { R } } { - } S { \mathrm { O } } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ , synergizing with the accelerator MPS to accelerate the deposition of copper ions on the cathode surface; also acting as an inhibitor, adsorbing on the cathode surface $\begin{array} { r l } { \mathsf { a s } \textbf { a } ^ { \infty } \mathbf { h o o l } \breve { \mathbf { k } ^ { \prime \prime } } } \end{array}$ to enable the inhibitor to function properly $( { \mathrm { F i g u r e } } \ 5 )$ . Chloride ions can also serve as a “chlorine bridge” between the electrode surface and $\boldsymbol { \mathrm { C u } } ^ { + }$ . This increases the concentration of subcopper ions on the electrode surface, reduces the double-layer capacitance, weakens polar ization, lowers nucleation rates, ultimately achieving favorable conditions for crystal nucleus growth. Research also suggests that certain leveling agents using I<sup>−</sup> as the counteranion exhibit significantly enhanced inhibitory capabilities compared to $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ as the anion. The reason for this is the synergistic interaction between I<sup>−</sup> and the overall structure of the leveling agent, resulting in a potent inhibitory efect.<sup>21</sup>

4.3. Inhibitors. In electroplating additives, inhibitors achieve the suppression of surface copper deposition by adsorbing onto the copper surface, enhancing cathodic polarization, and inhibiting the deposition of copper on the surface. Inhibitors are generally polyether substances with a certain molecular weight. Common inhibitors include polyethylene glycol (PEG), polypropylene glycol (PPG), and a copolymer of ethylene glycol and 1, 2-Propanediol (EPE). The molecular weight of PEG is around 6000 to 10000. Inhibitors have a larger molecular weight and are easily consumed during the electrodeposition process. Therefore, during electroplating, inhibitors primarily exhibit a gradient distribution on the surface ofthe plated piece. For PCB electroplated copper pillars, the bottom of microblind holes is relatively distant from the bulk solution, leading to a reduced distribution of inhibitors in this area. The concentration of inhibitors at the opening of the hole is closer to the concentration of inhibitors in the bulk solution. Additionally, as these polyol substances are excellent surfactants, they also function as wetting agents in copper electroplating. When the amount of inhibitor added is too small, resulting in insuficient wetting of the board surface, it causes the surface to appear red and dull.

It is important to note that inhibitors can only exhibit efective inhibitory efects when Cl<sup>−</sup> is present in the electroplating solution. In the presence of chloride ions in the solution, PEG strongly inhibits the deposition of metallic copper, usually causing an increase of several hundred millivolts in the $\mathrm { { o f } \ C u . } ^ { 2 \mathord { \uparrow } }$ 12 deposition overpotential

4.5. Interactions among Electroplating Additives. There is currently no fully unified understanding regarding the specific mechanism of accelerators. Currently, the more widely accepted view is the MPS-accelerated copper deposition mechanism proposed by Dow<sup>30</sup> and others (Figure 10). In this mechanism, MPS initially adsorbs on the electrode surface through the thiol group, and subsequently, its tail sulfonic acid group captures $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ in the solution and interacts with Cl<sup>−</sup> ions. The entire process involves an inner-sphere electron transfer mechanism. In the absence of Cl<sup>−</sup> ions in the plating solution, MPS or SPS will only exert inhibitory efects. The accelerating efect of SPS mainly results from the breaking of the disulfide bonds in its molecules into two MPS molecules under the influence of an electric field, and MPS is the substance that truly accelerates the process.

The most widely accepted theory regarding the mechanism of the inhibitory agent is that the formation of PEG-Cl<sup>−</sup>-Cu<sup>+</sup> hinders the deposition of copper. This theory has also been substantiated by various techniques, including electrochemistry, surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy, atomic force micros copy, and others.<sup>35,36</sup> In the case of the inhibitor, chloride ions coordinate with PEG to form PEG-Cu (I)-Cl complexes. Its adsorption on the copper surface enhances cathodic polarization, thus inhibiting the deposition of copper. Moreover, leveling agents in the plating solution can form complexes by coordinating with the copper surface through their active sites (such as N, S, Pyridine rings, etc.). The adsorption of this complex on the copper surface enhances the inhibitory efect of PEG-Cu (I)-Cl on the copper surface.

Numerous studies indicate the presence of significant interactions between inhibitors and accelerators, and the manifestation of the accelerating efect depends to a certain extent on the presence of the inhibitor. For instance, in a plating solution containing $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ but without PEG, the addition of SPS did not show a significant accelerating efect, and the resulting plated coating was not bright. Mofat et al.<sup>37</sup> demonstrated that the competitive adsorption of SPS and PEG on the copper surface involves the competition for adsorption sites. They argue that the appearance of the accelerating efect is attributed to the disruption of the cathodic inhibition layer by the sulfonic acid group. Moreover, the rate of SPS replacing PEG adsorbed on the copper surface is dependent on the overpotential. The higher the overpotential, the faster SPS replaces PEG.

Dow et al.<sup>38</sup> proposed that when JGB serves as a leveling agent, there is a synergistic efect between JGB, PEG, and chloride ions, enhancing their inhibitory efects. This enhanced efect is realized through the formation of PEG-JGB-Cl<sup>−</sup> complexes generated during the electroplating process. The synergistic efect is related to the convection intensity, causing the inhibition of PEG-JGB-Cl<sup>−</sup> complexes in high convection areas and the accumulation of SPS at the bottom of blind holes, thereby achieving overfilling of the blind holes. Bandas et al.<sup>39</sup> studied the catalytic efect of amine leveling agents on SPS at the interface between copper and the electroplating solution, revealing that the influence of leveling agents on accelerators is related to the molecular weight of the leveling agent.

The primary challenge in acidic copper electroplating lies in the incomplete understanding of the mechanisms of additives in the copper plating system, especially those of accelerators and leveling agents. Among them, the mechanism of leveling agents is of paramount importance. As leveling agents are vital for achieving uniform copper coatings, the challenge lies in correctly selecting and using appropriate additives when altering electroplating conditions, particularly in high current density electroplating.<sup>38</sup> Currently, in industrial electroplating practices, the current density for through-hole electroplating is generally strictly controlled below 3 A/dm,<sup>2</sup> and for plating blind holes, it is even lower, typically strictly controlled below 2 A/dm.<sup>2</sup> There are two main impacts of increasing current density.

First, it seriously diminishes the uniformity of the coating, resulting in greater diferences in thickness between the copper surface and the copper coating inside the hole. Excessively thin hole copper can lead to severe damage to the electrical performance and reliability of PCBs, which is strictly prohibited in electroplating production. Second, increasing current density will impact existing additive systems, necessitating the develop ment of new additive systems. However, developing an entirely new electroplating solution system has become increasingly challenging, requiring higher costs and more funding. Furthermore, higher current density will accelerate the consumption of accelerators, increase the dificulty of additive control, and significantly impact coating quality.

Accelerators can be tailored toward organic additives devoid of sodium ions, with the objective of minimizing the impact of sodium ion infiltration on chip electrical performance. Future inquiries into leveling agents should concentrate on polyquater nary ammonium salts, small-molecule nitrogen-containing heterocyclic compounds, and inorganic molecules. Additionally, polymers enriched with multiple active functional groups, including ethers, hydroxyl groups, and imidazoles, emerge as a promising research direction for innovative leveling agents.
