As a result, it is of great importance to screen metals with low electron mean free path in the replacement of Cu in order to improve the property of IC. Among these metals with relatively low mean free path, Co was investigated widely as interconnect line after balancing the production cost and IC property.<sup>6–11</sup> Since cobalt not only is of low fine-line resistivity, but also is of strong electromigration resistance.<sup>12,13</sup>

Applying electrodeposition method to prepare Co thin films is a cost-friendly, fast, and easy-operating method, and has been applied in many fields.<sup>14–17</sup> Achieving bottom-up growth of cobalt is the key to manufacturing the interconnect line, while the superconformal electrodeposition of cobalt can be obtained by exploring additive,<sup>18</sup> and optimizing the electrodeposition parameters, including the composition of bath solution,<sup>19</sup> current density,<sup>20</sup> pH<sup>21</sup> and so on. Besides, Co film with different structure and crystal phase can be obtained by changing electrodeposition parameters.<sup>22</sup> Generally, the Watts-based electrolyte or buffered sulfate electrolyte can be used to deposit Co film, in which boric acid has been added to stabilize the increasing pH in plating bath caused by polyborates and primarily triborate and occupy block surface sites to inhibit HER as well as facilitate cobalt deposition by the surface complex with cobalt.<sup>23–25</sup> In order to achieve bottom-up growth of cobalt deposit, appropriate additives should be introduced into plating bath to achieve growth rate difference in the blind vias.<sup>26–28</sup> And, this difference is consistent with the diffusion-adsorption mechanism.<sup>29–32</sup>

Josell et al.<sup>28</sup> realized the superconformation filling of TSVs with high aspect ratio by adding polyethyleneimine (PEI) as suppressor into the plating solution, which is composed of cobalt sulfate, cobalt chloride and boric acid. The deposition mechanism is due to the occurrence of S-NDR characteristics after the breakdown of the adsorption of PEI on the cathode surface, in which active-passive transitions are formed in TSVs with the applied voltage. Hydrogen induction deactivation mechanism was proposed to explain the influence of additive XF on superfilling of cobalt by Wu et al.<sup>33</sup> The growth rate different within blind vias was ascribed to the fact that the deactivation rate of additive is higher than the compensatory rate by mass transport. Huang et al.<sup>34</sup> added the dioxime additive as suppressor to achieve Co defect-free filling. Co(DMG) complex can be formed between dioxime and cobalt ions so as to inhibit the Co reduction. When the voltage rises to the breakdown threshold, Co begins to deposit on the cathode surface. Under the influence of convection, an obvious inhibition gradient was formed during the deposition process, which is consistent with S-NDR mechanism.

In this study, Malachite Green (MG), was selected as a suppressor for cobalt electrodeposition. It has been verified that MG adsorbed on the cathode surface to inhibit the reduction of copper and titanium.<sup>35</sup> And the influence of MG on Co metal deposition process have also been discussed before,<sup>36</sup> so this paper mainly studies the influence of MG adsorption on the hydrogen evolution process. The electrochemical tests, including cyclic voltammetry (CV) and linear sweeping voltammetry (LSV), were applied to research the inhibition ability of MG on the deposition process of cobalt, while the influence of MG on HER was also studied by EQCM tests. Superconformal electrodeposition of cobalt was achieved and induction-diffusion-adsorption mechanism was proposed to illustrate the synergistic effect of MG and pH.

The effect of MG on cobalt reduction process.—The electrochemical behaviors of MG were obtained from CV in order to study the influence of MG on cobalt reduction process. The influence of MPS on electrochemical behavior can be regarded as an accelerator for the electrodeposition of cobalt with a depolarization effect according to LSV analysis in Fig. S1. Figure 1 shows the CV curves of 10ppm MG in the bath with the different rotation rate so as to study the influence of mass transport. It can be seen that the current density begins to increase sharply when potential reaches to $- 1 . 2 4 \mathrm { V }$ (vs MSE) without rotating. When the rotation rate increased from 0 rpm to 800 rpm, the threshold potential of Co ion reduction shifted negatively from −1.24 V to −1.31 V (vs MSE) on the negative-going sweep, which can be attributed to the adsorption of the $\mathrm { \overline { { M } } G } ^ { 3 8 }$ and the change of surface coverage. The adsorption MG can be used as site-blocking by decreasing the active surface area for cobalt ions reduction. And the current density of the reduction process gradually decreases with the increasing rotation rate, due to the faster replenishment of MG from the bath to the cathode surface. In addition, the current loop at around −1.26 V was observed, demonstrated that the overpotential of cobalt nucleation is large. The slightly increase of current at about −1.15 V to −1.24 V was mainly attributed to the reduction of hydrogen ion and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } . ^ { 3 9 , 4 0 }$ No metal deposits were found on the cathode surface (not shown here). In this case, the total current density vs potential curve exhibits S-shape negative diffierential resistance (S-NDR) behavior,<sup>28,41,42</sup> which attributes to the breakdown of the blocking inhibitor layer (MG layer).

It should be noted that the current density for $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ reduction also changed between −1.16 V and −1.24 V with rotation speed increased from 0 rpm to 800 rpm shown in Fig. 1(b). $\mathrm { A t } - 1 . \bar { 1 } 6 \mathrm { V }$ , the current density for $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ reduction reached to −0.3 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ at 0 rpm and −0.7 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ at 800 rpm, which is attributed to the acceleration of $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ reduction with the increasing speed. Besides, the slope before reaching −1.19 V is different from that after reaching −1.19 V, illustrating that the partial current was attributed to reduction of hydrogen ion (reaction $1 ^ { 4 3 } )$ before reaching to $- 1 . 1 9 \mathrm { V } ,$ , as well as the current caused by the water reduction (reaction $2 ^ { 4 4 } )$ when potential was within −1.19 V to −1.22 V.<sup>24,43</sup>

The CV curves of different concentrations of MG on electrochemical behavior were tested, as shown in Fig. 2. It can be seen that the significant hysteretic voltammetric curves appeared after MG was introduced into the electroplating bath even though the concentration is quite low (2 ppm), demonstrating that the additive MG is of excellent inhibition ability for the reduction of cobalt. It should be noted that the strong inhibition effect might be caused by strong adsorption and coordination between MG and cobalt ions studied in our previous work.<sup>45</sup> Besides, the breakdown potential shifted negatively from about $- 1 . 2 5 \mathrm { V }$ to lower than −1.40 V with the MG concentration increasing from 2 ppm to 20 ppm, while there is a relationship between the increase of threshold potential and the concentration of $\mathbf { M G } ,$ illustrating that the threshold value is related to the adsorption and transport of MG. Meanwhile, the S-shape negative differential resistance (S-NDR) can be observed when the MG concentration is higher than 10 ppm since the current density rises sharply when the cathode potential is lower than the breakdown potential. Furthermore, the current density of $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ reduction was also accelerated with the increase of MG.

The acceleration of MG on HER.—Because the standard reduction potential of $\mathrm { \dot { C } o } ^ { 2 + }$ to Co metal (−0.28 V vs NHE) is more negative than that of H<sup>+</sup> reduction to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 }$ (0 V vs NHE), the side reaction (hydrogen evolution reaction, HER) would occur inevitably and have a negative effect on the current efficiency of Cobalt deposition in an acidic bath. As a result, the influence of MG on HER should be taken into account respectively. The influence of MPS on HER has been investigated and MPS has little effect on HER, as shown in Figs. S2 and S3.

What’s more, voltammetry curves were used to further study the influence of MG on HER without Co ion in the bath. The solution contains of the same composition of plating bath except that the $\mathrm { C o S O } _ { 4 } { \cdot } 7 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ was replaced by $\mathrm { K } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 }$ in order to match the conductivity of electrolyte. Co-seeded platinum electrode was selected as the cathode was shown in the Fig. 4. It can be seen that the current density increases with the increase of additive concentration at about −1.0 V. The process of hydrogen evolution was significantly accelerated even though 2 ppm MG added into plating bath. The accelerating effect on HER can be enhanced with the increase of MG concentration. The MG could absorb on the cathode surface as active sites to promote the HER, which is consistent with EQCM analysis (Fig. 3). It should be noted that the current density obtained in EQCM analysis is slightly different from that of cyclic voltammetry analysis, which is due to the fact that rotation electrode was applied in cyclic voltammetry tests while there was none convection in EQCM test.

The process of hydrogen evolution was significantly accelerated after MG was added into plating bath<sup>46</sup> and the hydrogen evolution current increased with the increasing concentration of MG. In other words, the higher coverage of adsorption MG on electrode surface, the higher current density for proton reduction (Fig. 1). Furthermore, the hydrogen evolution current obtained is lower than that collected from EQCM, which indicated the complex CoMG might also act as a catalyst for HER.<sup>47,48</sup> In summary, the MG absorbed on the cathode surface to inhibit cobalt ions by occupying the active site on the surface but to boost the HER during the cathodic reduction.

According to the above description, the addition of MG inhibited the deposition of cobalt, but accelerated HER process at the same time at lower overpotential. This indicates that the MG will strongly adsorb on the cathode surface and occupy the active site, which plays an inhibitory role on cobalt deposition. However, MG occupying the active site is beneficial to the reduction of $\mathrm { H } ^ { + } / \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ as a catalyst.

The acceleration of MG on HER will promote the appearance of hydroxide at the electrode surface, the intermediate formation of CoOH<sup>+</sup> or Co(OH) might also been appeared during the deposition of cobalt metal. While the buffer effect of boric acid and the bulk pH value indicate that no $\mathrm { C o ( O H ) } _ { 2 } { } ^ { 2 4 }$ precipitates will be formed. The intermediate was mainly composed of $\dot { \mathrm { C o O H } ^ { + } } _ { \mathrm { ( a d s ) } } \left( \mathrm { E q } . ~ 3 \right) ^ { 3 7 }$ and the intermediate will adsorbed on the electrode surface.

The influence ofpH on current efficiency.—The effect of MG as an acceleration for HER would still result in an increasing of the local pH, especially at the bottom of the vias. Therefore, the current efficiency (CE) for $\mathrm { C o } ^ { 2 + }$ <sup>+</sup> reduciton with different pH was studied, as shown in Fig. 5. The deposition current density was selected as 2 mA·cm<sup>−2</sup>, 5 mA·cm<sup>−2</sup>, and $8 \mathrm { m A } { \cdot } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ respectively and the corresponding potential transients were shown in Fig. S7. The CE for the deposit was calculated by anodic stirring charge. It can be seen the proportion of current for ${ \mathrm { C o } } ^ { 2 + }$ reduction increased gradually with the increasing of total current density or decreasing of rotation, resulting in higher CE. Although the concentration of ${ \mathrm { C o } } ^ { 2 + }$ is significantly greater than that of $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ in the deposition bath, the CE of $\mathrm { ~ \overrightarrow ~ { ~ H ~ } ~ } ^ { + }$ reduction is primary at low current density. From Fig. 5, when current density was $^ { \circ } 2$ mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } ,$ , the CE of ${ \mathrm { C o } } ^ { 2 + }$ reduction was as low as 10% at pH 3. Under these conditions, changing either the reduction rate or transport rate of $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ has noticeable effects on the CE of ${ \mathrm { C o } } ^ { 2 + }$ deposition.<sup>29,39,40</sup> In addition to the concentration effect, proton reduction kinetics was confirmed to be faster than that of cobalt deposition at lower overpotential.<sup>49</sup> Therefore, the effect of MG on the proton reduction process should also be taken into account at lower overpotential deposition, especially at lower pH.

The surface morphology of cobalt deposit.—The surface morphology was analyzed to verify the acceleration of MG on HER, as shown in Figs. 6 and S5. SEM images were obtained with and without the existence of the additive MG. As can be seen from Fig. 6a, the Co grain are densely stacked blocks. When the MG concentration is 10 ppm, the grain size becomes smaller and there are much more nanoscale voids on the grain, as shown in the Fig. 6b. It can be concluded that the addition of MG results in the grain refinement because of the inhibition of MG on cobalt deposition. Meanwhile, the MG act as the accelerator for hydrogen evolution which make hydrogen bubble increase and overflow from the coating surface. However, the voids in the plating layer have a negative effect on the physical and chemical properties of the Co deposition and proper wetting agent should be introduced. Therefore, 20 ppm MPS and 10 mM chloride ion were added in the bath in order to obtain cobalt coating with high quality, as shown in Figs. S6a and S6b. After optimizing plating composition and process parameters, a compact uniform film without nanoscale voids can be obtained with or without stirring. The further verification of the contact angle under water was shown in Figs. S6c and S6d and the plating layer was placed face down under water and with a bubble attaching to the surface. The contact angle was $1 3 9 ^ { \circ }$ and $1 4 7 ^ { \circ }$ respectively with or without stirring, which means the released hydrogen during the entire reduction process can be quickly removed from the surface.

Electroplating.—The electroplating test was carried out in order to observe the influence of MG and pH on the bottom-up growth of cobalt. The test condition in filling experiments was the same as that in electroanalytical experiments except for stirring way. The ohmic losses difference caused by different stirring way can be neglected (Fig. S8). Electroplating test were investigated at the potential range of −1.19 V and −1.22 V since superconformal electrodeposition could be achieved due to intense pH and strong inhibition of MG. As shown in Fig. 7, there is almost no cobalt reduced when the cathode potential is −1.19 V. Referring to the previous voltammetry curve, when the external potential at −1.19 V, the main electrochemical reaction in the via is hydrogen ion reduction. When the deposition potential is −1.20 V, it can be seen that the deposition layer begins to appear at the bottom and side wall. According to Moffat’s description of the metal filling process in TSV,<sup>28,50,51</sup> the blocking effect caused by the coverage of inhibitors on the electrode makes the deposition efficiency of metal on the sidewall higher than that on the surface, which can form a passive-active transition. From the Fig. 7(b), it can be seen that the rapid deposition rates take place in the lower portion of the via, while the sidewall and outside surface remain in the passive state. What’s more, the boundary of the passive-active transition gradually rises at more positive potential in Fig. 7(c). The transition forms mainly due to the difference of the vias coverage caused by the breakdown and diffusion-limited process of the MG.<sup>28,52</sup>

Although boric acid is added to the bath as buffer, it can be seen from the Fig. 5 that the deposition efficiency of the same pH value at different rotational speeds is significantly different, especially at a lower pH value. Next, the filling conditions of cobalt metal under different pH values were studied, as shown in Fig. 8. When the bath was adjusted the pH to 3 by dilute sulfuric acid, almost nothing is deposited in the feature, as shown in Fig. 8(a). This indicates that the reaction occurring at this condition is mainly the reduction of H<sup>+</sup>, and the absorption of MG makes no cobalt deposit in the feature. After the pH value of the bath was up to 3.5, thin film was deposited on the central bottom rather than the bottom corners of the feature, as shown in Fig. 8(b). This model of deposition appears to differ from the higher deposition rate on the sidewall, which is based on the passive-active transition model. In other words, the MG inhibition effect still exist in the feature, and the cobalt deposit at the central bottom may be caused by some accelerant. In the absence of MG images (Fig. S10), the thickness of Co deposit in the feature, such as the bottom and the surrounding field, is nearly the same as that on the surface. Therefore, the local accelerant was probably regard as the formation of $\mathrm { C o O H ^ { + } _ { a d s } }$ at the bottom,<sup>53</sup> which caused by the rising in pH, rather than the breakdown of the MG. A local pH increases owing to hydrogen ion consumption and mass transport limitations,<sup>37</sup> especially when MG is adsorbed at the bottom.

The formation of local pH gradient is a process of time accumulation because the mass transport of proton is faster than that of suppressor. The coupling of MG depletion effects in feature filling with the local increasing pH could provide the explanation for the subsequent shift from the passive to active zone at the bottom. When different rotation speeds and concentration are applied at −1.20 V, the filling of metal Co was completely different, as shown in Fig. S11. The phenomenon of conformal deposition at 0 rpm indicates the conformal growth of cobalt since effective MG concentration gradient was not established. As the convection intensifies, there is no cobalt deposit on the outer surface and sidewall of the via since effective MG concentration gradient based on diffusion-limited within the feature was established.<sup>54</sup>The passive-active profile should be steady-state in nature, which is reflected in the potential-dependent incorporation balanced by the suppressor depletion gradient in the deposit.<sup>52</sup> However, this transition state gradually expands over time [Fig. 9(c)], which may be due to the disruption of inhibition caused by pH evolution, which is related to time evolution. After the stable passive-active transition zone is completed, the bottom-up growth process proceeds smoothly as shown in Figs. 9(d) and 9(e).

At the initial state, the cathode surface covered with inhibitor MG which suppress the Co reduction and promote the HER. During the electrodeposition, the deposit suppression gradient was formed because of the diffusion-limited of MG. The passive-active transition zone come into being, and then the zone grows until it covers the entire trench due to the induction HER of MG. Meantime, the effective pH gradient is also established due to the mass transport limitation of hydrogen ion, resulting that the current efficiency at the bottom is higher, as shown in stage b in Fig. 10. Compared with the formation of inhibition gradient, the disruption of MG caused by HER is weaker, which is more conducive to the bottom-up superfilling process. In summary, the induction-diffusion-adsorption mechanism, namely diffusion-adsorption effect caused by MG gradient and pH gradient as well as induction effect of MG on HER, was proposed to illustrate the bottom-up growth of cobalt.

The additive Malachite Green (MG) was used as an effective suppressor for cobalt deposition. The suppressing effect of MG on cobalt electrodeposition was investigated according to cyclic voltammetry and the mass transport of MG is diffusion-controlled. The induction acceleration of MG on HER was obtained by coupling EQCM and cyclic voltammetry as well as surface morphology was used to confirm the acceleration of MG on HER, while the influence of pH on current efficiency was also studied. The formation of hydroxide ions at the electrode surface caused by the HER which leaded to the formation of $\mathrm { C o O H } ^ { + } \mathrm { ( a d s ) } .$ The induction-diffusionadsorption mechanism was proposed to illustrate the bottom-up growth of cobalt. The MG gradient formed within blind vias due to the limitation of mass transport resulting the inhibition difference at different parts (the growth rate at the bottom is higher than that of the opening), while the pH gradient and the formation of $\mathrm { C o O H ^ { + } }$ (ads) caused by MG induction is beneficial to the Cobalt filling in the feature.

Electroless-plated cobalt alloys with tungsten typically exceeding 5 at.% are the common barrier materials for copper metallization. As cobalt is a new interconnect material for advanced microchips, it is worth studying the advanced cobalt-interconnect metallization process that involves extremely diluted cobalt-tungsten (CoW) alloys with an eliminated impurity resistivity and enhanced electromigration reliability. To this aim, we fabricated three different CoW nanolines with 0.03, 0.06 and 0.11 at.% of W using an electroless process, and examined their electromigration behaviors under accelerated stressing conditions, using Co lines as a control. All three W contents, especially 0.06 at.%, mitigate Co electromigration. The mechanism for the electromigration mitigation is due to an improvement of the film s nanomechanical and surface wetting properties, as well as grain-structure refinements. A full account of the relationship between the film properties, grain structures and electromigration testing results is given, reasonably explaining the cause of the reliability optimization.

The measured data of $\mathrm { C o W _ { l } }$ and $\mathrm { C o W _ { h } }$ (high tungsten content) obviously deviates from the inverse variation trend for $\mathbf { C o } ,$ , CoW<sub>l</sub> and $\mathrm { C o W } _ { \mathrm { m } } .$ This deviation can be attributed to the strong affinity of W for oxygen [41], which likely results in a higher sticking coefficient of W atoms on the SiO₂ substrate compared to Co atoms [42]. This interfacial reaction likely facilitates the formation of tungsten oxide between the $\mathrm { C o W _ { h } }$ and $S \mathrm { i O _ { 2 } , }$ thereby enhancing adhesion strength. Such behavior has also been reported in Co-Zr, Co-Al [43] and Co-W-B [44] barriers for Cu metallization. The high concentration of W in $\mathrm { C o W _ { h } }$ promotes the diffusion of W atoms and the subsequent formation of tungsten oxide. This process, coupled with the high surface energy of 69 mJ $\mathbf { m } ^ { - 2 }$ , results in a moderate adhesion energy of 52.7 MPa. Note that. The data of Table 2 apparently suggest that the magnitude of the adhesion strength, along with the film’s hardness, is a key electromigration-mitigation factor, which in turn places the electromigration-reliability ranking of the four different Co deposits in decreasing order from $\mathrm { C o W _ { m } , C o W _ { h } , C o W _ { l } }$ to Co.

Here, the content of the W in Co is minor (0.03, 0.06 or 0.11 at.%), and thus the effective valence $Z ^ { * }$ , diffusivity D and electrical resistivity ρ of the alloyed Co are assumed to be the same as those of the unalloyed Co. Stressing the Co and W-added Co lines with an identical current density under the same temperature should induce the same electromigration flux at equilibrium according to Eq. (5). Thus, the reason for the W-added Co lines to yield a higher resistance to a variety of flux divergences showing a reduced void growth rate and extended electromigration lifetime, as implicitly confirmed by their smaller n factors, is related to the higher film mechanical properties. As stated, compressive and tensile stresses tend to build up, respectively, in the anode and cathode sides of a damaged region around the grain boundaries or material interfaces. The relaxation of the stress gradient by a back-diffusion process accelerates the formation and growth of the voids there [52]. The high adhesion strength and hardness of the W-added $\mathbf { C o } ,$ especially $\mathrm { C o W } _ { \mathrm { m } } ,$ contribute to the inhibition of stress relaxation during electromigration stressing, thus mitigating electromigration and prolonging interconnect’s lifetime. A thin polycrystalline conductive film with a higher adhesion strength and hardness would have a stronger substrate’s binding force and a tighter (or tougher) grain structure, which would put it more resistant to electromigration voiding or thermal stressing [53, 54]. Indeed, the SEM micrographs in Fig. 3 show that the thermal stability of the Co film is worse than that of the $\mathrm { C o W _ { m } }$ film; the Co interconnect line also has an inferior electromigration reliability, as compared to all W-added Co interconnect lines.

The STEM-HAADF image of the unalloyed Co line (Fig. 7c) exhibits a ‘clean, smooth’ contour, suggesting a relatively low defect density; the line also gives a ‘perfect’ lattice fringe image (Fig. 7d) and [0001] zoneaxis Fourier transform pattern of HCP-Co (inset, Fig. 7d). By contrast, the $\mathrm { C o W _ { m } }$ line comprises a stacking of equiaxed grains (Fig. 7b), seemingly offering a more complicated grain structure that could inhibit grain-boundary electromigration. Moreover, the $\mathrm { C o W _ { m } }$ line exhibits an HAADF image with an intricate, rough contour (Fig. 7e), suggesting a relatively high defect density. Its high-resolution TEM image (Fig. 7f), taken along the [0001] zone axis, clearly shows the existence of stacking faults on (0001) basal planes, associated with a streaky diffraction pattern of HCP-Co (inset of Fig. 7f). Comparing the unalloyed $\mathbf { C o } ,$ the equiaxed $\mathrm { C o W _ { m } }$ has a more complex grain structure and a higher density of immobile planar defects, which would offer a maze of diffusion routes to retard the void-growth rate.

In sum, the mitigation of Co electromigration by the alloying of extremely diluted W is directly related to an improvement of the film’s mechanical properties and a reduction in the film’s surface energy. Grain-structure refinement also plays a role in the reliability reinforcement.

An all-wet SAM-seeding and electroless-plating process has been developed to form thin films of Co and extremely diluted CoW alloys with controlled thin-film properties, including deposition rates, alloy compositions, deposit surface morphologies and microstructure stability against thermal stressing. We then extend this all-wet process to fill these metal films into SiO<sub>2</sub> trenches, eventually fabricating nanolines of three different CoW alloys for electromigration-behavior evaluations, using nanolines of Co as a reference. The electromigration mitigation for all three nanolines of Co alloys with 0.03 at.%, 0.06 at.% and 0.11 at.% of added W, termed $\mathrm { C o W _ { l } , C o W _ { m } }$ and $\mathrm { C o W _ { h } } ,$ respectively, under accelerated current stressing conditions of the order of $1 0 ^ { 7 } \mathrm { A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ has been confirmed. Most noticeably, the $\mathrm { C o W _ { m } }$ line containing a moderate amount of W, while only 0.06 at.%, yields a significantly reduced current density scaling factor of 0.33, which is much smaller than that of the Co line (0.50). So, it also yields a much slower void growth rate, associated with an electromigration lifetime at least twice as long as that of the Co line. While a variety of advanced TEM analyses fail to locate the trace amount of W which is less than one atom in about 1000 cobaltmatrix atoms, the 0.06 at% added W markedly elevates the adhesion strength and hardness of Co from 35.8 to 56.1 MPa and 14.8 to 17.5 μN $\mathrm { n m } ^ { - 1 } ,$ respectively. Moreover, it also reduces Co surface energy from 70 to 60 mJ $\mathbf { m } ^ { - 2 }$ , favoring the wetting of the electroless deposits onto the underlying substrate. A fourth benefit given by the optimum W content, as found from advanced STEM/TEM analysis, is that the big electromigration-accelerating blocking grains, as exist in the Co line, are absent from the $\mathrm { C o W _ { m } }$ line. The full account of the thin-film properties being investigated correlates well with the reliability performance of the four different metallic thin films/interconnects under thermal/electricfield stressing. It also reasonably explains why the ranking of their electromigration reliability being increased from $\mathbf { C o } ,$ CoW (0.03 at.%), $\mathrm { C o W _ { h } }$ (0.11 at.%) to $\mathrm { C o W _ { m } }$ (0.06 at.%).

It is significantly important to develop novel suppressor to achieve cobalt superconformal filling. Linear sweeping voltammetry (LSV) and impedance spectra (EIS) were coupled together to study the effect of novel dye suppressor nitrotetrazolium blue chloride (NBT) on cobalt electrodeposition. The adsorption behavior of NBT on cobalt substrate was investigated by applying density functional theory (DFT) calculation, molecular dynamics (MD) simulation and in situ Raman spectra, while the interaction between NBT and cobalt ions $( \mathsf { C o } ^ { 2 + } )$ is analyzed based on topology analysis and interaction region indicator (IRI) analysis. Synergistic suppressing mechanism, namely adsorption effect and coordination effect, was proposed to explain the suppressing effect of NBT during cobalt electrodeposition. The cobalt surface morphology analysis under the influence of NBT demonstrates that NBT is of grain refinement, while XRD analysis indicates that the formation of Co hcp (100) is formed preferentially. The superconformal filling of cobalt is achieved in microvias with different diameters. The cobalt layer is of excellent quality due to low surface deposit thickness (SDT). The SDT values are 15.9 μm, 8.8 μm and 4.9 μm for 150 m, 100 m and 50 m.

Electroplating technology is key fabrication process to obtain cobalt interconnect [14]. It is essentially important to introduce proper additives to achieve superconformal growth of cobalt [15,16] since the growth rate at the plane and opening of vias is higher than that in the bottom and sidewalls as a result of mass transfer limitation within vias and edge effect at the opening [17,18]. Several additives used for cobalt superconformal filling has been reported in the literature. Josell et al. investigated branched polyethyleneimine (PEI) as suppressor and proposed S-shaped negative differential resistance (S-NDR) model to predict bottowm-up filling of cobalt [19], while Huang et al. studied the effect of oxime additive and believed that amine groups could coordinate with ${ \mathsf { C o } } ^ { 2 + }$ to suppress the cobalt electrodeposition [20–22]. He et al. studied the influence of inhibitor polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) on cobalt electrodeposition as well as cobalt superconformal electrodeposition was achieved at trench with high aspect ratio [23]. In contrast, Ma et al. proposed adsorption-coordination inhibition mechanism to explain the suppressing effect of malachite green (MG) during cobalt electrodeposition and achieve superconformal filling [24].

In this work, a kind of dye molecule Nitrotetrazolium Blue chloride (NBT), was used as novel suppressor on cobalt electrodeposition. Electrochemical methods including linear sweeping voltammetry (LSV) and electrochemical impedance spectra (EIS) were used together to study the influence of NBT on kinetics of ${ \mathsf { C o } } ^ { 2 + }$ reduction. Density functional theory (DFT) calculation was accepted to obtain the quantum chemical parameters of NBT. Besides, theoretical calculation, molecular dynamics (MD) simulation and in situ Raman spectra were used to study the adsorption of NBT on cobalt substrate. Topology analysis and interaction region indicator (IRI) analysis were accepted to study the coordination between NBT and cobalt ions $( \mathsf { C o } ^ { 2 + } )$ . The suppressing mechanism of NBT is explained by proposing synergistic suppressing mechanism. The influence of NBT on morphology and crystal orientation is investi gated by SEM and XRD, respectively. Cobalt superconformal growth is achieved at microvias with different diameters.

Fig. 1 (a) shows the effect of NBT on electrochemical reaction. Generally, the increased cathodic polarization indicates that the metal electrodeposition is suppressed. In order to exclude the influence of NBT on hydrogen evolution reaction, LSV curves were measured without the existence of cobalt ions, as shown in Fig. S1. It can be seen that NBT can improve HER at a limited extent. As a result, the strengthened cathodic polarization will reflect the suppressing effect of NBT on cobalt deposition. The cathodic polarization is −1.180 V when NBT concentration is 0 mg/L. After the introduction of NBT, it can be found that even trace NBT can effectively increase the overpotential (more than 35 mV for 5 mg/L). Besides, the cathodic polarization sees an increase from −1.215 V to lower than −1.250 V with NBT increasing from 5 mg/L to 20 mg/L, which illustrates that suppressing effect for the electrodeposition of cobalt is intensified with the increase of NBT concentration and NBT is an effective suppressor for cobalt electrodeposition.

In summary, synergistic suppressing mechanism was proposed to illustrate the excellent suppressing ability of NBT during cobalt electrodeposition. On one hand, NBT is of excellent adsorption ability on cathodic surface since it is positively charged and is full of $\mathfrak { p i }$ electron cloud of benzene and nitrogenous heterocyclic ring, which can reduce the active sites for reduction of ${ \mathsf { C o } } ^ { 2 + }$ (Adsorption effect). On the other hand, the nitrogenous heterocyclic ring opening due to accepting electrons from cathodic surface leads to that NBT can coordinate with ${ \mathsf { C o } } ^ { 2 + }$ when ${ \mathrm { C o } } ^ { 2 + }$ go through the NBT adsorption layer, which further increase the energy barrier (Coordination effect).

The effect of NBT on cobalt layer morphology was studied by SEM, as shown in Fig. 6. The inserted figure shows the grain size distribution and mean grain size. The cobalt layer is relatively compact when NBT ranges from 0 mg/L to 15 mg/L. However, it should be noted that the cobalt layer is full of large and coarse grains (mean grain size of about 416 nm) without NBT. The quality of cobalt layer can be effectively improved by introducing NBT, as shown in Fig. 6 (b) to (d). The cobalt layer becomes more uniform when NBT concentration rises from 5 mg/L to 15 mg/L, indicating that NBT can improve the surface morphology. Besides, the grain size is about 356 nm when NBT concentration is 5 mg/L. In contrast, the grain size is reduced to about 264 nm and lower than 240 nm when NBT concentration is 10 mg/L and 15 mg/L, respectively. The phenomenon of decreased grain size with rising of NBT concentration indicates that NBT is of grain refinement and the improved surface smoothness is conducive to lowering the losses of signal transmission.

Use of sodium hypophosphite causes incorporation of P in the cobalt matrix. Miksic et al. [40] provided the earliest report on the amount of P present in Co matrix deposited with different hypophosphite concentration. They found that increasing hypophosphite concentration from 0.047 M to 0.24 M resulted in an increase of the P content from 0.5% to 2.5%. Frieze et al. [41] varied the hypophosphite concentration within slightly wider range (0.05 M to 0.5 M). They were able to increase the amount of P from 1% to 5%. Schlesinger et al. They also conclusively observed the tendency of decreasing grain size with increasing amount ofP which was previously hinted by the observations of Cortijo et al. [43]. During nucleation and subsequent growth of Co film on the substrate surface, P atoms act as growth inhibitor resulting in smaller grain size [41, 44]. Dark field transmission electron micrograph [45] and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy [46] along the grain boundaries suggest that P atoms accumulate along the grain boundaries preventing further grain growth.

Wetting agents, also known as surfactants, are generally used to improve the wettability of a substrate by reducing its surface tension. This allows the electroless bath solution to make better contact with the entire surface, leading to more uniform deposition. Although use of surfactants is not very common in electroless cobalt bath, sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS) has been reportedly used in some cases where deposition was done on polyethylene terephthalate [24] or boron nitride substrate [70].

Accelerators enhance the deposition rate on a substrate. They can be categorized into two types. The first type is an accelerator solution into which an activated substrate is dipped before being placed in an electroless bath. The second type is an accelerator that can be added directly to the electroless bath in small quantities. $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } O H }$ , NaOH, $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 }$ etc. fall in the first category. Osaka et al. [71] compared the accelerating effects of 1 M $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } O H } ,$ 1 M NaOH, and $1 . 1 2 \mathrm { M } \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 }$ during deposition of $\mathrm { { C o - P } } .$ NaOH reportedly demonstrated maximum accelerating effect although the differences between them were found to be small. Shen et al. [72] found that addition of triethanolamine (TEA) directly into a hydrazine bath as an accelerator enhanced the deposi tion rate of pure cobalt up to five times. TEA forms a complex with cobalt ions in the bath which is believed to be more easily reduced. Trace amount (up to \~ 0.01 mMol) of thiourea in the bath can also be considered as accelerator as it can increase the deposition rate [66, 73].

Electroless deposition is possible at room temperature $( 2 5 { - } 4 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ [55, 74]. With increasing temperature, the deposition rate of metal ions increases almost linearly [75–77]. Figure 5b shows the plot of film thickness versus plating time in different bath temperature. From the plot, it is clearly evident that higher the temperature, lesser the needed time to attain a certain film thickness. Although it can be assumed that still higher deposition rate is possible at temperature more than $9 0 ^ { \circ } \mathbf { C } ,$ maintaining pH at this high temperature is very difficult. Hence, $7 0 – 9 0 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ is found to be the ideal range of bath temperature for electroless cobalt plating. Generally, increasing the bath temperature accelerates the deposition rate because higher temperatures promote faster chemical reactions and increase the diffusion rates of ions to the substrate surface. However, excessively high temperatures can lead to bath instability and spontaneous decomposition. Optimal temperature control is thus crucial for achieving desired plating kinetics and obtaining uniform, dense, and welladhered coatings. Rahman et al. [75] observed that at higher temperature, P content seems to increase in deposited Co-P layer contradicting the earlier claim of Liu et al. [77] who found no dependence of amount of P in the deposit on bath temperature.

In electroless plating, both ultrasonication and stirring serve the same overall purpose, which is to ensure a uniform and high-quality metal deposition on the surface of the object being plated. Ultrasonication uses high-frequency sound waves to create microscopic vibrations in the solution to dislodge gas bubbles and enhance mass transfer [82]. In electroless Co-P plating, particularly in solutions with low cobalt sulfate concentration as fewer cobalt ions available, the diffusion process becomes more critical for maintaining a steady supply of ions to the substrate surface. The ability of ultrasonication to improve diffusion has a greater impact on accelerating the deposition rate in such scenarios [64]. Ultrasound irradiation reduces the activation energy of the electroless deposition reaction. This essentially means the reaction requires less energy to occur, allowing for a comparable deposition rate at a lower temperature [83]. The mechanism behind this improvement is attributed to ultrasonic cavitation. The collapse of cavitation bubbles on the solid surface generates micro-jets which effectively clean the catalytic surface by removing contaminants leading to a larger active surface area for catalysis [84]. Yu et al. [85] found that at high ultrasonication power (100 W), the film exhibits cracks on the surface. This is likely because excessive agitation disrupts the film growth process, leading to weak bonding between the deposited particles and creating cracks. They recommend 90 W for deposition of relatively smaller and more regular shaped crystallites.

Magnetic properties ofelectroless Co films, particularly coercivity, have been extensively studied from the beginning. Coercivity is the ability of a ferromagnetic material to resist external magnetic field without being magnetized. Tuneable coercivity of electroless Co-P combined with ultra-thin nature of the deposited film makes it a candidate of interest for high density magnetic recording medium [8, 9, 78]. Ouchi et al. [125] fabricated CoNiP nanodot arrays shorter than 50 nm with high perpendicular magnetic coercivities, using electroless deposition process (Fig. 10a). This is a crucial property for perpendicular magnetic recording technology to increase storage density. Co-P films are promising for magnetic rotary encoders, enabling magnetization into 2048 magnetic pole pairs with uniform output [126]. This improves resolution and accuracy for angle and displacement measurements.

Electroless Co-P deposits typically have a fine-grained structure, which contributes to their low friction coefficients and good wear resistance. However, the wear and friction behavior of the deposit can be further improved by annealing the deposit at an elevated temperature. Annealing causes the metal grains to grow, which results in a more uniform and stronger deposit. Klingenberg et al. [127]reported the microhardness (VHN) of Co-B to be 716 kg-f/mm<sup>2</sup> and of Co-P to be 883 kg-f/mm<sup>2</sup> after heat treatment at 350 °C. Composite coating like Co-SiC can exhibit high hardness even without heat treatment [116]. Self-lubricating Co-WS film (Fig. 10b) with very low coefficient of friction can be produced via electroless route [115]. It is also reported that presence of cobalt in electroless film enhances corrosion resistance in acidic [128] and saline environment [14].

Electrolysis involves the decomposition of water into hydrogen and oxygen gases. The material of the electrodes can affect the rate of hydrogen and oxygen production. Noble metals (Ru and Pt) are often used due to their catalytic properties but they are expensive. Transition metal-based catalysts (Co–B[52], Co-Mo-B [53], Co-P [31, 129], Co-P-B [130] etc.) offer more economical options. Electroless deposition is explored as a promising method for achieving uniform and adherent catalyst layers on electrode surface. Catalytic activity of Co-P significantly depends on phosphorus content, with the coating containing 11 wt% P achieving optimal hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) performance, notably a low overpotential of 98.9 mV at 10 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ [131]. Efficiency of Co-P-B catalysts stems from synergistic electronic interactions, where electron transfer from B to Co, often modulated by P, creates active sites and optimizes adsorption capabilities [132, 133]. Whether synthesized as coatings on Ni foam for enhanced hydrogen evolution from ammonia borane [132] and sodium borohydride hydrolysis [134], or as amorphous nanoparticles [133] for overall water splitting, Co-P-B materials demonstrate superior reaction rates, lower activation energies, and excellent stability, making them promising candidates for sustainable hydrogen production. Electron micrograph of Co-coated Ni foam developed for catalytic water splitting is shown in Fig. 10c.

Adding small percentage of micro or nano-sized ceramic particles $( \mathrm { A l } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 3 }$ , SiC, MgO, WC, etc.) to metals can make them stronger and tougher as the hard ceramic particles act like tiny obstacles, making it harder for the metal to deform or break. Poor wettability can be a problem in metal matrix composites. If the metal does not adhere well to the ceramic particles, the composite material will be weaker and more likely to fail. One way to improve wettability is to coat the ceramic particles with a different material. This coating can act as a bridge between the metal and the ceramic, making it easier for the metal matrix to spread out and cover the ceramic particles. In recent decades, cobalt is being proven to be a good choice for coating ceramic particles in metal matrix composites [70, 119, 120]. Nambiar et al. [139] successfully developed aluminum matrix composites reinforced with cobalt-coated carbon nanotubes and Al2024 powder, designed for aircraft and automotive applications. A crucial finding was that a 10 µm electroless cobalt coating thickness was essential for maintaining reinforcement integrity and preventing defects during fabrication, thereby enhancing composite properties for these uses.

Electroless plating significantly enhances the performance of ceramic particle-based composite coatings obtained through cladding or thermal spraying, particularly for wearresistant applications. By coating SiC [140], WC [136, 141–143], or WC–Co [144–147] powder particles with Ni–P, Co-P, or Ni-Co, desirable features like a more uniform distribution of the binder, higher sintered densities, and improved interfacial bonding can be ensured.

Diffusion barriers (Fig. 10f) are crucial in microelectronic devices to prevent unwanted interdiffusion of atoms between different materials, which can lead to device failure. Electroless Co-P [4, 5, 108], Co-W–P [86, 105, 155], and Co-W-B [50] can be employed as interfacial layer in microelectronic contacts to prevent the inter diffusion of materials such as copper [156] and lead-free solders [5], ensuring the long-term reliability of electronic devices. A minimal 0.1% addition of manganese oxide (MnO) particles to electroless Co also reportedly improves its resistance to electromigration by physically blocking atomic movement [157]. Electroless deposited Co-P-W films, particularly those with over 12% P and 2% W, serve as excellent barrier layers in structures like through-silicon vias [158]. Compared to chloride free Pd activation, a PdCl /HCl-based activation process is noted to yield superior, residue-free deposition for such Co-P-W capping layers [159].

Enhanced Deposition Rate and Bath Efficiency: A persistent challenge is the low deposition rate and bath efficiency. Future research should focus on novel reducing agents, catalysts, or additives to accelerate kinetics without compromising quality or stability.

Electroless cobalt plating is a versatile technique capable of depositing a wide range of cobalt-based coatings, including pure cobalt and various binary and ternary alloys such as Co-P, Co-B, Co–Ni-P, Co-W–P, and Co-W-B. By carefully adjusting the composition of the plating bath and operating conditions, it is possible to tailor the properties of the deposited coatings to meet specific application requirements. These coatings offer numerous advantages, including improved corrosion and wear resistance, enhanced magnetic information storage capabilities, ability to serve as effective barrier layers against copper diffusion or acting as a catalyst in H generation via electrolysis. While many potential applications have been explored, there is still significant room for further research and development in this area. This review aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the electroless cobalt plating process by serving as a valuable resource for information on the various chemical baths and operating conditions employed by previous researchers.

# Suppressing-accelerating effect of Nitrotetrazolium Blue chloride in boosting superconformal cobalt filling

Achieving cobalt superconformal (bottom-up) growth is significantly important. Electrochemical methods, including cyclic voltammetry, electrochemical impedance spectra and EQCM-derived Coulomb-voltage curves, were used to confirm the suppressing influence of new suppressor Nitrotetrazolium Blue chloride (NBT). In situ Raman spectroscopy was used confirm that NBT can effectively adsorb on cobalt surface. Besides, EQCM-derived Coulomb-voltage illustrates that it is more beneficial for cobalt electrodeposition at high pH. The NBT effect on hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) was studied by LSV and chronoamperometry. Finite element simulation is used to investigate the accelerating effect of NBT on HER and convection. Suppressing-accelerating effect is proposed to illustrate effect of NBT. NBT can not only suppress the cobalt deposition but also can accelerate local convection by intensifying HER, which can in turn strengthen NBT adsorption. SEM analysis demonstrates that convection and NBT can refine grain. The search for suitable additives is the core to fulfill the bottom-up electrodeposition mechanism. Generally, the electrodeposition rate of cobalt changes in diferent positions of the hole due to changing thermodynamics across the additive concentration gradient.<sup>21,22</sup> When the deposition rate at the bottom of the hole is higher than that at the upper part of the hole, it can obtain the void-free superfilling deposition of cobalt in the microvias, holes, or trenches from bottom to to p.<sup>23−25</sup> These additives have efects on controlling the deposition process and have influence on the surface morphology, crystal structure, and electrical properties of the cobalt films.<sup>26−29</sup> The research on cobalt electroplating additives has focused on finding compounds that can achieve superfilling while improving plating properties. However, there are few reports and research studies in this field, particularly for the superfilling processes at present.

In this work, we propose a cobalt electrodeposition additive which can be used for superfilling. The inhibition efect of alkyne-PEG4-amine (AP4A) was investigated by electrochemical methods, including cyclic voltammetry and chronopotentiometry. Quantum chemical calculations were applied to confirm the inhibition efect of the AP4A molecule on electrodeposition. The results of the cobalt electrodeposition experiment showed that AP4A has significant influence on electrical properties, surface morphology, and crystal structure. In superfilling of nanometer scale structures with high aspect ratios, the additive AP4A was used to achieve bottom-up cobalt electrodeposition successfully. This study provides a targeted solution for superfilled cobalt plating, which has a good role in promoting the development of electroplating in the future.

3.4. Cobalt Superfilling. In the electrodeposition process, the constraints of the hole geometry lead to higher electric field and mass-transport conditions at the top of the hole.<sup>36,37</sup> The current and ion concentration at the top of the hole is often higher than at the bottom; as a result, cobalt tends to deposit more rapidly at the top than at the bottom, resulting in the formation of structures containing voids. Besides, as the current density increases, the possibility of void formation also rises, which is attributed to a more pronounced concentration of current at the top of the hole and an increased restriction on mass-transport at the bottom. Therefore, in terms of current parameter settings, the electrodeposition was carried out using segmental currents and starting from a small current (Table 2) in order to optimize the filling process, improve the filling eficiency, and reduce the defects (such as pores and voids) in the process.

Based on the above study, cobalt superfilling electrodeposition was performed with AP4A. The cross-sectional view (Figure 5) confirms AP4A’s capability as an inhibitor in cobalt superfilling. In this work, the concentration of AP4A is 5 ppm, which achieved bottom-up cobalt electrodeposition. The bottom-up filling mechanism is depicted in Figure 6. During the process of cobalt electrodeposition, AP4A molecules are adsorbed on the surface of the electrode, modulating the partial electric field strength and current density distribution. In addition, under the influence of mass transport, the molecules have a higher concentration at the top of the hole, leading to a more significant inhibitory efect and slowing down the rate of reduction of the cobalt ions. As a result, the electric field and concentration gradient developed in the presence of the AP4A molecules lead to a higher rate of deposition of cobalt ions at the bottom of the hole than at the top, resulting in the expected bottom-up superfilling.

In summary, this research successfully achieved cobalt superfilling in high aspect ratio nanometer scale structures under the action of AP4A. From the analysis of electrochemical tests and quantum chemical calculations, the cobalt electro deposition inhibitor AP4A shows a splendid ability for polarization, mainly resulting from the capacity for donating electrons of the amino group. In this work, the feasibility for achieving superfilling with additives is assessed by electrochemical experiments and quantum chemical calculations in the first place, which is verified by practical filling of electrodeposition. This research successfully identifies an additive molecule that can be used for cobalt superfilling and investigates its inhibition mechanism as well as its film properties, providing helpful insights into the relationship between molecule and microstructure, which is meaningful for realizing high-quality nanoscale cobalt inter connections and for the search of other potential additives.

Copper is the conventional material for metal interconnect in very large scale integration (VLSI). However, as the process node develops from 180 nm to a remarkable 7 nm [1,2], interconnect sizes continue to shrink, resulting in high resistance and high resistance–capacitance (RC) delay [3–5]. The reason is that copper has a relatively large electron mean free path (39 nm) and needs a relatively thick barrier layer to inhibit electron migration [6,7]. Cobalt is a promising alternative material with an average electron free path of approximately 10 nm and low electron migration [8,9]. Therefore, at the same nanometer scale, cobalt has lower resistance and smaller RC delay [10,11]. The key to replacing copper with cobalt is to be able to produce high-quality cobalt interconnects.

Thin film deposition technology is critical to realize high-quality cobalt interconnects. Physical vapor deposition [12,13] (PVD), chemical vapor deposition [14,15] (CVD), atomic layer deposition [16–18] (ALD), and electrodeposition [19–21] are the primary synthesis methods reported to date. PVD is a widely used film deposition technique, yet its filling efficiency and step coverage remain inadequate, primarily due to one-direction linear de position characteristics. This results in particles with large incidence angles failing to enter the trenches and instead depositing at the trench openings [22]. Consequently, the opening closes before the trench is fully filled [23]. To solve this problem, the industrial sector has de veloped specific PVD technologies, such as ionized PVD and collimated sputtering [24,25]. Nevertheless, the hole problem in small-sized channels still exists. In addition, CVD tech nologies have better filling capabilities, especially when trench widths are around several hundred nanometers, such as plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition [26]. ALD possesses the unique characteristic of layer-by-layer self-limiting growth, providing exceptional step coverage and film uniformity. However, its deposition rate is exceedingly low, making it particularly suitable for applications such as barrier layers and seed layers [27]. In contrast, electroplating technology is extensively utilized in damascene copper interconnect processes, where it enables bottom-up film growth and demonstrates remarkable filling capabilities [28,29]. During the electroplating process, precise control over parameters such as applied current, anode material, accelerants, inhibitors, planarization agents, and mass transport allows for the fine-tuning of deposition rate, grain size, morphology, impurity content, and stress [30]. This level of control highlights the considerable potential for further advancement of metal-interconnect trench-filling techniques.

Cobalt electroplating is an efficient and cost-effective method for achieving highquality cobalt interconnects [31,32]. By introducing certain organic additives into the plating solution, bottom-up cobalt superfilling can be realized. Superfilling refers to the phenomenon where the metal deposition rate at the bottom of a trench exceeds that in the side wall. This technique is particularly crucial for the fabrication of interconnects with high aspect ratios, as it effectively prevents the formation of voids, ensuring the integrity and reliability of the interconnects. To date, multiple super-conformal filling mechanisms have been proposed by different research groups. The S-shaped negative differential resistance [33,34] has been extensively applied to the overfilling processes of various metals, including copper [35], gold [36], nickel [37], cobalt [38], and zinc [39]. This model suggests that the adsorption and desorption behavior of inhibitors on the electrode surface leads to a nonlinear variation in current density within a specific potential range, resulting in an “S”-shaped curve. By optimizing inhibitor concentration and potential control, this model enables the realization of the bottom-up overfilling of metals in high-aspect-ratio structures. Rigsby et al. [40,41] introduced the differential current efficiency fill mechanism, emphasizing the critical role of the H<sup>+</sup> concentration gradient in overfilling processes. They observed that during the electrodeposition of cobalt, the pH gradient rapidly formed within the trenches due to proton transfer, resulting in a disparity between the current efficiency and deposition rate at the trench interior and the opening. This differential effect facilitated the bottom-up filling of cobalt. In parallel, Wu et al. [42] introduced the hydrogen reduction-induced deactivation mechanism, which elaborates on how changes in pH and H<sup>+</sup> concentration affect the inhibitory efficacy of additives, thereby triggering a bottom-up filling mechanism. That model showed that the self-initiated bottom-up filling of cobalt was driven by the reduction in and deactivation of inhibitors at the bottom of the trench, caused by hydrogen gas evolution, leading to a diminished inhibitory effect and subsequently promoting the deposition rate at the bottom. The adsorption energy determines the conformality of deposited cobalt layers, especially in complex geometries structures, but its role in achieving superconformal filling has been largely overlooked. Addressing this gap is essential for improving the precision and reliability of coating processes in advanced applications.

The electrochemical behavior during cobalt electrodeposition was analyzed using linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) and the electrochemical deposition method with constant current. The LSV test involved a negative sweep starting from 0 V to −1 V vs. $\mathrm { A g / A g C l }$ with a scan rate of $2 \mathrm { m V } { \cdot } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ , as shown in Figure 2a. In this study, a superfilling mechanism was proposed, in which superfilling was achieved by regulating the adsorption energy of molecules on the cobalt surface. Organic additives containing carbon–carbon triple bonds and oxygen-containing functional groups (BOZ, BEO, and BDE) were examined. The molecular activity and electrochemical behavior analysis revealed that BOZ and BEO exhibited stronger adsorption capabilities on the cobalt surface compared to BDE, owing to their carbon–carbon triple bonds. XRD results indicated that after the addition of BOZ, BEO, and BDE, the cobalt grain size significantly increased. The adsorption energy of BOZ, BEO, and BDE were −10.39 eV, −22.62 eV, and −8.43 eV, respectively. Cobalt superfilling into micro-size trench was achieved by using BDE molecules as additives with an absorption energy of 8 eV. Additives with an extrahigh adsorption energy may inhibit the deposition rate of Co equally both on top and at the bottom of the trench, which cannot benefit from superfilling. However, additive molecules with a suitable adsorption energy may inhibit the Co reduction reaction more strongly on top of the trench than at the bottom, because of the additive molecule concentration gradient caused by mass transport and additive consumption during electrodeposition.

# Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation

The major mechanism of corrosion inhibition effect by nicotinic acid (NA) is to form a passivation film which adsorbs on cobalt (Co) surface so as to strengthen the surface impedance and isolate the corrosion medium. In an alkaline environment (pH 10), NA exists in the form of Nic<sup>2−</sup> ions, which are negatively charged. Driven by electrostatic forces and Van der Waals forces between NA molecule (N atom and the carboxyl) and cobalt atom, Nic<sup>2−</sup> ions are appealed to the Co(OH)<sub>2</sub>, leading to the appearance of Co(II)-NA molecule groups. NA molecules produce a single or multilayer self-assembled Co(II)-NA film on the cobalt surface and further preven the corrosion on Co film.
Keywords: Cobalt interconnection Nicotinic acid Corrosion inhibitor Electrochemistry Molecule simulation

Cobalt (Co) is the interconnect metal of integrated circuits with the feature size of 10 nm and below, and Co corrosion is the main problem in cobalt interconnect chemical mechanical polishing (CMP). The introduction of inhibitors is one of the most ideal approaches to reduce corrosion. In this work, useful insights into the corrosion inhibition performance of nicotinic acid (NA), a green inhibitor, on cobalt film in alkaline medium were investigated via electrochemical characterization, surface analysis, quantum chemical calculation, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation, as well as the adsorption mechanism at atomic level was explored. NA belongs to anodic erosion inhibitor and its inhibition efficiency reached a maximum of 86.65 % at the concentration of 80 mM pH 10, which was identified by the contact angle and potentiodynamic polarization (PDP) test. The elec trochemical impedance spectra (EIS) suggested that the surface resistance was enhanced to prevent corrosion. Free energy obtained from the Langmuir model indicates that NA molecules are physically and spontaneously adsorbed on cobalt surface. XPS results further confirmed this point, which reveals that NA exists in the form of Nic<sup>2−</sup> in alkaline solution and forms a $\mathrm { C o ( O H ) _ { 2 } ( N i c ^ { 2 - } ) }$ molecule group (Co(II)-NA) on Co surface. Additionally, quantum chemical calculations based on density function theory (DFT) have approved that C–N bond and carboxyl group are the active sites of NA molecule and form the most significant electrostatic adsorption force with cobalt atoms. Moreover, it can be inferred from MD simulations that NA molecules are spontaneously and physically adsorbed on the cobalt surface at a certain angle. In a word, NA manifests its effectiveness in corrosion inhibition of cobalt and will become a potential cobalt CMP inhibitor. The research methods and results of this paper are beneficial to the study of the adsorption characteristics and inhibition mechanism of inhibitors on the metal surface, and provide a theoretical basis for optimizing the composition of Co CMP slurry.

In recent years, the addition of corrosion inhibitors has been proved to be an effective measure to inhibit corrosion of metal materials [9 11]. Many studies show that organic inhibitor molecules containing elements such as C, N, and O are often more effective in corrosion prevention, among which benzotriazole (BTA) is a common inhibitor and has been broadly commercialized [12 14]. The corrosion inhibition effect of BTA was firstly reported by Cotton et al. [15], and since then researchers have carried out a lot of researches on BTA $[ 9 , 1 6 , 1 7 ]$ . However, some current studies reported that BTA has a poor inhibition effect on Co corrosion in corrosive medium. Yang et al. [7] characterized the surface morphology of Co in the solution containing BTA and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ by SEM, and concluded that BTA could not effectively reduce the pitting caused by $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ on Co surface. Similarly, Lei et al. [18] suggested that BTA is no longer applicable to Co CMP by means of surface morphology test. In addition, the toxicity of BTA also limits its application in CMP [19,20]. Therefore, scholars have been committed to developing green and effective corrosion inhibitors for Co CMP, such as organic acid and vi tamins [21–23].

Notably, nicotinic acid, which belongs to the B3 group of vitamins, is widely used as an intermediate in the synthesis of various pharmaceuticals and shows favorable potential in corrosion inhibition effect. Mohamed et al. [23] investigated the polishing behavior and defects of cobalt samples with an aqueous mixture of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ,$ oxalic acid (OA), and nicotinic acid at pH 10. The results show that the alkaline solution including 80 mM NA can broadly reduce the corrosion current of cobalt samples and galvanic erosion between cobalt and copper, proving that NA can operate as an inhibitor for Co film in $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ solution. He et al. [24] concluded that NA offers a composite layer on the cobalt surface, and prevents further Co corrosion, while a combination of 10 mM NA and 5 mM TAZ minimized Co-Cu corrosion as measured by zero resistance galvanometer. Although it is confirmed that NA possesses an inhibition effect on cobalt, further studies on NA, such as the interaction process between NA and $\mathrm { C o } ,$ the adsorption mechanism of NA on Co surface and so on, have not been reported. Studying the adsorption of corrosion inhibitor on the metal surface is of great significance to explore the corrosion inhibition mechanism. This work mainly studies the inhibitory effect of NA on cobalt corrosion in alkaline medium, as well as the formation and mechanism of [NA-Co] complex.

Studies on the performance of inhibitor molecules only by conventional chemical experiments and characteristic methods are inadequate. The rapid development of theoretical chemistry provides a more scientific explanation for its research. Molecular simulation is a crucial approach to study the molecular chemical activity of corrosion inhibitors from a microscopic perspective [25,27–29]. The adsorption mechanism between inhibitors and metal substrates can be intuitively characterized by molecular simulation technology. Ma et al. [26] probed the effect of potassium oleate (PO) as a viable corrosion inhibitor for Cu films in $\mathrm { E D T A  – H _ { 2 } O _ { 2 } }$ based solution through combining chemical experiment analysis with molecular simulation. Density functional theory and molecular dynamics approaches were applied to study the inhibition mechanism at the atom level of PO on Cu(111) substrate. Yin et al. [16] evaluated the corrosion inhibition of BTA and TAZ at the molecular level via comparing quantum chemical descriptors. Therefore, it is necessary to further study the quantum chemical properties of NA and micro adsorption mechanism of NA on Co surface.

Considering that NA is an inexpensive, green, and easily available organic inhibitor, it was introduced into the alkaline (pH 10) solution. The molecular structure of NA is shown in Fig. 1. Contact angle and PDP measurements were carried out to determine the optimal concentration of NA. The passive film of NA was investigated by EIS, and the reaction between Co and NA was explored by XPS. Density functional theory was employed to study the properties of NA molecule. Several chemical descriptors were calculated to reveal active sites of NA molecule and the electron transfer characteristics between NA and Co atoms, as well as MD simulation was conducted to study the adsorption configuration, adsorption stability and adsorption sites of NA on Co surface. This work provides a more in-depth insight into the development of alkaline cobalt CMP slurry.

Cobalt coupons (2 cm \* 2 cm) cut from a 12-inch. cobalt blanket wafer were used to accomplish the contact angle test and electrochemical experiments. Before each experiment, the coupons were immersed in 0.025 M citric acid $\mathrm { ( C _ { 6 } H _ { 8 } O _ { 7 } , }$ , CA, 99 %) solution for 5 min to remove the oxide layer on the film surface, then rinsed with deionized water (DIW) and dried with nitrogen $\left( \mathrm { N } _ { 2 } \right)$ . After CA treatment, the cobalt specimens were immersed in NA $( \mathrm { C } _ { 6 } \mathrm { H } _ { 5 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 2 } ,$ 99.5 %) solutions with different concentrations (40, 50, 60, 70, 80 mM) for 5 min. The pH of each inhibitor solution was adjusted to 10.00 with KOH and $\mathrm { H _ { 3 } P O _ { 4 } } .$ Eventually, these cobalt coupons were rinsed with DIW and dried with $\Nu _ { 2 }$ to obtain different samples.

The Forcite module was employed to operate MD simulations. The ideal Co(111) surface was selected as the adsorption object owing to its high atomic density and low Miller index. The inhibitor molecule and Co (111) crystal system with the size of $6 \times 6 \times 8$ and containing a 40 Å vacuum layer were optimized before the start of each dynamics simulation. In order to obtain stable adsorption configuration of the inhibitor on the Co(111) surface, MD simulation was carried out at the ‘Universal force field and $\mathbf { \hat { Q } E q } ^ { * }$ charge. The total energy was calculated by the summation method of the atom-based electrostatic and van der Waals. All MD simulations were based on NVT thermodynamics with an absolute temperature of 298 K, a time step of 1 $\mathbf { f s } ,$ and a total simulation time of 1000 ps.

The adsorption of organic molecules on the metal surface will change its hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity and alters the contact angle of metal surface, while fresh metal surfaces usually present hydrophilicity, hence the contact angle reflects the adsorption effect of the inhibitor [30]. Fig. 2 illustrates contact angle of cobalt samples treated with different concentrations of NA and compared with that treated with CA. After CA treatment, the natural oxide layer on the cobalt surface was removed, and the contact angle of the cobalt surface reduced from $5 5 ^ { \circ }$ to 47◦, obtaining the fresh cobalt surface [31]. The contact angle increased to $6 7 ^ { \circ }$ following 40 mM NA treatment and increased steadily with the increase of NA concentration until the maximum contact angle reached $8 3 ^ { \circ }$ when the concentration was 80 mM. When the concentrations of NA were 90 and 100 mM, the contact angles were 82◦ and 83◦, respectively, which remained basically unchanged compared with that of 80 mM. These results show that when the concentration of NA is greater than 80 mM, the adsorption of NA molecules on the cobalt surface reaches saturation.

According to the contact angle results, PDP tests were carried out to evaluate the effect of corrosion inhibition of NA with the concentration less than 100 mM on cobalt electrode. Fig. 3 shows the PDP curves of cobalt electrode treated with different NA concentrations.

With the introduction of NA, both the anode and cathode branches of Tafel curves have the tendency to extend to the region of low corrosion current density. Compared with the cathode branches, the corrosion current density of the anode branches differs from one another markedly, i.e. the reduction reaction rate of dissolved oxygen at the cathode basically remains unchanged, while the metal ionization process occurring at the anode is inhibited. Accordingly, nicotinic acid belongs to the anodic corrosion inhibitor. The linear region of anodic branch, named as passivation region, proves that NA molecules gradually adhere to the cobalt surface to form a protective film and reduce the corrosion degree. It is noteworthy that the slope at the end of the 40 mM NA anode branch (circled in red) sinks, which is caused by the incompactness of the passivation film as the local corrosion medium may interact with the metal through the protective layer to aggravate the metal ionization. The illustration in Fig. 3 shows the PDP test curves of cobalt electrode in NA solutions with concentrations of 80, 90 and 100 mM, respectively. It can be seen that these three curves almost coincide, which indicates the surface corrosion of Co electrode is similar.

EIS measurement was used to analyze the passivation effect of physically adsorbed protective film on cobalt surface in alkaline medium. Fig. 5(a) shows the Nyquist impedance spectra of the Co electrodes in different concentrations of NA, which can better understand the structure of passivation layer. Since the Nyquist curve is a 1/4 arc, the charge transfer controls the erosion on cobalt/alkaline medium interface, and the equivalent circuit is a simple model formed by electron exchange on passivation film. In the event that the general shape of the impedance spectra does not change with the introduction of inhibitors, the reaction principle of the corrosive medium could be considered as unaffected [35]. Meanwhile the radius of the spectrum increases with the increase of NA concentration, suggesting that the adsorption film turns to be more completed [36]. The radius of imped ance spectrum reaches the maximum when the concentration of NA is 80 mM, which is consistent with PDP results. Nonetheless, the center of the 1/4 arc is apparently below the x-axis, known as the frequency dispersion effect, which is on account of the non-ideal capacitive behavior of the cobalt/medium interface generated by the non-uniformity of cobalt electrode surface.

XPS was introduced to confirm the chemical composition of cobalt samples to further analyze the reaction state of cobalt surface. The XPS spectra and corresponding Co 2p spectra of cobalt samples after being treated with CA and immersed in 80 mM NA are shown in Fig. 6. Fig. 6 (a) shows that the two curves have three distinct peaks (C, O, and Co). In contrast, the peak intensities of C, O, and Co soaked in NA are signifi cantly higher than that of soaked in citric acid. This phenomenon is consistent with the element of NA molecules, and it can be inferred that inhibitor NA and its relative products can successfully assemble on the cobalt surface, issuing in the change of peak intensity of homologous elements. In addition, the appearance of N peak on the Co sample’s surface is induced by the pyrazole ring in the NA molecule [32].

Frontier molecular orbital (FMO) theory has been widely applied in the field of chemical structure to evaluate the efficiency of inhibitors, as well as explore the mechanism of interaction between inhibitors and metal surfaces [42–44]. Hence, a series of quantum chemical parameters, such as the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) energy levels, and the energy gap (ΔE) were calculated by DFT method. Firstly, the structure of NA molecular was optimized, and then properties of the frontier orbital of NA molecule were evaluated.

Generally, the higher HOMO energy or a lower LUMO energy manifests a mightier capability of molecular electron pairs to transfer or vacant orbitals to accept electron pairs. For corrosion inhibitors, this also means a more violent trend of binding and adsorption with metal surface atoms, that is, more efficient corrosion inhibition competence [45]. On top of that, the molecule activity is strengthened with the decrease of ΔE $( \Delta E { = } \Delta E _ { L U M O } - \Delta E _ { H O M O } )$ , i.e. the reduction of ΔE promotes the impact of corrosion inhibition.

In this work, we focused on nicotinic acid as a potential corrosion inhibitor for cobalt CMP in alkaline medium, and the adsorption behavior of NA was systematically revealed by several characteristic techniques and molecular simulations. The results of contact angel and electrochemical test show that corrosion efficiency reached the maximum value of 86.65 % at the concentration of 80 mM. The adsorption of NA on cobalt surface follows the Langmuir adsorption isotherm, which is a spontaneous physical process. EIS further suggests that with the increase of NA concentration, the passivation film covered on cobalt surface became more complete, resulting in the increase of surface resistance. According to the results of XPS, NA molecules exist in the form of $\mathrm { N i c } ^ { 2 - }$ ions in alkaline environment, and physically assemble on $\mathrm { C o ( O H ) _ { 2 } }$ to form Co(II)-NA molecular groups to isolate the permeation of corrosive medium. DFT calculation and MD simulation indicate that NA molecule is adsorbed on the Co(111) surface at a certain angle through Coulomb force and van der Waals force, which are derived from the interaction of $\mathrm { N } { = } \mathrm { C }$ bond and carboxyl in NA molecule and surface cobalt atoms. The results of this work on passive film of NA on Co surface and its microscopic properties provide a theoretical basis for optimizing the composition of Co CMP slurry, and also provide support for subsequent researches of exploring synergistic effect of NA and other slurry components. In conclusion, NA is suggested to be an effective potential inhibitor for Co CMP in IC manufacturing process. Its physical adsorption on cobalt surface will help to improve the inhibitor removal effect in post CMP cleaning.
