In the process of electroless cobalt plating, the saccharin additive can significantly change the surface morphology, texture orientation, and conductivity of the cobalt coating layer. When the amount of saccharin was 3 mg·L<sup>–1</sup>, the cobalt coating transformed from disordered large grains to a honeycomb structure, with a preferred orientation of (002) facet on hexagonal close-packed (HCP) cobalt crystals. The resistivity of the cobalt film decreased to 14.4 μΩ·cm, and further decreased to 10.7 μΩ·cm after the annealing treatment. When the concentration of saccharin was increased, the grain size was gradually refined and a “stone forest” structure was observed, with the preferred orientation remaining unchanged. The addition of saccharin also slightly improves the purity of cobalt coating to a certain extent. Through the study of the crystallization behavior of cobalt electroless plating, saccharin molecules can adsorb to specific c-sites on the cobalt dense crystal plane, inhibiting the growth of abc stacking arrangement and inducing the crystal growth in ab stacking mode, thereby achieving optimal growth of HCP (002) texture.

With the continuous development of chips towards high integration, the chip interconnect size is constantly decreasing and copper interconnect technology faces huge challenges. When the interconnect size is reduced to below 7 nm, copper wire conducts exponential growth in resistivity due to its grain boundary scattering [1, 2], leading to chip overheating and increased power consumption, which in turn affects the computing speed and overall device performance [3]. On the other hand, copper interconnects require a barrier layer of approximately 2 nm tantalum nitride (TaN) to prevent copper metal from diffusing into the silicon dielectric layer, thus further increasing the interconnect resistance [4]. Metal cobalt has the advantages of short electron mean free path, resistance to electromigration and good compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing, which has been considered as a new type of interconnect material to replace copper [5–7]. Currently, the pioneer manufacturers such as Intel and TSMC are also proposing to adopt cobalt as a new interconnect metal for advanced chip manufacturing [8]. At present, the cobalt interconnects in silicon chip are realized through electroplating cobalt super-filling. Although there have been reports on the research of electroplated cobalt super-filling in chip microholes [9–11], compared with electrodeposited copper, electrodeposited cobalt is prone to forming holes and cracks due to such issues as hydrogen evolution, homogenization and poor coating quality [12]. Electroless plating is one of the most practical routs to realize cobalt plating in industrial-scale since it presents a good coverage ability, facile processing and low cost. Particularly, additives play a crucial role in electroless plating [13–16]. The appropriate additives not only can improve the quality of the chemical coating, but also enhance its properties such as density, corrosion resistance, wear resistance, and conductivity.

Saccharin (SAC) is a common organic, non-toxic small molecule that can be used as an additive in the electroplating process to improve the quality of coatings, reduce internal stress, refine grains, enhance the glossiness and reflectivity of coatings [17–19]. Altamirano-Garcia et al. [20] studied the effects of sulfates, chlorides, and saccharin on the electrodeposition of cobalt nickel alloys, and found that the addition of saccharin significantly improved the deposition current efficiency and suppressed hydrogen production, thereby improving the density of the alloy coating. Hoghoghifard et al. successfully improved the microwave absorption performance of nickel coated fabrics by adding saccharin to the plating solution [21]. They found that adding saccharin can reduce surface resistivity, refine grain size, enhance hysteresis loss, and ultimately improve the microwave shielding effect of the fabric. Kolonits et al. found that adding saccharin can significantly refine grain size, increase lattice defect density, and thus improve the hardness of nickel films [22]. Currently, researchers explored the additive mechanism through molecular dynamics simulations and calculations of quantum chemistry, which can effectively resolve molecular-metal interactions [23, 24]. Nevertheless, the researches on quantum chemical calculation of the electroless cobalt plating under the influence of additives are insufficient. Therefore, it is of great significance to establish a method based on quantum chemical calculation to study the effect of additives on cobalt plating.

# Investigation of polyvinylpyrrolidone as an inhibitor for trench super-filling of cobalt electrodeposition

Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) is studied in this paper as an inhibitor of cobalt electrodeposition. The suppres sion effect of PVP was analyzed through electrochemical methods, including cyclic voltammetry (CV) and galvanostatic measurements (GM) tests. It is indicated that PVP effectively suppresses the electrodeposition of cobalt and chloride ion accelerates this suppression. Further experiments verify that PVP inhibits the deposition of cobalt through the adsorption on the electrode surface. Quantum chemical calculations were employed to calculate the molecular orbitals of PVP and the electrostatic potential (ESP) energy of the involved molecules. The simulation results imply that the amide group acts as the main electrophilic attack region and facilitates nucleophilic reactions to bond with cobalt. High aspect ratio trench filling on silicon wafer was achieved with the addition of PVP, which confirms that PVP is an applicable inhibitor for the practical electrodeposition of cobalt filling. The mechanism of cobalt trench filling was proposed to explain the role of PVP in the electroplating filling. Besides, crystalline and morphological characterizations reveal that PVP is able to inhibit the specific crystal growth of cobalt. especially the growth of 220 crystal plane. affect the crystal morphology of cobalt and improve surface compactness.
## 3.1. Inhibition and maximum ofPVP inhibition

The inhibitive behavior of PVP in the solution was investigated through electrochemical measurements. Fig. 1 shows the significant decrease of cobalt stripping area and hysteretic voltammetric features in the solution with PVP. The current density decreases sharply in the presence of PVP (Fig. 1a). For example, after adding 5 mg/L PVP into plating solution, the stripping peak current density decreases from $2 1 \mathrm { m A } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ to $1 2 { \mathrm { m A } } / { \mathrm { c m } } ^ { 2 } .$ . In the meantime, the oxidation peak potential is also shifted negatively by 80 mV (from 0.36 V to 0.44 V vs Hg/ $\mathrm { H g } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 } ) .$ The change in stripping peak current density and oxidation peak potential both reveal that cobalt electrodeposition is inhibited by

PVP. The CV plot in Fig. 1b highlights that the cobalt deposition potential is negative correlated with the concentration of PVP which shows an enhancing effect on the polarization of cobalt electroplating. In addition, with the increasing concentration of PVP, cobalt electrodepositing was further inhibited, which is supported by the decreasing area of oxidation peaks.

The maximum state of PVP suppression was further studied. As is shown in Fig. 1c, the oxidation peak area of CV was calculated to illustrate the inhibition effect of PVP with different concentrations. The integral of the cobalt stripping peak area is defined as $\mathrm { Q } _ { 0 }$ without PVP and as Q with PVP, respectively [28]. The curve which displays the value of $\mathrm { Q } / \mathrm { Q } _ { 0 }$ as a function of the concentration of PVP can be divided into three stages (Fig. 1d). $\mathrm { Q } / \mathrm { Q } _ { 0 }$ values undergo a sharp drop with low concentration of PVP and a steady stage with the high concentration of PVP. Notably, an intermediate slope appears in the curve for the PVP concentration range between 15 mg/L and 81 mg/L. When the PVP concentration continues to increase to more than 81 mg/L, the inhibition of PVP in cobalt electroplating reaches maximum.

As well known, chloride ions could affect the quality of metal coating and influence the mechanisms of additives in metal electroplating bath [29, 30]. The impact of Cl in the PVP-involved electroplating system was analyzed through voltammetry curves (Fig. 2a). In contrast with the curves in Fig. 1a-b, the stripping peak current density decreases more sharply when 5 mg/L PVP was added into the solution. These results in CV curve imply that PVP can inhibit the electrodeposi tion of cobalt in both chloride-containing and non-chloride ion plating solutions. However, in the solution with Cl, less amount of PVP is needed to reach the saturation (Fig. 2b). As for the $\mathrm { Q } / \mathrm { Q } _ { 0 }$ value, this ratio decreases with increasing concentration of PVP and process is divided into two stages (Fig. 2b). The phenomenon of first stage that $\mathrm { Q } / \mathrm { Q } _ { 0 }$ values decrease sharply with adding PVP can be observed when the concentration of PVP is less than 10.65 mg/L. In the second stage, Q/Q values maintain relatively stable with further increased PVP concentration. In the absence of Cl (Fig. 1d), PVP in plating solution reaches the saturation at a much higher concentration. Furthermore, when 10 mg/L PVP was added, the oxidation peak area in solution with Cl $( \mathrm { Q } / \mathrm { Q } _ { 0 }$ value decreases from 1.0 to 0.42 in Fig. 2b) decreased more than the chlorine-free solution $( \mathrm { Q } / \mathrm { Q } _ { 0 }$ value decreases from 1.0 to 0.51 in Fig. 1d). It is indicated that PVP is a suppressant of electrodeposited cobalt which can negatively shifts the deposition potential of cobalt, and chloride ion helps to accelerate the suppression effect of PVP.

The increase of overpotential is attributed to the adsorption of PVP on the surface of cobalt. The reverse scan exhibits an obvious hysteresis in the solution with only 100 mg/L PVP (Fig. 2c), revealing an adsorption and re-adsorption process of PVP. After adding Cl into PVP solution, the CV curve in Fig. 2c displays a weaker hysteresis effect. Thus, the adsorption strength of PVP is enhanced and Cl makes the adsorption more stable. Fig. 2c also shows the synergistic effect between PVP molecules and chloride ions. Chlorine ions were added to the solution containing 100 mg/L PVP, and the absolute value of current density continued to decrease.

The interaction between PVP and cobalt cations in aqueous solution has been reported (Liu et al.) [17, 31]. In this work, when the PVP was added in the solution, it preferentially complexes with cobalt ion. $\mathsf { P V P - C O } ^ { 2 + }$ complexes affect the polarization of cobalt electrodeposition and thus inhibit cobalt deposition. As the concentration of PVP increases, an extra oxidation peak appears with stronger suppression. PVP molecules are absorbed on the electrode surface and chloride ions promote the adsorption of PVP.

The molecular frontier orbital theory suggests that the key of chemical reactions is the HOMO and LUMO of the molecules [20]. The distribution of HOMO and LUMO of PVP was simulated by molecular orbital method (Fig. 3). The HOMO value $\left( \mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { H O M O } } \right)$ of a molecule determines its ability to lose electrons outward, and the LUMO value $\left( \mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { L U M O } } \right)$ represents its ability to accept electrons. Higher E and lower $\mathtt { E } _ { \mathrm { L U M O } }$ partly reflect the reactivity of molecule [32]. The $\mathtt { E _ { H O M O } }$ value of PVP is 6.877 eV (Fig. 3e), compared with 7.338 eV of PEG [21], indicating that PVP has relatively stronger electron donating ability. The simulated values imply that PVP is more likely to interact with cobalt cations and have an impact on electrodeposition of cobalt. Fig. 3e shows that the nitrogen element and oxygen element of the amide group are the main contributors to the HOMO orbital, which acts as the main electrophilic attack region. The organics with higher value of $\mathtt { E _ { H O M O } }$ tent to have stronger electron donating ability to bond with the d-orbital of the metal. PVP with amide group may bond with cobalt, facilitates formation of PVP adsorption and inhibits cobalt electroplating. The electrostatic potential distribution on the surface of molecular van der Waals force of PVP is displayed in Fig. 3a, which is widely used to predict molecular electron donating ability, electro-accepting ability and electrophilic reaction sites [33]. Areas with low ESP value are the positions of high electron density, which are considered to be more affinitive to the cobalt surface [34, 35]. PVP has lowest ESP value of 131.3 kJ/mol compared with PEG [21] ( 131.6 kJ/mol) (Fig. 3a). The electron density map shows that the carbonyl of the amide group contributes greatly to the electron donating ability of PVP. The amide group probably acts as reaction sites in the electrodeposition reaction by the quantum chemical calculations.

Convection have significant influence on the process of electrodeposition. For the electroplating with rotating electrodes, the higher rotating speed of electrode leads to the greater convection in the solution. PVP can effectively inhibit the electrodeposition of cobalt in strong convection because the potential was quickly reduced by 160 mV when 5 mg/L PVP was added in strong convection (2000 rpm) (Fig. 3c). However, when 5 mg/L of PVP was added at low rotating speed (200 rpm), the potential was reduced by 100 mV and the inhibitory effect was slowly balanced after 2000s. Ji et al. found that electrolyte flow plays an important role in electroplating process [36]. The convection intensity of the solution inside the hole is lower than the one outside. The local convection affects the transport boundary layer in cobalt electroplating. As a result, more PVP molecules are be transmitted from solution to the electrode surface per unit time in strong convection. In Fig. 3c, PVP demonstrates a faster suppression in the strong convective condition, which is conducive to filling holes in electroplating. PVP molecules can be adsorbed on surface faster, resulting in different concentration distribution of additives at surface and bottom of trenches at the initial stage of electrodeposition. The cause of the secondary current density distribution is the concentration gradient of the additive [37,38]. In addition, the electroplating experiment was also conducted. As shown in Fig. 3d, the silicon trench is sealed in cobalt electroplating without inhibitor during the process of cobalt electroplating which is consistent with the above discussion.

Cobalt filling was achieved in silicon trenches, which confirms that PVP is capable of being an inhibitor in the electrodeposited cobalt filling. The silicon-based chip has a series of trenches in which a layer of gold was sputtered and the recess was filled by electrodepositing cobalt (Fig. 4). Fig. 4d is a cross-sectional slice of the electrodeposited cobalt-filled silicon trench with full cobalt super-filling. In this work, cobalt super-filling is achieved in silicon trench with the addition of 100 mg/L PVP. It is assumed that PVP molecules adsorb rapidly on the plated surface in the presence of Cl.

Cobalt bottom up filling mechanism is proposed in Fig. 5. In the initial stage of electrodeposition, PVP molecules were quickly adsorbed on the surface, strongly inhibiting the growth of cobalt on the surface. Therefore, the deposition rate at the bottom is greater than that at the surface. Diffusional limitation and CDA of PVP long chain molecule both contribute to the higher deposition rate at the bottom than the one at the surface of the trench and obvious bottomup filling is then expected.

The effect of PVP involved in the electrodeposition of cobalt was further investigated by the characterization of morphology. PVP demonstrates considerable effect on electrodeposited cobalt crystals. The XRD results in Fig. 6a indicate that PVP inhibits the cobalt electrodeposition by affecting the growth of cobalt specific crystal surfaces. The electrodeposited cobalt mainly forms cubic crystals in Fig. 6a. And, it is worth mentioning that PVP reduced the intensity of diffraction peak of cobalt along the direction of 220, indicating that the introduction of PVP inhibited the growth of 220 surface of cobalt without affecting the growth of other crystal planes.

The contact angle test indicates that PVP can improve the wettability of plating solution effectively. As is shown in Fig. 6c-d, the contact angle of the plating solution without PVP is more than $3 0 ^ { \circ }$ on the cobalt surface and is reduced to 15° after adding 100 mg/L PVP. Better wettability of the solution enables more hydrogen to be released in time [39] and enhances coating quality in cobalt electrodeposition. PVP can also be used as surfactant in electrodeposited cobalt because the amide group and carbon chains of PVP can act as polar hydrophilic and hydrophobic group respectively. Meanwhile, according to the theory of electro-capillary, polarization can reduce the surface tension and contributes to the desorption of hydrogen, which is consistent with the discussion above.

In addition, PVP can refine particles and makes the cobalt layer more compact. The SEM images of electrodeposited cobalt in the solution without PVP display different particle size and roughness of surface without inhibitor (Fig. 6e). Fig. 6f shows the SEM of electrodeposited cobalt layer after adding 100 mg/L PVP and the surface morphology of the coating changed obviously in contrast with the one without PVP.

The uniformity of the coating was clearly improved by 3D roughness tests (Fig. 6g-h), and cobalt surface becomes more compact. Sa represents the arithmetic mean of the height values of all the peaks and troughs on plane A in Fig. 6g and Fig. 6h. The larger the value of Sa, the greater roughness of metal surface. The Sa value of electrodeposited cobalt layer in the solution without PVP is less than the Sa value of cobalt layer with 100 mg/L PVP in the electroplating solution, validating that PVP can improve the uniformity of cobalt layer in cobalt electrodeposition. In summary, PVP is an effective cobalt electrodeposition inhibitor. Besides, PVP can effectively facilitate hydrogen desorption, affect the surface morphology, and improve surface uniformity of cobalt layer.

As a conclusion, PVP can increase the polarization of electrodeposition, affect the growth of cobalt particles growth and redistribute the cathodic current. PVP works as inhibitor for electrodeposited cobalt and the suppression mechanisms of PVP were demonstrated. Chloride ion can facilitate the adsorption of PVP and helps to accelerate the suppression effect of PVP. The amide group of PVP is probably the reaction site by quantum chemical calculations. Void free filling of silicon trenches was achieved by cobalt super-filling on a sputtered gold layer in this paper.

Cobalt electroplating has great application potential in the fabrication of interconnection in electronic devices. More types of additives with the function of manipulating cobalt deposition rate and improving deposition quality of cobalt layer will be attempted in the following research.

# Investigation of adenosine as a leveling additive with synergetic acceleration–suppression behavior for superconformal cobalt filling in X-shaped through-hole

Adenosine (ADO) was selected as a leveling additive for superconformal cobalt filling in X-shaped through-hole. Changes in deposition potential and the generation of new stripping peaks in cyclic voltammetry curves were observed in electrochemical tests of ADO-containing plating solution. The adsorption behavior of ADO on the cobalt surface was investigated using density functional theory calculations, molecular dynamics (MD) simulation, and electrochemical in situ Fourier transform infrared (E-FTIR) spectroscopy tests. Furthermore, the Co<sup>2+</sup> with ADO coordination was simulated via interaction region indicator analysis. Based on the changes of the ADO adsorption sites from the MD and E-FTIR analyses, an intramolecular synergistic acceleration–suppression mechanism was proposed to explain the effects of low-concentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression in cobalt deposition. Surface analysis revealed that ADO exhibited a grain refinement effect, and crystal analysis showed that the Co hcp (002) crystalline plane was preferentially formed. Finally, X-shaped throughhole with a maximum aspect ratio of 2:1 formed cobalt superconformal filling, with a surface deposition thickness of the cobalt layer as low as 1.2 μm and meanwhile a filling rate ≥90 %.

The bottom-up superfilling phenomenon of cobalt has been increasingly studied, and various micro-nanoscale mechanism models have been proposed. Such models include hydrogen-induced inactivation mechanisms [7,8], voltage-dependent suppression mechanisms [9, 10], S-type negative differential resistance mechanisms [11,12], and differential current efficiency filling mechanisms [13]. Rigsby et al. [12] proposed a differential current efficiency filling mechanism and achieved damascene filling of cobalt. Using the differential current filling mechanism, Ni et al. [14] introduced polyvinylpyrrolidone into electrodeposition of cobalt to achieve a superconformal silicon trench filling. Ma et al. [15,16] used the S-type negative differential resistance mechanism with malachite green and achieved micro blind hole filling of cobalt. Li et al. [17,18] achieved micro blind hole filling with different pore sizes using nitrotetrazolium blue chloride, applicable to S-type negative differential resistance mechanism theory. Huang et al. inves tigated the role of oxime additives and concluded that the amine group can suppress cobalt electrodeposition by coordinating with ${ \bf C o } ^ { 2 + } \ \bar { [ 9 , 1 0 , }$ 19]. In addition, it was proposed that Co $\left( \mathrm { O H } \right) ^ { - }$ was the intermediate for cobalt deposition [20], which explained the difference in cobalt deposition rates at different pH levels. Li et al. [21] delved into the efficacy of 5-alkynylpyrimidines as inhibitors for cobalt superfilling by curbing excessive growth in specific regions to ultimately obtain homogeneous and compact cobalt coating. Ni et al. [22] explored the combined effects of 3-mercapto-1-propanesulfonate and polyvinylpyrrolidone on the growth dynamics of cobalt pillars during electroplating and uncovered a synergistic interaction to efficiently modulate the morphology and dimensions of these pillars. Cao et al. [23] conducted the effects of dimethylglyoxime, 3-mercapto-2-propanesulfonate, and histidine on the growth characteristics and magnetic properties of cobalt electrodeposited on copper substrates and discovered notable impacts on the coating morphology, structure, and magnetic attributes. Li et al. [24] focused on the electroplating of nanocrystalline cobalt within sulfate baths with butynediol ethoxylate to produce coatings with exceptional crystallinity and superior surface morphology. Tong et al. [25] examined the role of alkyne-PEG4-amine as an inhibitor in cobalt superfilling, showing its superiority in hindering cobalt growth in select areas to achieve even and dense coating. Wu et al. [26] assessed the performance of phenyl methyl sulfoxide as an additive for cobalt superfilling to significantly enhance the coating uniformity and density and improve the reliability of the three-dimensional interconnect. Furthermore, the design of an in-situ micro-reactor electrochemical experiment is crucia for investigating cobalt valence in complex intermediates and tracking its reduction process effects [27].

Herein, using adenosine (ADO) as an additive with the lowconcentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression and the differential current efficiency filling mechanism during cobalt deposition, superconformal filling of cobalt in X-shaped through-hole was achieved. Through electrochemical analysis, ADO was observed to exhibit a depolarizing effect on ${ \mathrm { C o } } ^ { 2 + }$ deposition at low concentrations. However, at concentrations of ${ > } 1 0$ mg/L, ADO increased the polarization of cobalt deposition and considerably changed the cobalt deposi tion. Through density functional theory (DFT) calculations and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, this electrochemical effect was elucidated in terms of electrostatic potential (ESP) on the molecular surface and the adsorption energy of ADO on the cobalt surface, respectively. The shift in the type of ADO electrochemical action at different concentrations was elucidated in terms of the change in adsorption sites during electrochemical in situ Fourier transform infrared (E-FTIR) spectroscopy tests. Finally, cobalt filling with ultrathin surface deposition thickness (SDT) outside the hole was realized via the low-concentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression effect of ADO.

Fig. 1 showed the CV, and GM curves for ADO in a cobalt plating solution. Anodic stripping charge of cobalt Q was calculated from CV curves of Fig. 1a. In this way, $Q / Q _ { 0 }$ values could be obtained to find out the performance of ADO with the concentration of 5\~150 mg/L during cobalt plating; Q and $Q _ { 0 }$ was the anodic stripping charge from the plating bath with and without ADO, respectively [31]. $Q / Q _ { 0 }$ values for the condition of 5\~150 mg/L ADO were 107.55 %, 98.79 %, 84.96 % and 48.60 $^ { \% , }$ respectively. The addition of 5 mg/L ADO led to an accelerating performance of cobalt deposition while ADO with the concentration of higher than 5 mg/L resulted in a suppressor behavior of cobalt deposition. As shown in Fig. $^ { \mathrm { 1 b , } }$ the deposition peak had a positive shift at 5 mg/L, indicating that the deposition of cobalt was accelerated. When the concentration exceeded 10 mg/L, the deposition peak had a negative shift and exhibited S-type hysteresis, indicating that ADO could suppress cobalt deposition.

Electrochemical coupling analysis was performed to further investigate the low-concentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression of ADO. Cobalt deposition was first conducted for 200 s under a $\mathrm { \bar { 0 . 5 A / d m ^ { 2 } } }$ constant current condition, followed by stripping within the potential range $\begin{array} { r l } { \mathbf { 0 } \mathbf { f } - 1 . 0 \mathrm { t o } 0 . 3 \mathrm { V } . } \end{array}$ With an increase in the concentration of ADO, a stripping peak was generated at −0.7 V (Fig. 1c), which differed from the stripping peak position of cobalt [13,32]. It was speculated that ADO could generate complexes with ${ \mathsf { C o } } ^ { 2 + }$ and change the deposition-stripping process of cobalt. During the stripping process, the stripping peak was only observed during the first cycle of the CV test, the ADO solution alone did not produce a peak so the effect of the solution was negligible. Thereby confirming that the peak originated from the stripping of cobalt metal under the action of ADO.

As the ADO concentration increased, the process was divided into three phases (Fig. 1d). When the ADO concentration was 5 mg/L, the Q/ $Q _ { O }$ value was slightly elevated. During the concentration of 10\~50 mg/ L, the second stage phenomenon of rapid decrease of $Q / Q _ { O }$ value with the addition of ADO could be observed. In the third stage, the $Q / Q _ { O }$ values remained relatively stable, illustrating that the ADO in the bath had reached a supersaturated concentration [31]. Above result was approximately the same to the case in Fig. 1a, confirming that the low-concentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression effect of ADO during cobalt deposition. Given that the concentration of 50 mg/L situated close to the intersection of the second and third stages, where ADO had just reached saturation, 50 mg/L was selected as the optimal concentration for DC plating [14,31].

It was observed that ADO exhibited a low-concentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression effect during the electrochemical test. Combined with the results in Fig. 1d and e, in order to avoid the potential reversal phenomenon caused by the concentration, 50 mg/L was selected as the concentration of ADO for DC cobalt plating.

The surface ESP of the ADO molecule was within the range from −50.39 to 56.25 kcal/mol, and the higher surface ESP could result in the stronger electrostatic adsorption on the cathode surface [34,35]. The high ESP region of the ADO molecule was extremely dispersed, and the electrostatic adsorption on the cathode surface was in a multipoint adsorption state. The adsorption sites were –NH<sub>2</sub> of adenine moiety and –OH of nucleoside moiety. A lower ΔE suggested that ADO was more likely to receive and provide electrons on the cathode surface during electrochemical reactions while having a larger adsorption strength in the electric field [36–38]. With no MO distribution on the nucleoside group, so it exhibited only electrostatic adsorption and low adsorption strength on the cobalt surface. Thus, the electrochemical active site of ADO was the adenine group. According to the MO distribution characteristics and the electrochemical test results, it was hypothesized that the nucleoside group accelerates cobalt deposition, the adenine group suppresses cobalt deposition, and the adsorption site of the adenine group increased at a high concentration, rendering the suppression effect dominant [39,40]. However, the reliable correlation between simple HUMO-LUMO calculations and inhibition efficiency was questioned in early work [41]. Therefore, more relevant simulations of IRI and MD simulations were added to further support the explanation of ADO suppressesing function during cobalt electrodeposition.

Above change could attribute to the ESP distribution of ADO in Fig. 2: the nucleoside group with the largest ESP value preferentially adsorbed but adsorption intensity of adenine group could be improved with the increase of ADO concentration. The E-FTIR test and MD simulation showed that the adsorption of adenine groups increased with an increase in concentration, whereas the nucleoside group was always in the maximum adsorption state. Combined with the electrochemical phenomenon where ADO accelerated the cobalt deposition at a low concentration and suppressed the cobalt deposition at a high concentration, this showed that the nucleoside group accelerated cobalt deposition, and the adenine group suppressed the deposition of cobalt.

During the electrochemical testing, ADO was observed to have a low concentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression effect on cobalt deposition. The electrochemical tests, MD simulations, DFT cal culations, and E-FTIR tests explained the reasons for the acceleration at a low concentration and suppression at a high concentration. First, nucleoside groups accelerated cobalt deposition, whereas adenine groups form complexes with ${ \mathsf { C o } } ^ { 2 + }$ to suppress cobalt deposition. Thereafter, adenine groups adsorbed more on the cobalt surface with an increase of the concentration of ADO. Thus, the acceleration disappeared and the suppression increased with an increase of the concentration.

Fig. 6 showed the crystal morphology and contact angle changes in cobalt under different conditions as well as the changes in grain orien tation and the coating roughness data. As shown in Fig. 6a–c, the addition of ADO made the cobalt grains significantly smaller, which had the effect of refining the grains. In addition, the distribution of the grains was more uniform, and the uniformity of the plated layer improved. The addition of ADO significantly reduced the contact angle from 105.6◦ to 61.9◦, and the surface energy increased from $9 . 7 2 7 5 ^ { \ast } 1 0 ^ { - 3 }$ to $3 9 . 3 8 2 5 ^ { * } 1 0 ^ { - 3 } \ \mathrm { J } / \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 } .$ . The smaller surface contact angle improved the wettability of the plating solution [52,53], which was conducive to the faster release of hydrogen and the enhancement of the deposition uniformity [54–56]. During the electrochemical test, it was observed that ADO exhibited a low-concentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression effect. By analyzing the HOMO-LUMO and ESP values, discovered that the ADO adsorption sites could be categorized into two distinct groups: adenine and nucleoside. Subsequent MD simulations revealed that the specific adsorption sites were the –OH within the nucleoside group and the –NH within the adenine group. Furthermore, the E-FTIR test indicated that the –OH in nucleoside group were preferentially adsorbed, and as the concentration of ADO increased, the adsorption of the –NH in adenine group was enhanced. These findings were consistent with the ESP calculations, which identified the –OH in nucleoside group as the maximum point and the –NH in adenine group as the sub-maximum point. Combined with the results of electrochemical tests and IRI sim ulations, it is concluded that the nucleoside groups which containing multiple –OH played an accelerating role in cobalt deposition, while the adenine group which coordinated with $\mathsf { C o } ^ { 2 + }$ played a role in suppressing cobalt deposition. The difference in the adsorption intensity of nucleoside and adenine groups leads to the low-concentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression effect of ADO in the cobalt electrodeposition.

Unlike acidic Cu electroplating in which hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is negligible, Co electroplating is accompanied by HER given that $\varphi _ { \mathrm { C o } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { C o } } = - 0 . 2 8 \ : \mathrm { V }$ vs. SHE and $\varphi _ { \mathrm { H } ^ { + } / \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } } = 0 \ : \mathrm { V }$ vs. SHE [12,13]. In order to achieve bottom-up filling and avoid voids in the vias, a suitable inhibiting additive, such as sodium 2-mercapto-5-benzimidazolesulfonate (MBIS) [14], or dimethylglyoxime among others [15–25], is needed to regulate the kinetics of Co deposition. Several superfilling (superconformal deposition) models have been proposed to account for the additive-assisted filling process, including the S-shaped negative differential resistance (S-NDR) [15,26,27], the differential current efficiency fill (DCEF) model [28,29], and the hydrogen reduction-induced deactivation (HID) model [30,31].

The adsorption structure of MBIS on the Co electrode was further confirmed. The vibrational frequencies and intensities of MBIS were calculated using DFT based on harmonic approximation, and the results are displayed in Figure S5 and MOV 1 (see the details in Supporting Information online). To further investigate the mechanism, the molecular dynamics simulations were performed using classical force fields (see the details in Supporting Information online). Based on the aforementioned results and molecular dynamics simulations, the interfacial mechanism of MBIS on Co electrodes may be proposed (Figure 7). The hydrophobicity of MBIS aromatic rings disrupts the hydrogen bonding of interfacial $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } ,$ , leading to the formation of a more ordered $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ structure in favor of HER (1 of the left panel of Figure 7). The positively charged ${ \mathrm { C o } } ^ { 2 + }$ ions are driven towards the electrode surface by the electric field, forming an interfacial Co(II)-MBIS complex that requires higher energy input for its reduction (2, 3 of left panel of Figure 7). On one hand, the adsorption of MBIS reduces the number of surface active sites and decreases the apparent overall current. On the other hand, the formation of a Co(II) complex at the MBIS-modified Co electrode inhibit the Co deposition much more significantly than the HER, leading to a decrease in $\mathrm { F E } _ { \mathrm { C o } }$ and an increase in $\mathrm { F E } _ { \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } } .$ . As a proven additive in the Co superfilling, MBIS essentially displays the feature of a strong inhibitor against Co deposition. The inhibition effect of MBIS is highly dependent on its surface coverage: the higher the coverage, the stronger the inhibition against Co deposition. Thus, the mechanism of the Co superfilling in the vias could be qualitatively unraveled by assuming the existing difference of local surface MBIS coverage inside and outside the vias, which may arise from but not limited to the obstructed mass transport of MBIS and the pH difference caused by HER. The higher and lower MBIS coverages outside and inside the vias lead to slower and faster Co filling outside and inside the vias, respectively, ensuring the Co superfilling (right panel of Figure 7). Based on the above mechanistic understanding at the molecular level, we are constructing (will report in the near future) a simulation model of the Co filling process to quantitatively analyze the distribution of additives in the vias, as well as to predict the conditions for the Co superfilling.

In this study, we have delved into the inhibition mechanism of the additive MBIS in acidic Co electroplating using a synergistic approach inclusive of electrochemical and ATR-SEIRAS measurement as well as computational simulations.

The MBIS molecule adapts a nearly vertical adsorption configuration on the Co electrode via the formation of thiolate, reducing both partial currents for Co deposition and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 }$ evolution with a higher $\mathrm { F E } _ { \mathrm { C o } }$ and a lower $\mathrm { F E } _ { \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } } ,$ , as compared to the MBIS-free case. We have revealed at a molecular level that the adsorbed MBIS molecules disrupt the hydrogen bonding of interfacial water, and form a sort of interfacial $\mathrm { M B I S - C o } ^ { \overline { { 2 } } + }$ complex, thereby favoring a higher selectivity toward the hydrogen evolution than the Co deposition. Furthermore, variation in the MBIS coverage has been identified with varying pHs or potentials, offering crucial insights into the refinement of electroplating parameters. The MBIS coverage-dependent inhibition effect can qualitatively account for the Co superfilling process. Our work is valuable in understanding the interfacial structure and functionality of a typical inhibitor for superconformal Co plating and lends important guidance for filling simulations.
